3.q: Why is face-to-face communication often the most suitable method for delivering sensitive or difficult news to a stakeholder?
o: It reaches large, geographically dispersed audiences at the lowest cost
It removes the need to follow the conversation up afterwards
It allows tone, empathy and immediate reassurance to be conveyed in person
It creates a permanent written record of exactly what was said
3.w: Face-to-face communication conveys tone and body language and allows immediate, empathetic two-way response, suiting sensitive messages.

3.q: When reviewing a colleague's draft business case, which of the following would you expect to be a core component?
o: The finalised test scripts to be used in verifying each deliverable
The detailed activity schedule and the resource histogram for every member of the team
The expected benefits, costs, timescales and risks of the proposed investment
The configuration item register and the version history of every product
3.w: A business case justifies the investment by setting out its expected benefits, costs, timescales and risks, usually comparing options, so the sponsor can decide whether it is worth doing.

n.0: Test scripts are quality control documents prepared later for verification, not business case content.
n.1: Detailed schedules and resource histograms belong to the project management plan, not the business case.
n.3: Configuration records track products and versions during delivery; they are not part of the justification.

3.q: Which of the following is essential for parametric estimating to produce reliable results?
o: A fully completed work breakdown structure
Accurate historical data for unit costs or durations
Consensus reached through expert judgement
An approved stakeholder engagement plan
3.w: Parametric estimating depends on accurate historical cost or duration data per unit in order to scale estimates reliably.

3.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of quality management within a project?
o: To avoid the need for any configuration control
To provide contingency against any time overruns
To remove every single risk that the project might face
To ensure outputs and processes are fit for purpose
3.w: Quality management ensures that the outputs, benefits and the processes that deliver them meet stakeholder requirements and are fit for purpose.

n.0: Configuration management is still needed; quality management does not replace it.
n.1: Contingency against overruns is a reserve of time or money set through risk management.
n.2: No process can remove every risk; that is not the purpose of quality management.

3.q: During delivery a team reviews whether its agreed working procedures are being applied consistently across all workstreams. Which process is this?
o: Benefits management
Change control
Quality control
Quality assurance
3.w: Reviewing whether agreed processes and procedures are being applied is a quality assurance activity.

3.q: In the APM change control process, which stage comes last, directly after the plans have been updated?
o: Carry out a detailed evaluation of it
Make a recommendation to the sponsor
Implement the change and communicate it
Raise a fresh change request for review
3.w: The six stages are change request, initial evaluation, detailed evaluation, recommendation, update plans and implement. Implementing (and communicating) the change is the final stage, once the baseline and plans reflect it.

n.0: Detailed evaluation is the third stage, assessing impact before any decision is made.
n.1: Recommendation is the fourth stage, where the change is approved, rejected or deferred before plans are updated.
n.3: Raising a change request is the first stage. An approved change does not go back round the process.

3.q: A supplier fails to deliver components on time, delaying the schedule. What is the role of issue management in this situation?
o: To revise the scope so the affected tasks are removed
To document the issue, assign ownership and track its resolution
To plan the resources needed for the next project phase
To reassess the project's future risks and update tolerances
3.w: Issue management handles real disruptions such as a missed delivery by logging them, assigning an owner and tracking them through to resolution.

3.q: A director reviews the organisation's entire collection of projects and programmes to decide which to fund, pause or stop. Which discipline is this?
o: Programme management
Project management
Portfolio management
Operational management
3.w: Selecting, prioritising and controlling the whole collection of projects and programmes for strategic value is portfolio management.

3.q: Why can virtual tools such as shared whiteboards be advantageous for collaborative planning?
o: They remove the need to keep any project documentation
They are inherently more secure than meeting in person
They prevent disagreement between the project's stakeholders
They allow asynchronous contributions from remote participants
3.w: Shared online tools support collaboration even when participants are not all available at the same time.

3.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between change control and configuration management?
o: Both processes apply only after the project has been formally closed
Configuration management authorises changes; change control audits the schedule
Change control governs whether changes happen; configuration management maintains records of items and versions
They are the same process operating under two different names
3.w: Change control decides on changes while configuration management keeps the record of controlled items and their versions; the two are complementary.

3.q: A team leader recognises a member's contribution during a sprint review. What effect is this most likely to have?
o: It boosts morale and encourages continued high performance
It delays the delivery of future sprints
It demotivates the remainder of the team
It reduces collaboration across the team
3.w: Recognition reinforces positive behaviour and lifts morale, which can drive further high performance.

3.q: What is the defining feature of the way phases are arranged in a linear project life cycle?
o: All phases run in parallel from the very start of the project
Phases can be reordered freely according to team preference
Phases repeat in short cycles until the customer is satisfied
Each phase is largely completed before the next one begins
3.w: A linear life cycle runs its phases sequentially, with each substantially finished before the next starts.

3.q: During delivery a planned milestone is not achieved on its target date. What does this most usefully signal to the project manager?
o: That the risk register no longer needs to be maintained
That the project's scope has been formally reduced
That the project's budget has automatically been increased
That progress may be slipping and corrective action may be needed
3.w: A missed milestone is an early signal that progress is slipping, prompting the project manager to consider corrective action.

3.q: Why might a project manager carry out a PESTLE analysis during the initiation of a project?
o: To identify external factors that could influence the project
To map out the internal work breakdown structure
To set the payment schedule agreed with contractors
To evaluate the team's internal communication styles
3.w: PESTLE analysis is used to identify external, macro-environmental factors that may affect the project.

3.q: Why does a risk register support effective communication about risk on a project?
o: It provides a shared, consistent record all parties can reference
It records only the risks the sponsor wishes to see
It hides risk information from the wider stakeholders
It replaces the need for any progress reporting
3.w: By holding risk information in one consistent place, the register gives stakeholders a shared reference for discussing and reviewing risk.

3.q: At a decision gate review, who typically decides whether the project proceeds to the next phase?
o: An external team of auditors
The project manager acting alone
The governance board or sponsor
The project team collectively
3.w: Gate decisions are made by the governance board or sponsor to provide objective oversight and strategic alignment.

3.q: A sponsor insists that stakeholder feedback be included as a success measure. What does this illustrate about effective success criteria?
o: They must always be expressed in financial terms
They should include both objective and subjective elements
They should exclude any measure of user experience
They are best defined at project closure
3.w: Good success criteria combine measurable, objective outcomes with subjective elements such as stakeholder satisfaction.

3.q: Members drawn from several departments are struggling with unclear communication and low trust. Which challenge does this illustrate?
o: Difficulties with procurement planning
Cross-functional team dynamics
Work breakdown structure confusion
Disengagement of the project sponsor
3.w: Cross-functional teams frequently face communication and cohesion challenges arising from differing priorities and norms.

3.q: A colleague asks you to complete the sentence 'project management is the application of...' as accurately as possible.
o: ...governance rules to coordinate a portfolio of unrelated investments
...financial controls to maximise the return from routine operations
...processes, methods, knowledge and skills to achieve the project objectives
...standard operating procedures to sustain continuous business services
3.w: The recognised definition is the application of processes, methods, knowledge and skills to achieve the project objectives; the distractors describe operational and portfolio work.

3.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between the project sponsor and the project manager?
o: The sponsor sets direction and governance while the manager delivers
The sponsor manages daily delivery while the manager sets strategy
The two roles operate independently with no formal relationship
The sponsor handles finance while the manager makes technical choices
3.w: The sponsor provides strategic direction and governance, while the project manager delivers the project within those boundaries.

3.q: Resource levelling is most accurately described as which kind of scheduling technique?
o: Quality-limited, adjusting specifications to save resources
Resource-limited, adjusting the schedule to available resources
Scope-limited, deleting tasks until demand is affordable
Time-limited, never allowing the completion date to change
3.w: Resource levelling is resource-limited, adjusting the schedule to fit the resources available, which may extend the duration.

3.q: In a linear project the baseline for time, cost and scope is set at the start. What is the key challenge if significant changes are later needed?
o: There is no means of tracking the change
The whole project has to be restarted
Baselines cannot be documented at all
Any change must pass through formal change control
3.w: In a linear life cycle changes to the fixed baseline must be formally assessed and approved through change control.

3.q: A project manager sets up processes to ensure the final product meets the agreed requirements. What is the main purpose of quality management?
o: To make the project's procurement arrangements simpler
To reduce the number of stakeholders involved in the project
To ensure outputs are delivered to a consistent and acceptable standard
To increase the overall speed at which the product is delivered
3.w: Quality management exists to ensure that project outputs consistently meet the agreed standards and are fit for purpose.

3.q: How does a communication plan help to reduce misunderstandings on a project?
o: By reducing the amount of stakeholder engagement needed
By clarifying who communicates what, when and how
By transferring all communication tasks to suppliers
By restricting the team to informal conversations only
3.w: Clear responsibilities and defined channels support accurate, consistent communication throughout the project.

3.q: A senior user reviews the project management plan and questions the schedule. Why is their involvement important?
o: They represent end-user needs and shape quality expectations
They manage all of the third-party procurement
They are accountable for allocating project risk
They take over the project manager's role if delays occur
3.w: Senior users ensure the plan reflects business needs and the quality expectations of those who will use the deliverables.

3.q: Which of the following best describes the responsibility of a project team member?
o: Providing specialist skills and completing assigned tasks
Defining and owning the project business case
Approving transitions between project phases
Authorising procurement contracts with suppliers
3.w: Team members apply their specialist skills to complete assigned work packages and report progress to the project manager.

3.q: A client insists a release must launch on a fixed date, accepting that some lower-priority features may not be ready. Which technique fits?
o: Critical path analysis
Time boxing
Resource levelling
Analogous estimating
3.w: Holding the launch date fixed while allowing lower-priority features to drop is time boxing.

3.q: For a quick decision needing input from team members across three time zones, which method offers the greatest advantage?
o: A single face-to-face meeting at head office
A virtual meeting or video conference
A printed memo posted to each location
A physical noticeboard in the site office
3.w: Virtual methods connect geographically dispersed members quickly and cheaply, without the time and cost of bringing everyone together in person.

3.q: Which of the following is a key outcome of performing critical path analysis?
o: A detailed quality assurance plan for deliverables
An understanding of which tasks have scheduling flexibility
A stakeholder influence and interest chart
A revised procurement contract for the main suppliers
3.w: Critical path analysis distinguishes tasks with float from those without, showing where the schedule has flexibility.

3.q: Why do organisations apply project management to unique, time-limited pieces of work?
o: To guarantee that the work encounters no risks or unexpected events
To ensure the work continues indefinitely as part of routine operations
To achieve the defined objectives within agreed time, cost and quality constraints
To keep the project team occupied until a permanent role becomes available
3.w: The key purpose of project management is to achieve the project objectives within the agreed constraints, typically time, cost and quality.

3.q: Throughout the life of a project, who holds overall ownership of the business case and its continued validity?
o: The project sponsor
The project team
The project manager
The end users
3.w: The sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for ensuring the investment remains justified throughout the project.

3.q: A team colour-codes its risks red, amber and green to show their severity. What is this an example of?
o: Qualitative risk analysis
Quantitative risk analysis
Configuration management
Critical path analysis
3.w: Ranking risks by descriptive categories such as red, amber and green is a form of qualitative risk analysis.

3.q: A critical activity is forecast to overrun by two days. According to critical path analysis, what is the likely effect?
o: The project end date slips by two days unless recovered
The project end date is unaffected because of float
The project baseline automatically re-sets itself
Only non-critical activities are delayed by two days
3.w: A slip on a zero-float critical activity pushes out the project completion date unless corrective action recovers the time.

3.q: A sponsor approved a change, then discovered its full effect on cost and schedule had never been analysed. Which change control stage was missed?
o: Logging the change request
Detailed evaluation
Updating the plans
Implementing the change
3.w: Detailed evaluation is the stage that analyses the full impact of a change on scope, time, cost, quality, risk and benefits, and it must come before the recommendation.

n.0: Logging records the request at the start; it does not analyse its impact.
n.2: Updating the plans happens after approval and reflects the decision; it does not analyse the impact beforehand.
n.3: Implementing is the final stage and applies the change once plans are updated.

3.q: A manager unites the team around a shared goal and motivates them to commit to it. Which capability are they chiefly demonstrating?
o: Assurance
Scheduling
Procurement
Leadership
3.w: Uniting a team around a goal and motivating commitment is a demonstration of leadership.

3.q: How does an organisational breakdown structure (OBS) support role clarity within a project team?
o: By setting out the project's configuration control procedures
By identifying the deliverables that the project must produce
By showing how responsibilities are distributed through the organisation
By detailing the project's individual financial cost centres
3.w: The OBS clarifies who holds responsibility and who reports to whom, improving transparency of roles across the team.

3.q: A project manager prepares a backup supplier agreement, to be used only if the main vendor fails to deliver. What is this arrangement best called?
o: A contingency reserve
A transfer response
A fallback plan
An avoidance response
3.w: A fallback plan is a plan B, put into action only if the risk occurs. Here the backup supplier is used only if the main vendor fails.

n.0: A contingency reserve is an amount of time or money set aside for risk, not an alternative course of action.
n.1: Transfer passes the financial impact or management of the risk to a third party, for example through insurance or a contract.
n.3: Avoidance changes the plan so the threat cannot happen; the risk of the vendor failing still remains here.

3.q: In a project using iterative delivery, which aspect of the deployment baseline is most likely to change frequently?
o: The governance structure
The procurement method
The sponsor's role
The scope definition and priorities
3.w: Scope and priorities evolve throughout an iterative project, so the baseline adjusts to reflect them.

3.q: Why is scope in a linear project usually captured in a detailed baseline agreed before delivery starts?
o: So that scope can be decided only after the product is built
So that the team can alter deliverables freely without any record
So that any later change can be measured against an agreed, approved reference
So that stakeholders need not be consulted during planning
3.w: A fixed scope baseline gives an agreed reference so later changes can be assessed and controlled against it.

3.q: As sponsor, what should you do if the business case is found to be no longer valid during delivery?
o: Pause the project and update the business case for governance review
Instruct the team to continue with the work regardless
Increase the project's scope to add further value
Remove the project's risk management procedures
3.w: The sponsor must keep the business case valid; if it is not, work should be paused and approval sought for any change.

3.q: The project's actual spend has now exceeded its approved budget and finance has flagged it. How is this best classified?
o: An issue
A dependency
A tolerance
A risk
3.w: A confirmed overspend that has already happened and needs action is an issue, not a risk, which remains only a possibility.

3.q: Quality management is best understood as an umbrella covering which combination of activities?
o: Quality planning, assurance, control and continuous improvement
Estimating, scheduling, procurement and resource optimisation
Identifying, analysing, responding to and closing project risks
Concept, definition, deployment and transition of the outputs
3.w: Quality management is made up of quality planning, quality assurance, quality control and continuous improvement.

n.1: These are planning and resourcing activities, not the parts of quality management.
n.2: These are the stages of the risk management process.
n.3: These are the phases of a linear life cycle.

3.q: When developing the communication content of a project management plan, which group most needs clearly defined roles and timely updates in order to deliver the work?
o: The project team members
The regulatory authorities
The general public
The external suppliers
3.w: Project team members carry out the work, so they require clear responsibilities and regular, relevant updates to perform effectively.

3.q: At what point during a project should quality management activities be applied?
o: Only if a defect is reported by the customer
Throughout the life cycle, from planning through to delivery
Only before any planning has begun
Only at the very end, once the product is finished
3.w: Quality management runs throughout the life cycle, building quality in rather than checking only at the end.

3.q: A developer implements a software change from an informal request, and it later proves incompatible with existing modules. Which process breakdown occurred?
o: Stakeholder mapping was not kept properly up to date
Change control was bypassed and configuration was not enforced
Quality control was applied too heavily to the work
Risk escalation was skipped during the delivery phase
3.w: The change was not authorised through change control and was not verified or integrated through configuration management, so both controls failed.

3.q: How do change control and configuration management together protect the integrity of a project's deliverables?
o: One identifies risks; the other transfers them to a supplier
One trains the users; the other reviews the benefits realised
One fixes the budget; the other sets the delivery schedule
One ensures changes are properly authorised; the other keeps items consistent and correctly versioned
3.w: Change control ensures only authorised changes proceed, while configuration management keeps deliverables consistent and correctly versioned.

3.q: What is the main objective of risk analysis in project management?
o: To approve outstanding change requests more quickly
To assess the likelihood and impact of each identified risk
To transfer every identified risk to external suppliers
To remove all uncertainty from the project's plans
3.w: Risk analysis evaluates how likely each identified risk is to occur and how much it would affect the project's objectives.

3.q: Within the discipline of benefits management, a 'benefit' is most accurately defined as what?
o: A measurable improvement resulting from an outcome, seen as advantageous
A tangible product created by the project's delivery work
A risk that has occurred and now requires resolution
A task that must be completed before another can begin
3.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement, arising from an outcome, that is perceived as advantageous by stakeholders.

3.q: Which estimating technique is best suited when detailed information is unavailable and a quick estimate is needed?
o: Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
3.w: Analogous estimating provides a quick, high-level estimate based on past projects when detailed data is not yet available.

3.q: How do a product breakdown structure and a work breakdown structure support scope definition when used together?
o: They set out the project's risks and outstanding issues
They identify the communication channels and reporting lines
They link the deliverables to the work required to produce them
They record the financial transactions made for the stakeholders
3.w: Together the PBS and WBS connect what must be delivered to the work required to deliver it, giving a complete view of scope.

3.q: Which word most accurately captures the essential nature of a project risk?
o: Certainty
Milestone
Uncertainty
Deliverable
3.w: A risk is fundamentally an uncertain event, distinguishing it from certainties, deliverables or milestones.

3.q: A sponsor wants the life cycle to continue after handover until the benefits in the business case have been realised. Which life cycle supports this?
o: Linear life cycle
Hybrid life cycle
Extended life cycle
Iterative life cycle
3.w: The extended life cycle adds adoption and benefits realisation after transition, so it continues until the planned benefits are realised.

n.0: A standard linear life cycle ends at transition, when the outputs are handed over.
n.1: A hybrid life cycle combines linear and iterative approaches; it does not by itself extend beyond handover.
n.3: An iterative life cycle delivers in time boxes but ends with deployment of the solution.

3.q: Which factor most commonly makes it difficult to build trust within a newly assembled project team?
o: Members already know each other's strengths perfectly
Members have no individual roles to fulfil
Members have a long shared history of working together
Members are unfamiliar with one another's ways of working
3.w: In a new team, members are unfamiliar with each other's styles, so trust takes time to establish.

3.q: A project manager must brief forty stakeholders in different offices within an hour. Which method offers the strongest advantage here?
o: A briefing poster displayed on every office noticeboard
A printed newsletter posted out to each of the offices
A one-to-one face-to-face meeting with each person
A virtual broadcast or video conference to all of them
3.w: Virtual methods are fast and reach many dispersed people at once, so a broadcast or video conference can brief all forty stakeholders within the hour.

n.0: A poster is a physical method: it may not be seen in time and gives no chance for questions.
n.1: A printed newsletter is slow to produce and distribute, so it cannot reach everyone within an hour.
n.2: Forty one-to-one meetings in different offices cannot be held within an hour.

3.q: In a linear life cycle the scope, timeline and budget are fixed at the start and rarely change. What does this indicate about the deployment baseline?
o: It changes on a daily basis
It is used only after the project closes
It is set early and used to manage performance
It is created during the benefits review
3.w: In a linear life cycle the deployment baseline is fixed early and used as a stable reference for controlling delivery.

3.q: On an agile project, which responsibility most clearly belongs to the product owner rather than the project manager?
o: Prioritising the backlog so it reflects the greatest user value
Managing the project's overall budget and schedule
Reporting overall delivery progress to the project board
Securing the resources needed for the delivery team
3.w: The product owner owns and prioritises the backlog to maximise value delivered to users, distinct from the project manager's delivery oversight.

3.q: During which stage of the issue resolution process is the effect of the issue on the project's objectives determined?
o: Assess the impact
Track to closure
Agree the resolution
Identify and log
3.w: After the issue is identified and logged, its impact on the objectives is assessed so the sponsor has the information needed when it is escalated.

n.1: Tracking to closure monitors the agreed actions until the issue is resolved.
n.2: The resolution is agreed after the impact has been assessed and the issue escalated.
n.3: Identifying and logging records the issue; its impact is worked out in the next stage.

3.q: In an iterative project life cycle, what typically happens at the end of each development iteration?
o: The final product is signed off and the project closes
Stakeholder feedback is gathered to shape later iterations
All remaining risks are transferred to suppliers
The business case is rewritten from scratch
3.w: Each iteration ends with a review that gathers stakeholder feedback, informing and adapting the next iteration.

3.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between a PBS and a WBS?
o: The PBS defines the deliverables and the WBS defines the work to create them
The PBS defines the risks and the WBS defines the risk responses
The PBS sets the budget and the WBS sets the time limits
The PBS defines the costs and the WBS defines the people involved
3.w: The PBS identifies the product's deliverables, while the WBS defines the work needed to produce those deliverables.

3.q: When an organisation talks about 'portfolio management', which statement best captures what that discipline is concerned with?
o: The selection, prioritisation and control of projects and programmes to meet strategic goals
The delivery of a group of related projects to achieve a single change outcome
The day-to-day control of one project's scope, cost, schedule and quality
The coordination of routine business activities to sustain steady operational performance
3.w: Portfolio management selects, prioritises and controls the organisation's projects and programmes to align them with strategy; the others describe a programme, a single project and operations.

4.q: Critical path analysis shows a task that can be delayed without affecting the overall project timeline. What is this an example of?
o: Float
Budget slippage
Configuration drift
Scope creep
4.w: Float, or slack, is the amount of time an activity can be delayed without affecting the project's completion date.

4.q: A project holds a face-to-face kick-off meeting with key stakeholders. What is a genuine advantage of this approach?
o: It removes the need for any later follow-up communication
It lowers the travel and venue costs for the project
It speeds up the project's procurement decisions
It helps build trust and stronger relationships early on
4.w: Face-to-face interaction helps build relationships, trust and alignment at the start of a project.

4.q: Which sequence correctly shows the main stages of the issue resolution process?
o: Log, escalate to sponsor, assess, agree resolution, track to closure
Log, assess, agree resolution, escalate to sponsor, track to closure
Log, assess, escalate to sponsor, agree resolution, track to closure
Assess, log, escalate to sponsor, track to closure, agree resolution
4.w: An issue is identified and logged, its impact is assessed, it is escalated to the sponsor, a resolution is agreed (using change control if the baseline changes) and it is tracked to closure.

n.0: The impact must be assessed before escalation so the sponsor has the information needed to decide.
n.1: An issue breaches tolerance, so the resolution is agreed with the sponsor after escalation, not before.
n.3: The issue must be logged before it is assessed, and it cannot be closed before a resolution is agreed.

4.q: What is the purpose of configuration verification within the configuration management process?
o: To confirm that configuration items match their approved specifications
To redefine the project budget once the baseline has been agreed
To approve the protocols used for stakeholder communication
To review supplier invoices submitted during the delivery phase
4.w: Verification and audit confirm that configuration items conform to their approved specification and that records accurately reflect their status.

4.q: A team regularly reviews the work completed so far, checking each output against its specification; which process is this?
o: Risk assessment activity
Resource optimisation activity
Communication planning work
Quality control of outputs
4.w: Quality control includes regular reviews and inspections to ensure deliverables meet their agreed specifications.

4.q: At handover, the sponsor asks for evidence that the project met its objectives. Which element should the project manager refer to?
o: The communication plan produced during delivery
The success criteria agreed at project initiation
The work breakdown structure for the project
The procurement strategy used for the project
4.w: The success criteria agreed at initiation provide the benchmark against which achievement of the objectives is judged at closure.

4.q: At which point in a project is analogous estimating typically most useful?
o: Early on, when little detail exists but similar past projects do
Late in delivery when every work package is fully specified
Only after the critical path has been finalised
Only once the product has been handed over to operations
4.w: Analogous estimating draws on similar completed projects, making it valuable early when detailed information is scarce.

4.q: A project leader is described as providing 'direction'. What does this element of leadership involve?
o: Setting a clear vision and guiding the team towards shared objectives
Updating the configuration status of controlled items
Approving invoices submitted by the project's suppliers
Logging every risk that could affect the project outcome
4.w: Providing direction is the leadership function of setting a vision and guiding the team towards shared objectives.

4.q: A colleague asks you to complete the sentence 'scope management is the process whereby...' using APM terminology.
o: ...threats and opportunities to the objectives are identified and managed
...people and equipment are allocated to the project's planned activities
...progress is reported regularly to the sponsor and other stakeholders
...outputs, outcomes and benefits are identified, defined and controlled
4.w: APM describes scope management as the process whereby outputs, outcomes and benefits are identified, defined and controlled. Doing this well prevents scope creep.

n.0: Identifying and managing threats and opportunities describes risk management, not scope management.
n.1: Allocating people and equipment to activities is resource management and scheduling.
n.2: Regular reporting to the sponsor and stakeholders is progress reporting and communication.

4.q: Within issue management, what is the purpose of having a defined escalation route?
o: To decompose the project's scope into work packages
To raise problems beyond the manager's authority to those who can resolve them
To identify uncertain events long before they occur
To measure the benefits delivered after project closure
4.w: An escalation route lets issues beyond the project manager's authority reach those who can resolve them.

4.q: How does setting clear and achievable objectives for team members influence their performance?
o: It removes any need for the leader to monitor progress
It transfers accountability for delivery entirely to the team
It guarantees that no risks will affect their work
It gives them focus and a shared sense of direction, improving performance
4.w: Clear, achievable objectives focus effort and give direction, which lifts individual and team performance.

4.q: Midway through a busy period, a manager treats a unique system upgrade exactly like routine operations. Why is this approach likely to fail?
o: The upgrade's uniqueness and finite scope need project management
Routine operations demand far more governance than projects
Operations and projects require exactly the same controls
The upgrade cannot involve any of the operational staff
4.w: A unique, time-bounded upgrade requires project management disciplines, which differ from the steady controls used for business as usual.

4.q: A deadline is fixed and cannot move, but resource peaks must be reduced. Which optimisation technique should the project manager apply?
o: Resource smoothing, using float without changing the end date
Crashing, adding cost to shorten the critical path
Fast tracking, overlapping activities to save time
Resource levelling, accepting a later completion date
4.w: When the end date must hold, smoothing evens out resource peaks using available float without delaying completion.

4.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the phases of a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Optimisation
Definition
Concept
Deployment
4.w: The four phases of a typical linear life cycle are concept, definition, deployment and transition; optimisation is not one of them.

4.q: Why is identifying the critical path important to the success of a project?
o: It enables better control of time-sensitive tasks that affect the duration
It improves the project's overall stakeholder engagement strategy
It determines which procurement options the project will use
It ensures only the most skilled members are assigned to tasks
4.w: Knowing the critical path lets the project manager focus attention on the tasks that directly drive the completion date.

4.q: A benefit register entry reads 'annual IT maintenance savings of £50,000 by Year 2'. What does this represent?
o: A project deliverable
A change request
A project risk
A quantifiable benefit
4.w: This is a measurable, time-bound financial benefit that should be tracked to assess the project's value.

4.q: A plan is being produced to set out how requirements will be confirmed throughout delivery; which process does this describe?
o: Quality control of outputs
Quality assurance of processes
Change control of the scope
Quality planning for the project
4.w: This is quality planning, which decides how quality will be measured and verified before work is carried out.

4.q: A newly logged issue has just been assessed for its impact. What happens at the next stage of the process?
o: It is logged in the issue register for the first time
It is tracked to closure and the lessons are captured
Its probability of occurring is analysed and scored
It is escalated to the sponsor to agree a resolution
4.w: An issue is, by definition, breaching or about to breach tolerance, so after assessment it is escalated to the sponsor, who agrees the resolution.

n.0: Logging is the first stage and has already happened.
n.1: Tracking to closure is the final stage, after a resolution has been agreed.
n.2: Probability scoring applies to risks; an issue has already happened, so it is certain.

4.q: Unlike an issue, what defining feature does a risk always carry on a project?
o: An effect that has already been felt by the team
A guaranteed negative effect on the budget
A degree of uncertainty about whether it will occur
A requirement for immediate corrective action now
4.w: A risk always carries uncertainty about whether it will occur, unlike an issue which has already happened.

4.q: A project manager compares actual cost and progress against the plan approved before delivery to identify variances. What are they comparing against?
o: The risk register
The deployment baseline
The quality plan
The stakeholder analysis
4.w: Variances are measured against the deployment baseline, the approved plan for scope, cost and schedule.

4.q: What is the purpose of the estimating funnel in project planning?
o: To identify the benefits associated with each deliverable
To select the most competitive supplier for the work
To measure the performance of the project team
To progressively narrow cost and time estimates as more information becomes available
4.w: The estimating funnel refines estimates and reduces tolerance over time as project knowledge increases.

4.q: A developer finds that a technical constraint will prevent on-time delivery of a feature. What should they do next?
o: Raise the issue with the project manager and suggest options
Withdraw from the task and await reassignment
Notify the project sponsor of the problem directly
Escalate to the governance board for a decision
4.w: Team members are expected to raise emerging issues with the project manager and collaborate on possible solutions.

4.q: A project posts updates only on a physical noticeboard, and remote staff never see them. Which disadvantage of this method does this reveal?
o: It is far too fast for considered messages
It provides no permanent written record
It reaches only those physically present
It prevents any interpretation of tone
4.w: Physical, paper-based communication only reaches people at the location, excluding remote or dispersed stakeholders.

4.q: In a linear life cycle, moving from the definition phase into the deployment phase typically requires what?
o: Completion of user training and formal handover to operations
Approval at a decision gate confirming plans are ready for delivery
Realisation of the benefits set out in the business case
The first sprint retrospective to reprioritise the backlog
4.w: Phase boundaries in a linear life cycle are controlled by decision gates that authorise progression once plans are ready.

4.q: In which situation is a physical, printed communication method likely to be most beneficial?
o: When real-time collaborative editing is required
When rapid decisions must be reached within the team
When stakeholders are remote and rely on mobile devices
When working with non-digital audiences or in technology-restricted settings
4.w: Printed documents ensure accessibility where technology access is unreliable or absent.

4.q: Which of the following is a typical output of the quality control process on a project?
o: Records of inspections and test results for the deliverables
The schedule of independent process audits to be carried out
The quality management plan produced for the whole project
The list of quality standards the project will adopt
4.w: Quality control produces inspection and test records for deliverables; the other items are outputs of quality planning or assurance.

4.q: Because a time box cannot be extended, what is the likely fate of the lowest-priority items if time runs short?
o: They are delivered by lowering the required quality
The time box is lengthened until they are all finished
They automatically become the highest-priority items
They are dropped or deferred to a later time box
4.w: With the deadline fixed, the lowest-priority items are dropped or deferred to a later time box rather than the period being extended.

4.q: Before work begins, a project manager agrees measurable success criteria with all parties. What does this primarily achieve?
o: It removes the need to produce a business case for the investment
It transfers accountability for the benefits to the operational teams
A shared, agreed definition of what success will look like for the project
It guarantees that the project will be delivered within its budget
4.w: Agreeing success criteria at the outset gives every party a common, agreed understanding of what the project must achieve.

4.q: During initiation the project manager drafts cost and risk information while the sponsor decides on strategic justification. What does this show?
o: The two roles collaborate, with the manager informing and the sponsor owning the case
The two roles entirely duplicate each other's responsibilities and effort
The sponsor is responsible only for producing the detailed cost estimates
The project manager holds ultimate accountability for the whole investment
4.w: Developing the business case is collaborative: the project manager provides delivery information while the sponsor owns and justifies the investment.

4.q: A project sets up a version-controlled folder with controlled access for all configuration items. Which activity does this address?
o: Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration control
4.w: Configuration control includes the procedures that govern controlled access and the storage of approved item versions.

4.q: A project manager combines a per-square-metre rate with a similar building's actual cost to sense-check figures. Which two methods are being used?
o: Analytical and Delphi estimating
Bottom-up and comparative estimating
Qualitative and residual estimating
Parametric and analogous estimating
4.w: Applying a unit rate is parametric, while comparing against a similar building's actuals is analogous estimating.

4.q: Which statement best describes what is meant by a deployment baseline in project management planning?
o: The initial draft of the business case prepared before the project is approved
The record of lessons learned captured once the project has been handed over
The formally agreed scope, cost, schedule and resources against which delivery is managed
The register of risks and issues maintained throughout the delivery phase
4.w: A deployment baseline is the agreed reference for scope, time, cost and resources against which delivery is measured and controlled.

4.q: Which combination of elements is typically fixed within a project's deployment baseline?
o: Team roles, supplier contracts and lessons learned
Quality standards, audits and benefit reviews
Stakeholder interests, risks and communication channels
Scope, schedule and cost agreed for delivery
4.w: The deployment baseline captures the approved scope, schedule and cost that define what will be delivered.

4.q: A defect is discovered while the final product is being tested; which process is responsible for detecting it?
o: Change control process
Quality control of outputs
Risk management activity
Issue resolution activity
4.w: Quality control detects defects through the inspection and testing of deliverables.

4.q: Which statement best describes the difference between a product owner and a project sponsor?
o: The sponsor provides strategic oversight, while the product owner manages feature value
The product owner approves gateway reviews, while the sponsor delivers the outputs
The sponsor manages the backlog, while the product owner controls the funding
The product owner owns the business case, while the sponsor manages delivery tasks
4.w: The sponsor secures funding and strategic alignment, whereas the product owner focuses on feature value and customer priorities.

4.q: A sponsor asks how the project will make sure quality is managed, not just checked at the end. What is the best response?
o: Quality will be measured solely by the final cost
Quality will be left entirely to the supplier to judge
Quality will be planned, assured and controlled throughout delivery
Quality will only be inspected once the product is finished
4.w: Quality management spans planning, assurance and control throughout delivery, not just a final check.

4.q: What is the main purpose of holding a post-project review once delivery is complete?
o: To assess the morale of the members of the project team
To allocate the project’s resources to the next planned project
To capture lessons learned and evaluate how the project performed
To gain approval for the final budget submitted by the project
4.w: A post-project review evaluates performance and captures lessons learned so that future projects can benefit from the experience.

4.q: Which underlying principle lies at the very heart of the time boxing scheduling technique?
o: The cost is fixed and the quality is reduced to meet it
The team size is fixed and the deadline moves to suit it
The time available is fixed and the scope is adjusted to fit it
The scope is fixed and the time is extended until it is complete
4.w: Time boxing fixes the period and flexes the scope to fit, rather than extending time to complete a fixed scope.

4.q: A project manager lists each recipient, message, channel and timing in a communication plan. Which further detail should be added?
o: The full risk register scoring
The project's complete cost breakdown
The detailed critical path of the schedule
Who is responsible for issuing each communication
4.w: A communication plan should also record who is responsible for issuing each communication, alongside recipient, message, channel and timing.

4.q: What is typically carried out during the resolution step of the issue management process?
o: Assigning the issue to a responsible team member
Determining the overall severity of the issue
Recording the issue formally in the register
Taking corrective action to resolve the issue
4.w: The resolution step involves implementing the planned corrective action to deal with and close out the issue.

4.q: A PMO balances resource allocation and risk exposure across a suite of unrelated IT and marketing projects. What is being demonstrated?
o: Operational management
Programme governance
Portfolio management
Project assurance
4.w: Balancing investment, resources and risk across unrelated projects to serve organisational strategy is portfolio management.

4.q: A high-impact risk was reduced by early action, and the manager records this in the register. Why does this matter?
o: It automatically triggers a review of the team's performance
It provides an audit trail of the risk treatment actions taken
It ensures the stakeholder matrix is kept fully up to date
It activates a formal contract change notice with suppliers
4.w: Recording responses and their outcomes in the register provides transparency and an audit trail that supports future learning.

4.q: Which of the following is most likely to be included in a project communication plan?
o: A list of the sponsors of previous, unrelated projects
The technical hardware specifications of the outputs
The individual salaries of the project team members
The frequency and method for each stakeholder group
4.w: A communication plan sets out who needs what information, why, when and how often, by what method, who is responsible, and how feedback is gathered.

n.0: Sponsors of unrelated projects are not part of this project's audience.
n.1: Technical specifications belong in requirements documents, not the communication plan.
n.2: Salaries are confidential personnel data, not communication planning.

4.q: In Belbin's model, which team role is most associated with exploring opportunities outside the team and developing external contacts?
o: Resource Investigator
Coordinator
Implementer
Team Worker
4.w: The Resource Investigator is an outgoing networker who explores opportunities and brings in ideas and contacts from outside the team.

4.q: Which activity is most characteristic of the concept phase within a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Defining the business need and justification for change
Completing the post-project benefit reviews
Allocating detailed work packages to the delivery team
Producing and signing off the final test results
4.w: The concept phase articulates the need, high-level options and justification for the project before detailed planning begins.

4.q: A change request has just been logged on a project. What is the next stage in a typical change control process?
o: Close the project's business case
Assess the impact of the proposed change
Update the risk register and take no further action
Immediately implement the change to save time
4.w: After a change is logged, its impact on time, cost, scope and quality is assessed before any decision to authorise it.

4.q: A team lists activities like 'write code' and 'run tests' but never identifies the deliverables these produce. Which structure is missing?
o: A cost breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
An organisational breakdown structure
A product breakdown structure
4.w: The product breakdown structure identifies the deliverables; without it the team risks planning work without confirming what it must produce.

4.q: What is the primary purpose of benefits management within the delivery of a project?
o: To reduce the project's overhead costs
To ensure that suppliers are paid on time
To keep the project delivery on schedule
To define, track and realise the intended value of the project
4.w: Benefits management ensures the project delivers measurable value that supports the organisation's business objectives.

4.q: One manager plans and controls the work; another energises and directs the people. Which is chiefly exercising leadership?
o: Both equally, because leadership simply means administration
Neither, since the two activities are identical
The manager who energises and directs the people
The manager who plans and controls the work
4.w: Leadership is about energising and directing people towards a vision, whereas planning and controlling the work is management.

4.q: A project manager needs a standard risk register template and guidance on preparing for a gateway review. Which role usually provides this support?
o: The scrum master
The project sponsor
The project governance board
The project management office (PMO)
4.w: The PMO provides templates, tools, assurance and support to help projects plan and prepare for reviews.

4.q: In a project to digitise patient records, which activity best demonstrates benefits management?
o: Tracking supplier invoices during the system rollout
Identifying, measuring and realising improvements in access to patient data
Ensuring clinical staff are trained before the system goes live
Producing the project's quality register
4.w: Benefits management focuses on identifying, measuring and realising value, such as improved access to patient data.

4.q: How do project management, programme management and portfolio management typically relate to one another within an organisation?
o: A project may stand alone, or sit in a programme and/or a portfolio
Projects, programmes and portfolios are independent and never interact
Programmes and portfolios are just other names for very large projects
Portfolios sit within programmes, which sit within individual projects
4.w: A project may stand alone, sit within a programme, and/or sit within a portfolio. Programmes coordinate related projects for benefits; portfolios prioritise change against strategy and capacity.

n.1: They interact closely: programmes coordinate projects and portfolios prioritise both.
n.2: Programmes and portfolios are distinct ways of managing change, not just big projects.
n.3: This reverses the relationship; portfolios are the highest level, not the lowest.

4.q: Midway through a project a client requests several enhancements to the agreed product. What should the project manager do first?
o: Add the changes to the next iteration in order to save time
Submit a formal change request for the change to be reviewed
Update the work breakdown structure and proceed with the changes
Amend the entries in the configuration log to reflect the changes
4.w: The first step is to raise a change request so the change can be logged and its impact assessed before any implementation.

4.q: How can a well-run risk management process increase stakeholder confidence in a project?
o: By removing the need for any progress reporting
By promising that no risks will ever occur
By showing threats are being identified and actively managed
By hiding potential threats from the project board
4.w: Demonstrating that risks are being systematically identified and managed reassures stakeholders that the project is under control.

4.q: What does configuration management rely on to determine whether a proposed update can be safely implemented?
o: Approval given through the change control process
The project's overall work breakdown structure
The procedures used for escalating project risks
The project's stakeholder map and analysis
4.w: Configuration management only applies changes that have first been formally assessed and approved through change control.

4.q: A new CEO cancels two projects, starts three, and groups related initiatives into one programme. Which type of management is being applied?
o: Programme assurance
Change control
Portfolio management
Operational leadership
4.w: Prioritising, terminating and initiating initiatives across the organisation to reflect strategy is portfolio management.

4.q: How does a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) help to reduce duplication of effort on a project?
o: By ranking the project's activities in their order of criticality
By defining the communication channels between the stakeholders
By assigning each member of the team to a specific budget code
By clarifying who is responsible and accountable for each task
4.w: By assigning clear responsibility and accountability, the RAM prevents overlap and confusion about who should do each task.

4.q: Suppliers across time zones face delays because responsibilities are unclear. Which core purpose of project management is being undermined?
o: Establishing a clear framework of control and governance
Removing the need for stakeholder input entirely
Delivering the final product without any change
Minimising all administrative overhead on the project
4.w: A key purpose of project management is to provide clear control and governance, including defined roles and responsibilities for decision-making.

4.q: At what point in the issue resolution process are actions assigned to named owners?
o: When the issue is first identified and logged
When the issue's impact is first being assessed
When the resolution is agreed with the sponsor
When the issue is tracked through to its closure
4.w: Once the issue has been escalated, the sponsor and project manager agree the resolution and assign the actions needed to carry it out.

n.0: Logging captures the issue; the actions are not yet known at this point.
n.1: Assessment works out the impact; the response has not yet been agreed.
n.3: Tracking to closure follows the actions that were assigned when the resolution was agreed.

4.q: During testing a stakeholder suggests altering the interface, and the team updates the prototype without formal approval. What risk does this pose?
o: It reduces the project's reliance on captured lessons learned
It improves team morale but delays the realisation of benefits
It helps the team to finalise the configuration log early
It may cause scope creep and misalignment with the baseline
4.w: Changing a product without change control means the impact is not assessed, risking scope creep and divergence from the agreed baseline.

5.q: How does a communication plan help when several stakeholder groups with differing needs are involved?
o: It allows senior leadership to be left out of all updates
It restricts every communication to a single email channel
It requires the same message to be sent to every group
It lets the manager tailor messages to each audience's needs and influence
5.w: Communication plans support stakeholder-specific approaches, improving the relevance and effectiveness of engagement.

5.q: A change in organisational strategy puts a project at risk of cancellation. Who is responsible for deciding whether it should continue?
o: Project sponsor
Project manager
Product owner
Project planner
5.w: The sponsor assesses continued strategic alignment and has the authority to continue or cancel the project.

5.q: Which feature most clearly distinguishes an iterative life cycle from a linear one in terms of its phases?
o: Its phases are repeated to develop the solution incrementally
Its phases exclude any form of review or feedback
Its phases are always carried out by external suppliers
Its phases are performed strictly once in a fixed order
5.w: The defining difference is repetition of phases to build the solution incrementally rather than a single pass.

5.q: In which section of a business case would you expect to find the project's forecast financial return?
o: The quality plan
The executive summary
The investment appraisal
The communication plan
5.w: The investment appraisal presents the financial justification, such as cost–benefit analysis or return on investment.

5.q: A late supplier delivery has already caused a delay beyond the agreed tolerance. What is the most appropriate first action for the project manager?
o: Tell procurement that the project will now be cancelled
Log it as an issue and assess its impact on the schedule
Record it in the risk register as a possible future threat
Hand the whole project over to the product owner to fix
5.w: The delay has happened and breaches tolerance, so it is an issue. The project manager logs it, assesses the impact and then escalates it to the sponsor.

n.0: Cancelling the project is a decision for the sponsor or governance board, not a first response.
n.2: A risk is uncertain and in the future; this delay has already happened.
n.3: The project manager stays responsible for managing the project and escalating issues.

5.q: A team reviews trends in renewable-energy legislation to see how they could shape a new facility's design. Which tool are they most likely using?
o: SWOT analysis
PESTLE analysis
MoSCoW prioritisation
Cost-benefit analysis
5.w: PESTLE analysis identifies and assesses external factors, such as legislation, that could influence project outcomes.

5.q: What is the main purpose of risk management on a project?
o: To improve the chance of meeting objectives by managing uncertainty
To replace the need for a project management plan
To transfer all responsibility for the project to the sponsor
To eliminate every possible risk before the project begins
5.w: Risk management aims to increase the likelihood of achieving objectives by identifying and responding to uncertainty, not to remove all risk.

5.q: A project team meets regularly to review threats and plan responses before they occur. What core purpose of risk management does this serve?
o: Guaranteeing that the original plan will never change
Transferring all responsibility for outcomes to the sponsor
Reducing the impact of uncertainty on project objectives
Recording issues only after they have disrupted delivery
5.w: Regularly reviewing and responding to threats in advance reduces the impact of uncertainty on the project's objectives.

5.q: Which of the following is not a characteristic of a project?
o: An objective to deliver a unique output
A permanent team structure that continues indefinitely
A temporary nature, disbanding once objectives are met
A defined start point and a defined end point
5.w: Projects are staffed by temporary teams assembled for the objective and disbanded on completion, so a permanent structure is not a project characteristic.

5.q: The sponsor asks the project manager to update the delivery milestones in the business case. What does this indicate about their relationship?
o: The sponsor leads strategy while the project manager supplies delivery detail
Project governance is being deliberately bypassed
The project manager holds ownership of the strategic goals
The sponsor is performing the project manager's role
5.w: This reflects appropriate collaboration: the sponsor leads on strategy and the project manager provides delivery information.

5.q: A project plan shows 'design approved' as a milestone. What does this most likely represent?
o: The list of resources assigned to the design work
The completion of a significant deliverable or decision point
The amount of effort required to produce the design
The total cost of the design phase of the project
5.w: A milestone marks a significant achievement or decision point, such as an approval, rather than effort or cost.

5.q: Why is a milestone shown on a schedule with zero duration rather than as a bar spanning several days?
o: Because it can never appear anywhere on the critical path
Because it is the most expensive element in the schedule
Because it marks a single point in time and represents no work itself
Because it always has the most float of any scheduled item
5.w: A milestone marks a single point in time and involves no work, so it has zero duration, unlike an activity shown as a bar.

5.q: A post-project review finds that weak stakeholder engagement led to missed requirements; what should be done with this insight?
o: Ignore it because the project has now closed
Use it to place blame on the stakeholders
Delete it to protect the project's reputation
Document it as a lesson learned for future projects
5.w: Lessons learned should be captured and shared so that stakeholder engagement improves on future projects.

5.q: A team inspects completed deliverables to confirm they meet the agreed requirements; which process are they performing?
o: Quality planning of outputs
Quality control of outputs
Risk management activity
Stakeholder management work
5.w: Quality control involves inspecting and testing deliverables to verify they meet the agreed quality requirements.

5.q: A business case compares 'do nothing', 'do the minimum' and 'do something' approaches. Why is this comparison valuable?
o: It defines the criteria for project handover
It reduces the overall scope of the project
It demonstrates value for money and the case for change
It accelerates the procurement of suppliers
5.w: Comparing these options shows the value of proceeding and supports the strategic case for change.

5.q: What is a common issue with relying solely on virtual communication platforms?
o: They are vulnerable to internet outages or system failures
They remove the need for any project documentation
They function without issue in every geographic region
They require no training for people to use them
5.w: Poor connectivity or system failures can disrupt communication entirely when it depends only on virtual platforms.

5.q: Why is the temporary nature of a project important to the way it is managed?
o: It ensures defined objectives are delivered within a bounded time frame
It removes the need for any stakeholder involvement during delivery
It guarantees the team can immediately be reused on other work
It aligns all delivery activity strictly to the financial year
5.w: Being time-bounded focuses the project on achieving its specific objectives within defined constraints rather than continuing indefinitely.

5.q: A project has quality procedures in place but never reviews whether the team follows them; what is missing?
o: Risk management activity
Scope management activity
Issue control activity
Quality assurance of processes
5.w: Without checks to verify process adherence, quality assurance is not being properly implemented.

5.q: Why are the plans and baseline updated after a change is approved but before it is implemented?
o: So that the change no longer needs a formal decision by anyone
So progress is measured against the agreed, current baseline
So that no further change requests can be raised on the project
So that the original change request record can then be deleted
5.w: Updating plans comes before implementation so that the work, and the measurement of progress, are controlled against a baseline that already reflects the approved change.

n.0: The decision has already been made at the recommendation stage; updating plans does not replace it.
n.2: Further change requests can be raised at any time and go through the same process.
n.3: Change records are kept as an audit trail; they are not deleted once a change is approved.

5.q: A gateway review finds the deliverables no longer align with business strategy. Who is responsible for recommending that the project stops or is redirected?
o: Project governance board
Project team
Project manager
PMO administrator
5.w: The governance board has the authority to intervene when a project no longer aligns to strategy or exceeds risk thresholds.

5.q: A project manager finds the team has no Monitor Evaluator among its Belbin roles. Which risk is this most likely to create?
o: A shortage of new and creative ideas
Too great a reliance on outside stakeholders
Excessive attention to minor details
Weaker critical analysis and poorer decision-making
5.w: The Monitor Evaluator supplies objective, analytical judgement; without one the team may reach poorly considered decisions.

5.q: Which advantage does a recorded virtual meeting offer that a face-to-face meeting usually does not?
o: It guarantees immediate emotional reassurance to all
It can be replayed later by those who could not attend
It always conveys body language much more clearly
It removes any possibility of a technical failure
5.w: A recorded virtual meeting can be stored and replayed, giving absent members access to the discussion later.

5.q: Which of the following is the strongest success criterion for a new healthcare IT system?
o: Users agree the system improves the patient experience
Every stakeholder is invited to the project meetings
No existing member of staff changes their role
All project invoices are settled within thirty days
5.w: An outcome-focused, user-centred measure such as improved patient experience reflects the benefits the project is intended to deliver.

5.q: Beyond gaining initial approval, what continuing purpose does the business case serve as the project progresses through delivery?
o: It replaces the need to maintain a project schedule during delivery
It records the version history of each of the configuration items
It provides the reference for checking that the investment remains justified
It sets out the acceptance tests to be run on the final product
5.w: The business case is reviewed throughout delivery to confirm the investment remains viable and continues to justify the project's continuation.

5.q: What is one benefit of defining clear success criteria at the beginning of a project?
o: They remove the need to produce a stakeholder map
They guarantee that the schedule cannot slip
They avoid the need for a post-project review
They provide a clear benchmark for evaluating performance
5.w: Clear success criteria give a measurable benchmark for judging whether objectives were achieved and for justifying decisions.

5.q: An agile team adapts its backlog regularly throughout delivery. What does this indicate about scope management on the project?
o: Scope is left undefined until testing begins
Scope is adapted continuously as the project evolves
Scope is fixed and unchanged after the concept phase
Scope is fully defined at the start and then locked
5.w: Regular backlog refinement reflects iterative scope management, in which scope adapts to evolving priorities and feedback.

5.q: What is the purpose of producing a risk response plan?
o: To document the acceptance criteria for the project's final deliverables
To define how the team will react once issues have been logged
To develop the project's work breakdown structure
To set out the actions that will reduce, avoid, transfer or accept each risk
5.w: A risk response plan records the agreed action for each risk, whether to reduce, avoid, transfer or accept it.

5.q: How does configuration management help to maintain the integrity of project deliverables?
o: By approving or rejecting each change request that stakeholders raise
By allocating individual team members to specific project tasks
By identifying each item and controlling and recording its versions
By removing change restrictions so the team can work more flexibly
5.w: Configuration management identifies the configuration items and controls and records their versions and status, so everyone works from the correct, current version and only authorised changes are made.

n.0: Deciding whether a change is approved or rejected is the job of change control, not configuration management.
n.1: Allocating people to tasks is resource management, often shown in a responsibility assignment matrix.
n.3: Configuration management tightens control over changes to items; it does not remove restrictions.

5.q: A project team recognises potential cyber-attacks as a threat to delivery. What has this activity achieved?
o: It has identified a risk
It has closed the risk
It has analysed the risk's impact
It has accepted the risk
5.w: Recognising cyber-attacks as a possible future threat means the team has successfully identified a risk.

5.q: Where would a project manager typically record and track a problem that has already arisen during delivery?
o: In the business case
In the communication plan
In the risk register
In the issue log
5.w: A problem that has arisen is an issue and is recorded and tracked in the issue log, distinct from the risk register used for potential events.

5.q: What principally happens during the transition phase of a typical linear project life cycle?
o: The high-level idea is assessed for viability and strategic fit
Detailed plans, schedules and budgets are produced and baselined
Outputs are handed over to users and the project is formally closed
The main deliverables are designed, built and progressively tested
5.w: In the transition phase the outputs are handed over into use and the project is closed down.

5.q: A linear project finalised its scope during the concept phase. What is the likely consequence when new requirements emerge during delivery?
o: The change will be managed through strict change control
The scope will be re-planned freely at every stage
The change will be absorbed into the work automatically
The team will simply reprioritise its next sprint
5.w: Linear projects fix scope early, so new requirements arising later are handled through a formal, strictly controlled change process.

5.q: Which of the following is a key advantage of face-to-face communication on a project?
o: It removes any need for written follow-up or documentation
It reduces the travel and scheduling costs for the team
It permits immediate feedback and the reading of body language
It guarantees that stakeholders will agree with the message
5.w: Face-to-face communication conveys non-verbal cues and allows misunderstandings to be clarified immediately.

5.q: The team records that adverse weather might delay outdoor work next month. How is this best classified?
o: A change, because it alters the agreed scope
An issue, because it is affecting delivery now
A risk, because it is uncertain and may occur in future
A constraint, because it limits the schedule
5.w: An uncertain future event that may or may not happen is a risk, distinguishing it from an issue that has occurred.

5.q: When is a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) most useful during a project?
o: When defining the project's overall scope and its schedule
When conducting the project's lessons learned review at closure
When assigning clear ownership of deliverables and decision-making
When establishing the communication channels with stakeholders
5.w: The RAM is most valuable when ownership and accountability for deliverables and decisions must be made explicit.

5.q: A sponsor asks how delivery progress will be monitored. Which document should the project manager refer to as the key benchmark?
o: The organisational chart
The procurement policy
The deployment baseline
The risk log
5.w: The deployment baseline holds the agreed scope, time, cost and resources against which progress is compared.

5.q: A learner confuses scope management with schedule management. Which statement correctly explains how the two disciplines differ?
o: Scope management controls cost, while schedule management controls quality
Scope management defines the work required, while schedule management sequences it in time
Both are simply identical processes operating under two different names
Scope management sequences the work, while schedule management defines what is required
5.w: Scope management defines what work is required, whereas schedule management arranges that work in time; they are distinct disciplines.

5.q: A responsibility assignment matrix is typically created by combining which two structures?
o: The communication plan and the procurement strategy
The product breakdown structure and the benefits map
The cost breakdown structure and the risk register
The work breakdown structure and the organisational breakdown structure
5.w: A RAM maps the work packages of the WBS against the people or teams in the OBS to assign responsibilities.

5.q: What challenge might a project manager face when leading a team spread across multiple geographic locations?
o: Standardising tools that are already uniform everywhere
Reducing over-involvement from the team
Reconciling differing cultures and communication styles
Coping with excessive face-to-face interaction
5.w: Differences in culture and communication style can cause misunderstanding and tension, requiring the leadership approach to be tailored.

5.q: In an extended life cycle, which phase follows transition and focuses on users embedding the new outputs into their everyday ways of working?
o: The foundations phase
The adoption phase
The deployment phase
The definition phase
5.w: The extended life cycle adds adoption, where the outputs are embedded in business as usual, and then benefits realisation.

n.0: Foundations is a phase of the iterative life cycle, before any development.
n.2: Deployment comes before transition and is where the outputs are built.
n.3: Definition comes early and sets the requirements and plans.

5.q: Why is it important to formally close risks during the risk management process?
o: To prevent risks from being escalated to the project’s stakeholders
To keep the risk register accurate and focused on active threats
To transfer the lessons learned directly into the project issue log
To reduce the number of meetings the project team must hold
5.w: Closure removes risks that are no longer relevant, keeping the risk register current and focused on active threats and opportunities.

5.q: A change request has just been approved at the recommendation stage. Which stage of the change control process comes next?
o: Update the plans and baseline
Carry out a detailed evaluation
Implement the change straight away
Log the original change request
5.w: After the decision, the plans, baseline and configuration records are updated. Only then is the change implemented, so the work is controlled against the revised baseline.

n.1: Detailed evaluation happens before the recommendation, not after it.
n.2: Implementation is the final stage and follows updating the plans, not the decision itself.
n.3: Logging the change request is the first stage and was completed before evaluation began.

5.q: A deliverable performs exactly the job it was intended to do. In quality terms, this makes it what?
o: Non-conforming, and therefore automatically defective
Low grade, and therefore of poor quality
Over-specified, and therefore inherently wasteful
Fit for purpose, and therefore of good quality
5.w: A deliverable that does exactly the job intended is fit for purpose, which is the essence of quality.

5.q: A sponsor complains they only hear about problems once they are severe. Which reporting improvement would most directly address this?
o: Reporting progress regularly with early variance alerts
Reporting exclusively on completed deliverables
Reporting only when the sponsor formally requests it
Reporting only at the project's closure stage
5.w: Regular reporting with timely variance information gives early warning, preventing problems from being discovered only when severe.

5.q: Midway through an iterative project, stakeholders reprioritise features. What effect does this typically have on the deployment baseline?
o: It invalidates the baseline, so it must be deleted
It updates the baseline to reflect the revised priorities
It freezes the baseline until the project closes
It has no effect, as the baseline is permanently fixed
5.w: An iterative deployment baseline is expected to evolve, so reprioritised features are absorbed by updating the baseline for the next iterations.

5.q: Which of the following is the range of outcomes a decision gate can authorise for a project?
o: Only continue, since a gate can never stop a project
Continue to the next phase, amend the plan, or stop the project
Only stop, since a gate cannot allow continuation
Reassign the entire project team to other work
5.w: A decision gate can decide to proceed, amend or stop, not merely authorise continuation.

5.q: Why is effective leadership important to team performance within a project environment?
o: It removes the need for the team to hold any meetings
It motivates the team and supports collaboration towards shared goals
It guarantees that project risk will be completely eliminated
It ensures that all project contracts are signed on time
5.w: Leadership sets direction and motivates and aligns individuals so that the team works collaboratively towards the project’s shared goals.
