5.q: Which of the following is a recognised disadvantage of video conferencing in projects?
o: Prolonged calls can cause fatigue and reduced concentration
It cannot be recorded for those unable to attend
It is always more effective than meeting in person
It guarantees that every participant contributes equally
5.w: Extended video calls can cause fatigue, which reduces attention and engagement.

5.q: What is a key leadership challenge when managing a newly formed project team?
o: Resolving undefined roles and responsibilities
Delivering specialist technical training
Drafting the legal contracts for suppliers
Avoiding any emotional engagement with the team
5.w: Early in a project, roles are often ambiguous, and the leader must clarify them to prevent confusion and inefficiency.

5.q: A project manager uses critical path analysis to find which tasks must finish on time to avoid delaying the project. What is being managed?
o: Critical path activities
The quality of project resources
The overall project budget
Formal stakeholder approval
5.w: Critical path activities have zero float, so they must be completed on time to prevent the project end date from slipping.

5.q: A team decides to take no pre-emptive action against a possible delay to key components. Which risk response is this?
o: Transfer
Acceptance
Avoidance
Mitigation
5.w: Acceptance means acknowledging a risk and taking no pre-emptive action unless it actually materialises.

5.q: Compared with business as usual, project work is generally characterised by higher levels of which factor?
o: Uncertainty, because the outputs are unique
Repetition, because the tasks are standardised
Predictability, because the work is routine
Stability, because the team is permanent
5.w: Because projects deliver unique outputs, they carry greater uncertainty and risk than the routine, repeatable work of operations.

5.q: What is a key benefit of agreeing a procurement strategy at the start of a project?
o: It removes the need to monitor suppliers once contracts are signed
It gives a structured, consistent approach to acquiring goods and services
It replaces the need to produce a business case for the project
It guarantees that internal resources are always selected in preference
5.w: An early procurement strategy provides a consistent, transparent framework for obtaining resources and services externally.

5.q: In the context of scope management, how is 'change control' best defined?
o: The process for identifying and recording all project stakeholders
The process for levelling resources across the project schedule
The process for closing risks once they no longer apply
The process for formally requesting, assessing and approving changes to scope
5.w: Change control is the process by which changes to scope are formally requested, evaluated and authorised.

5.q: Which of the following is typically included in a benefits management plan?
o: The ownership, timing and measurement of each benefit
The baseline schedule data for the project
The list of items excluded from scope
The communication escalation procedures
5.w: A benefits management plan sets out who owns each benefit, when it is expected and how it will be measured.

5.q: Which of the following is not part of managing a project?
o: Identifying and managing project risks
Resolving issues that arise during delivery
Continuously delivering an ongoing business function
Communicating with project stakeholders
5.w: Project management concerns temporary, defined outputs; the continuous delivery of a business function is business-as-usual, not project work.

5.q: A schedule is revised to delay a task by three days so a shared specialist can finish another job first. Which technique is this?
o: Time boxing
Resource levelling
Resource smoothing
Risk transfer
5.w: Resource levelling resolves a resource conflict by moving task timings to match availability, even where this affects the schedule.

5.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of carrying out a benefit review on a project?
o: An evaluation of whether the expected business benefits have been delivered
A discussion of scope changes held with the project’s suppliers
A report on the availability of the team once the project ends
An internal audit of the time-tracking systems used by staff
5.w: A benefits review assesses whether the anticipated benefits set out in the business case have actually been realised.

5.q: Which of the following would be the weakest choice of project success criterion?
o: Delivery within the approved budget tolerance
Achievement of the required technical specification
Stakeholder satisfaction above an agreed threshold
An improvement in team morale during the project
5.w: Team morale is subjective and not directly tied to the project's deliverables, making it a poor, hard-to-measure success criterion.

5.q: In an agile project, which stakeholder clarifies the acceptance criteria and ensures user needs are reflected in the plan?
o: The PMO analyst
The product owner
The scrum master
The project sponsor
5.w: The product owner represents the customer and defines the requirements, including what acceptable delivery looks like.

6.q: Which of the following is a potential drawback of virtual communication methods?
o: They provide the same rich body-language cues as meeting in person
They remove every difficulty associated with differing time zones
They always ensure the confidentiality of shared information
They can suffer technical problems and reduced personal connection
6.w: Virtual tools can create barriers through technical limitations and weaker non-verbal engagement.

6.q: A key stakeholder's objection has halted work on site, and the resulting delay now exceeds the project manager's tolerance. Which process should be used to handle this?
o: Scope management
Risk identification
Configuration management
Issue management
6.w: The problem has happened and breaches tolerance, so it is an issue: it is logged, assessed, escalated to the sponsor and resolved through issue management.

n.0: Scope management identifies, defines and controls outputs, outcomes and benefits; it does not handle this problem.
n.1: Risk identification deals with uncertain future events, but this has already happened.
n.2: Configuration management controls and records versions of items, not stakeholder problems.

6.q: During delivery, a scope change is identified that will affect cost and schedule. What is the first step the project manager should take?
o: Continue as planned and ignore the change
Reassign the work without recording it
Compare the proposed change against the deployment baseline
Notify stakeholders that the project will close
6.w: Proposed changes are first assessed against the deployment baseline to determine their impact and whether approval is required.

6.q: In a linear life cycle, which of the following is a main purpose of the transition phase?
o: Designing and building the project's outputs
Handing over outputs and closing the project
Developing and approving the outline business case
Setting the deployment baseline for the work
6.w: Transition hands the outputs over to users and business as usual, gains acceptance, releases resources, and closes the project, including capturing lessons learned.

n.0: Designing and building outputs happens in deployment.
n.2: The outline business case is developed in the concept phase.
n.3: The deployment baseline is set at the end of definition.

6.q: In a project, what is quality management fundamentally intended to ensure about the deliverables?
o: That they are delivered before the agreed schedule
That they are produced at the lowest possible cost
That they involve the fewest possible team members
That they are fit for purpose and meet the agreed requirements
6.w: Quality management ensures deliverables meet agreed requirements and are fit for purpose.

6.q: How does an early stakeholder analysis help a project manager anticipate potential opposition to a project?
o: By guaranteeing that no stakeholder will ever oppose the project's aims
By revealing which stakeholders may resist, so their concerns can be addressed early
By transferring responsibility for opposition to the project sponsor
By removing any need to communicate with opposing stakeholders
6.w: Analysis reveals which stakeholders may resist, allowing their concerns to be understood and addressed early in engagement.

6.q: A project manager prepares a one-page summary schedule for executives showing only the key dates. What are these key dates called?
o: Work packages
Baselines
Milestones
Dependencies
6.w: Key dates shown on a summary schedule are milestones, giving senior stakeholders a high-level view of progress.

6.q: In what way does an effective risk management process improve decision-making on a project?
o: It removes uncertainty so no judgement is required
It provides a structured understanding of threats and opportunities to inform choices
It ensures decisions are only made at project closure
It replaces the need for a project board to make decisions
6.w: By assessing threats and opportunities, risk management gives decision-makers a structured basis for informed choices.

6.q: Who is typically responsible for ensuring that a project's benefits are realised after its outputs have been delivered?
o: The project quality manager
An individual project team member
The project sponsor or business owner
The project manager
6.w: The project manager delivers the outputs, but the sponsor or business owner owns the realisation of benefits once the project is complete.

6.q: A supplier misses a key delivery, so the project manager records it and assigns it to the procurement lead. Which stage of issue resolution is this?
o: Analysis of the issue's impact on objectives
Identification and assignment of the issue
Closure of the issue once it is verified
Resolution of the issue through corrective action
6.w: Logging the issue and giving it an owner are part of the initial identification and assignment stage of the resolution process.

6.q: In what way can parametric estimating help to improve the accuracy of a project estimate?
o: By relying on group brainstorming sessions to reach an agreed figure
By applying historical cost-per-unit data and scaling it to the work required
By comparing the whole project against one broadly similar completed project
By assigning a single fixed cost to every stage of the project
6.w: Parametric estimating applies measured historical rates per unit of work, which can be scaled to give a more accurate and defensible estimate.

6.q: How can a project leader who consistently models the standards and behaviours they expect influence their team?
o: It guarantees that no conflict will ever arise
It removes the need for any team ground rules
It transfers leadership responsibility to the team
It sets a clear example that encourages similar behaviour and effort
6.w: Leading by example sets the standard others follow, encouraging the behaviour and effort that support performance.

6.q: A project manager explains why a linear deployment baseline feels more rigid than an iterative one. Which explanation is correct?
o: Both fix the baseline rigidly before any delivery starts
Linear fixes it early, while iterative refines it each iteration
Iterative fixes it early, while linear evolves over time
Both leave the baseline entirely open until closure
6.w: A linear life cycle establishes a firm baseline early, whereas an iterative life cycle refines the baseline across successive iterations.

6.q: When resource levelling is applied because resources are limited, what is the likely effect on the schedule?
o: The project cost is guaranteed to fall to its lowest level
The project end date may be extended to fit resource availability
The scope automatically expands to absorb the spare capacity
The critical path is removed from the schedule entirely
6.w: Resource levelling is resource-limited, so activities are rescheduled to available resources and the end date may move out.

6.q: Two team members carried out a task differently after a briefing because neither confirmed what was meant. Which aspect of communication failed?
o: The wrong communication medium was chosen
There was no feedback to confirm shared understanding
The message was too short to be archived
The message was sent to too many recipients
6.w: Without feedback to confirm shared understanding, the message was interpreted differently, so the communication was not effective.

6.q: Which statement best describes how a risk register is used across the life of a project?
o: It is a living document reviewed and updated throughout
It is completed once at initiation and then archived
It is produced only after the project has closed
It is used solely to record issues that have occurred
6.w: A risk register is a living document, reviewed and updated throughout delivery as risks change, close or newly emerge.

6.q: Why does stakeholder analysis help a project manager use limited engagement time efficiently?
o: It transfers responsibility for engagement to the project sponsor
It replaces the need for a communication plan later in delivery
It highlights where to focus effort by ranking influence and interest
It confirms that all stakeholders require identical levels of contact
6.w: By ranking influence and interest, analysis shows where engagement effort will have most value, allowing resources to be focused.

6.q: Why does a linear life cycle generally require tighter scope control than an iterative one?
o: Because scope is only ever agreed after delivery has ended
Because its baseline is fixed early, so change disrupts the plan
Because it has no defined deliverables that need protecting
Because it welcomes unlimited change at any point in delivery
6.w: A linear baseline is set early, so uncontrolled change threatens the plan and demands rigorous control.

6.q: How does having a documented communication plan give the project manager a consistent basis for project communications?
o: It records who receives what information, how and when, so messages stay consistent
It removes the need to identify the project's stakeholders at all
It guarantees the project will be delivered comfortably within its budget
It transfers responsibility for delivery across to the stakeholders
6.w: The plan records who receives what, how and when, giving the project manager a consistent, agreed basis for all communications.

6.q: At which points in the life cycle do the sponsor and project manager jointly review the business case?
o: Only once the project has been formally closed
Solely at the point a change request is raised
At project initiation and at key decision gates
Only after the benefits have been fully realised
6.w: They review the case together at initiation and at decision gates to confirm the justification remains valid.

6.q: Which action is most appropriate during the risk closure stage of the risk management process?
o: Reviewing the outcomes and updating the lessons learned
Increasing the project's contingency budget for reassurance
Converting each closed risk into a formal change request
Assigning new owners to risks that have already expired
6.w: Closure involves recording outcomes and capturing lessons learned to improve risk handling on future projects.

6.q: Two projects run side by side: one linear, one iterative. Which difference in their deployment baselines should the project manager expect?
o: The linear baseline flexes weekly; the iterative stays fixed
The iterative baseline flexes; the linear stays largely fixed
Both baselines remain completely unchanged throughout
Neither project establishes a baseline at any point
6.w: The iterative project's baseline evolves with each iteration, while the linear project's baseline is largely fixed after early approval.

6.q: Which configuration management activity defines how items will be controlled and versioned throughout a project?
o: Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
6.w: Configuration planning sets out the framework, roles and procedures for how configuration items will be managed across the project.

6.q: How do change control and configuration management jointly relate to a project's baseline?
o: Configuration management authorises baseline changes; change control archives the previous plan
Neither of the two processes has any bearing on the project's baseline
Change control authorises amendments to the baseline; configuration management records the updated, controlled baseline
Both freeze the baseline permanently so that it can never be altered
6.w: Change control governs whether the baseline may be amended; configuration management maintains the record of the controlled, updated baseline.

6.q: In an iterative project, which mechanism is most commonly used to manage what gets built next?
o: A locked scope baseline signed at initiation
A single change request covering the whole project
A fixed work breakdown never revisited after concept
A prioritised, evolving backlog reviewed each cycle
6.w: Iterative scope is managed through a prioritised backlog that is reviewed and reordered each cycle.

6.q: Which decision would most appropriately sit with the project's governance arrangements rather than the project manager?
o: Whether the project should continue past a decision gate
The wording of a routine weekly status update
Which team member is assigned to a particular work package
How a specific technical task should be carried out
6.w: Decisions about whether the project proceeds at a gate rest with governance, keeping strategic authority separate from day-to-day delivery.

6.q: In a linear life cycle, in which phase is the project scope defined in detail and baselined?
o: The concept phase
The definition phase
The deployment phase
The transition phase
6.w: Definition is where requirements are defined in detail, the project management plan is produced and the deployment baseline (including scope) is set. From then on, scope is controlled through change control.

n.0: Concept develops the idea, the outline business case and feasibility. Scope is only outlined at a high level, not defined in detail or baselined.
n.2: Deployment delivers the work against the baseline set earlier. Scope is controlled here, not first defined.
n.3: Transition hands the outputs over to users and closes the project. Scope was fixed long before this point.

6.q: What is a key benefit of a communication plan to the project manager?
o: It prevents any conflict from arising within the team
It ensures consistent, structured messaging reaches the right people
It guarantees that the project will be delivered successfully
It removes the need to maintain any project documentation
6.w: A communication plan helps deliver the right message, to the right people, at the right time in a consistent format.

6.q: A project manager sequences activities and sets their timings before delivery begins. Which project management activity is being carried out?
o: Quality control
Benefits management
Scheduling
Risk analysis
6.w: Determining the timing and sequence of activities, and the resources needed, is the purpose of scheduling.

6.q: How does the estimating funnel support communication with stakeholders?
o: By removing tolerance ranges from progress reporting
By fixing the project scope at the outset
By guaranteeing that suppliers deliver within budget
By showing how estimate confidence increases over time
6.w: The funnel explains why estimates change and become more precise, helping stakeholders understand and trust the figures.

6.q: How does active listening help a project leader to improve team performance?
o: It slows down necessary project decision-making
It builds trust and allows issues to be addressed early
It removes the need for any formal reporting
It promotes a culture of blame within the team
6.w: Active listening creates a safe environment where concerns can be raised and resolved before they escalate.

6.q: Which of the following techniques is most commonly used to carry out quality control?
o: A formal lessons learned report
Inspection and testing procedures
The work breakdown structure
Critical path analysis of tasks
6.w: Inspection and testing are key techniques in quality control, confirming that outputs meet requirements.

6.q: Which of the following is a typical activity carried out during quality planning?
o: Monitoring the changing attitudes of the project’s stakeholders
Approving the procurement contracts entered into by the project
Defining the acceptance criteria that deliverables must meet
Identifying the residual risks remaining after responses are applied
6.w: Quality planning determines the standards and acceptance criteria that deliverables must meet and how quality will be achieved.

6.q: How does a communication plan help ensure stakeholders receive consistent information even when different team members send updates?
o: It replaces the need for a project schedule during delivery
It defines the agreed messages, channels and timing that everyone follows
It prevents team members from ever contacting stakeholders directly
It requires the project manager personally to send every single message
6.w: By defining agreed messages, channels and timing, the plan keeps information consistent regardless of which team member issues it.

6.q: A project manager notices discrepancies between the latest deliverable and the configuration baseline. Which process should be reviewed first?
o: Procurement management
Scheduling control
Communication planning
Configuration management
6.w: Configuration management keeps deliverables aligned with the current approved baseline, so it should be reviewed when discrepancies appear.

6.q: When should a project's success criteria be reviewed during the life cycle?
o: At initiation, regularly during delivery, and again at handover
Only once the benefits have been realised
Only at project closure
Only at the start of the project
6.w: Success criteria should be defined early, monitored during delivery to maintain alignment, and evaluated at handover.

6.q: You are running a construction project with a linear life cycle and fully defined requirements. What is the correct sequence of phases?
o: Initiation, Development, Execution, Review
Concept, Feasibility, Development, Handover
Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition
Concept, Definition, Deployment, Closure
6.w: The APM linear life cycle runs Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition. Older material used implementation and handover and closure for the later phases.

n.0: These are not APM phase names for a linear life cycle.
n.1: Feasibility is an iterative phase name, Development and Handover are not BoK7 linear phase names, and Definition is missing.
n.3: The final linear phase is Transition, which includes handover and closure.

6.q: Why is scheduling considered essential to managing the delivery of a project?
o: It defines the overall scope of the work the project will deliver
It establishes the cost breakdown structure for the whole project
It provides a framework to monitor progress and identify delays early
It removes the need for a project manager to oversee delivery
6.w: A schedule sets out when activities occur, giving a baseline against which progress is monitored and delays identified and managed.

6.q: How is scope typically handled in an iterative project compared with a linear one?
o: It is refined progressively as each iteration is reviewed
It is set by suppliers rather than the project team
It is defined only after delivery finishes
It is frozen at the outset and never revisited
6.w: Iterative scope is refined cycle by cycle in response to review and feedback, unlike a fixed linear baseline.

6.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the stages of the APM change control process?
o: Initial evaluation of the request
Post-implementation review
Updating the plans and baseline
Recommendation on the change
6.w: The six stages are change request, initial evaluation, detailed evaluation, recommendation, update plans and implement. A post-implementation review is not one of them.

n.0: Initial evaluation is the second stage: a quick check of whether the request merits a full assessment.
n.2: Update plans is the fifth stage: the baseline, plan and configuration records are updated before implementation.
n.3: Recommendation is the fourth stage: the change is approved, rejected or deferred by the appropriate authority.

6.q: In an agile project a stakeholder maintains the product backlog and decides which features are developed next. Which role is this person performing?
o: Project sponsor
Scrum master
Product owner
Project manager
6.w: The product owner owns the backlog and maximises value by deciding the order in which features are delivered.

6.q: A project manager wants to anticipate how the wider environment might influence a new venture. Which analysis best serves this purpose?
o: A PESTLE analysis of political, economic, social and other external factors
A responsibility assignment matrix mapping tasks to team roles
A risk register listing only internal delivery threats
A work breakdown structure decomposing the project's deliverables
6.w: PESTLE is used to scan the external environment, whereas the other tools address internal work, roles or logged threats.

6.q: What does a flexible deployment baseline allow a team to do in an iterative project?
o: Avoid the need for governance reviews
Work without any documentation or tracking
Respond to evolving user needs as they emerge
Make changes without any impact on the project
6.w: A flexible baseline lets an iterative team remain responsive to changing requirements while still planning and tracking work.

6.q: Why might an organisation choose to manage several related projects together as a programme rather than entirely separately?
o: To guarantee that each project finishes strictly within its own isolated budget
To achieve coordinated benefits that the individual projects could not deliver alone
To remove the need for any individual project to have its own objectives
To convert temporary project work into permanent operational business activity
6.w: A programme coordinates related projects so that combined, aligned benefits are realised that separate projects could not deliver individually.

6.q: Which statement most accurately describes what a hybrid project life cycle brings together within a single project?
o: A single linear sequence repeated so the team can refine the output twice
Linear phases for stable, well-understood work alongside iterative cycles for evolving requirements
Continuous iterations throughout, with no predefined phases fixed in advance
Two consecutive linear life cycles, each producing a separate final deliverable
6.w: A hybrid life cycle blends a plan-driven (linear) approach for defined work with an adaptive (iterative) approach for evolving elements within one project.

6.q: A new team member asks how the discipline of project management should best be defined in practice.
o: The steady supervision of recurring departmental duties within fixed annual budgets
The organising of resources purely to reduce day-to-day operational running costs
The prioritising of competing initiatives to reflect the organisation's changing strategy
The application of knowledge, tools and techniques to deliver objectives within agreed constraints
6.w: Project management applies knowledge, tools and techniques to deliver objectives within the constraints of time, cost and quality; the distractors describe operations and portfolio activity.

6.q: After a response reduces a risk's likelihood, what should happen to that entry in the risk register?
o: It should be updated to reflect its revised assessment
It should be deleted immediately from the register
It should be moved into the project's issue log
It should be left unchanged to preserve the original
6.w: The register is updated so that the revised probability and residual exposure are recorded, keeping the risk picture accurate.

6.q: A team defines, plans and controls its processes so that outputs satisfy customer expectations; what is the purpose of this?
o: To provide the cheapest possible product to the customer
To shorten the overall project life cycle
To ensure deliverables meet stakeholder-defined standards
To transfer quality responsibility across to the suppliers
6.w: The purpose of quality management is to define the agreed quality requirements and ensure they are met throughout the project.

6.q: A client receives a product that looks impressive but fails to meet several contractual requirements. How would its quality be assessed?
o: It is high quality, because of its technical complexity
It is high quality, because it exceeded the client's expectations
It is low quality, because it does not meet the agreed requirements
It is acceptable quality, because the client was impressed by it
6.w: Quality is judged against the agreed requirements, so a product that fails to meet them is of low quality regardless of its appearance.

6.q: What best distinguishes a project audit from a post-project review carried out after closure?
o: Audits are informal discussions, whereas reviews are formal inspections
Audits apply only to iterative projects, whereas reviews apply to linear ones
Audits assess benefits, whereas reviews assess only the schedule
Audits check compliance and governance, whereas reviews capture performance and lessons
6.w: Audits examine whether the project complied with organisational processes and governance, while post-project reviews focus on results and lessons learned.

6.q: You are delivering a new company intranet. Which of the following actions best reflects a project management activity?
o: Developing a risk register to manage delivery uncertainty
Running day-to-day maintenance on the existing intranet
Forwarding supplier invoices on to the procurement team
Producing the weekly staff timesheets for the HR team
6.w: Actively managing delivery risks is part of the structured, controlled approach that characterises project management.

6.q: Which of the following best describes the difference between an issue and a risk?
o: A risk relates to cost, whereas an issue relates to quality
A risk must be escalated, whereas an issue does not
A risk is recorded in the schedule, whereas an issue is not
A risk is a future uncertainty, whereas an issue is a current problem
6.w: A risk is an uncertain future event, while an issue is a problem that has already occurred and must be resolved.

6.q: How does a risk differ from an assumption on a project?
o: A risk has occurred; an assumption cannot occur
There is no difference between the two terms
A risk is always true; an assumption is always false
A risk is an uncertain future event; an assumption is taken to be true
6.w: A risk is an uncertain event that might happen, while an assumption is something accepted as true for planning.

6.q: Which statement best describes resource smoothing as a method of resource optimisation?
o: Adjusting activities within their available float to reduce peaks in resource demand
Cutting lower-priority activities in order to shorten the schedule
Adding extra staff directly to the activities on the critical path
Extending the schedule as required to remove all float from the plan
6.w: Resource smoothing reschedules activities within their available float to even out peaks in demand without extending the project end date.

6.q: What distinguishes genuine leadership from merely instructing a team to comply?
o: It concentrates on producing detailed progress reports
It motivates people to commit willingly towards shared goals
It focuses on allocating resources evenly across all tasks
It relies on enforcing rules so people obey through instruction
6.w: Leadership motivates people to commit willingly to shared goals, rather than securing mere compliance through instruction.

6.q: A city-centre event project faces growing scrutiny over its impact on local air quality and pollution. Which PESTLE category does this most relate to?
o: Technological
Environmental
Political
Legal
6.w: Pollution, air quality and sustainability concerns fall under the environmental category of PESTLE.

6.q: During the change control process, what is the main purpose of the impact assessment stage?
o: To close any related issues automatically
To remove the change from the register permanently
To implement the change as quickly as possible
To understand the effect on time, cost, scope and quality before deciding
6.w: Impact assessment evaluates the consequences on time, cost, scope and quality so an informed authorisation decision can be made.

6.q: While revising the project management plan, a project manager notices there has been no input from the senior supplier. What risk does this pose?
o: Delivery capability and logistics could be misaligned
The project may receive excessive funding
Stakeholder interest will rise unexpectedly
The benefits are likely to be over-delivered
6.w: Without supplier input the plan's delivery logistics may be unrealistic or misaligned with the supplier's capacity.

6.q: Which statement best describes the role of end users within a project?
o: They own the business case and ensure the benefits are realised
They define the strategic objectives and agreed scope of the project
They direct governance activities and approve the supplier contracts
They use the final product or service and give feedback during development
6.w: End users interact with the deliverables and provide feedback that helps ensure the product or service is practical, usable and effective.

6.q: A project manager wants to anticipate how their new team's behaviour will change as it matures. Which model is most relevant?
o: Tuckman's stages of team development
A responsibility assignment matrix
A PESTLE analysis
Belbin's team roles
6.w: Tuckman's model describes forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning, helping anticipate how a team develops over time.

7.q: A client requests a change to a configured product, and it must be assessed and approved before work begins. Which process provides this formal evaluation?
o: Stakeholder engagement
Risk management
Change control
Scope definition
7.w: Change control provides the formal route for assessing and approving or rejecting a change before it affects any configuration items.

7.q: Why is the closure stage important within the issue resolution process?
o: It assigns the issue to an owner for the very first time
It confirms the issue is resolved and records any lessons learned
It decides whether the issue should be escalated further
It determines the issue's likely impact on the schedule
7.w: Closure confirms the issue has been dealt with and captures lessons that may help on future work.

7.q: Why is it inappropriate for a project sponsor to delegate ownership of the business case entirely to the project manager?
o: The project manager already owns the project's risk and quality registers
The project manager is not permitted to view the business case at any stage
Ownership must remain with the sponsor, who is accountable for the investment's benefits
Delegating it would automatically cancel the project's approved funding
7.w: The sponsor owns the business case because they are accountable for realising the investment's benefits; that ownership cannot be handed to the project manager.

7.q: A new appraisal system must be handed to HR within six weeks. What best distinguishes this project from HR's business-as-usual work?
o: The HR department holds greater control over the project budget
The project has a defined end date and delivers a unique output
The project exists to support HR's routine daily operations
The project is concerned only with engaging its stakeholders
7.w: A project delivers a one-off output within defined constraints and then closes, whereas HR's ongoing work is repeatable business-as-usual.

7.q: During which phase of a typical linear life cycle is the initial idea first tested for feasibility and strategic fit?
o: Transition
Deployment
Concept
Definition
7.w: The concept phase tests the initial idea for feasibility and strategic fit before detailed planning begins.

7.q: Why is it important to tailor progress reports to different stakeholder groups?
o: To provide information relevant to each group's interest and influence
To remove the need for formal governance meetings
To avoid carrying out any project audits
To reduce the amount of communication within the team
7.w: Stakeholders have differing interests and influence, so tailoring reports ensures each group receives meaningful and relevant information.

7.q: What does a well-structured communication plan help a project team to ensure during delivery?
o: That all identified project risks are resolved automatically
That every project meeting is cancelled to save time and cost
That the right people receive the right information at the right time
That only face-to-face meetings are used throughout the project
7.w: A communication plan sets out who needs what information, when and how, so the right people are kept informed at the right time.

7.q: A manager lists features of project work to contrast it with business as usual. Which feature genuinely applies only to projects?
o: Delivering a steady, repeatable stream of outputs
Continuing indefinitely with no planned closure
Being temporary, with a defined start and end
Being run by a permanent operational department
7.w: A project is temporary, with a defined start and end, whereas business as usual is repetitive and ongoing.

7.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of decision gates?
o: They let the sponsor decide whether the project continues
They replace all other assurance and quality control activities
They ensure that only the final output is ever reviewed
They remove the need to engage with the stakeholders
7.w: Decision gates are points between phases where the sponsor or governance board decides whether the project continues, reviewing the business case, progress and readiness.

n.1: Gates complement assurance and quality control; they do not replace them.
n.2: Gates occur between phases throughout the life cycle, not only at the end.
n.3: Stakeholder engagement continues throughout; gates do not remove the need for it.

7.q: Why is it beneficial for a project to establish its quality management approach right at the start?
o: To ensure outputs meet requirements and are fit for purpose
To deliver the project in the shortest time possible
To transfer all quality responsibility across to the suppliers
To remove the need for any project documentation later
7.w: A quality management approach set from the outset helps ensure deliverables meet the required standards and are fit for purpose throughout the life cycle.

7.q: What is the role of success criteria when they are set out within a business case?
o: To give the measures by which project success will be judged
To set performance targets for individual team members
To record the communication preferences of the stakeholders
To track the duration of each scheduled activity in the plan
7.w: Success criteria are the qualitative or quantitative measures by which the success of the project is judged. They are agreed at the start, monitored during, and used at handover.

n.1: Individual performance targets are a line management matter, not the project's success criteria.
n.2: Communication preferences belong in the communication plan, based on stakeholder analysis.
n.3: Activity durations are tracked through the schedule, not the success criteria.

7.q: A document management system has been handed over to operations. Which activity would typically follow within the extended project life cycle?
o: Evaluating actual benefits against those forecast
Drafting the project initiation documentation
Holding the initial project kick-off workshop
Running performance tests on the old system
7.w: Comparing benefits actually achieved against those forecast is a central activity of the extended life cycle.

7.q: External stakeholders report that they are not receiving relevant project information. Which document should the project manager review first?
o: The risk register's list of threats and their owners
The quality plan's checklists and acceptance criteria
The communication plan's stakeholder list and distribution schedule
The benefits register's expected outcomes and measures
7.w: The communication plan defines who should receive which information and when, so its stakeholder mapping and schedule are the first thing to check.

7.q: In which life cycle is the deployment baseline most likely to be established firmly at a single point early in delivery?
o: Any life cycle where requirements keep changing
An iterative life cycle using repeated increments
A linear life cycle with defined, stable requirements
A life cycle that omits planning altogether
7.w: A linear life cycle sets a firm baseline early because requirements are defined and stable, unlike the evolving baseline of iterative delivery.

7.q: Which of the following is least likely to be a genuine stakeholder in a project management plan?
o: The team members delivering the work packages
A supplier with no involvement in the project
The end users who will operate the output
The project sponsor authorising the plan
7.w: A stakeholder has an interest in or is affected by the project; a supplier with no involvement has no such stake in the plan.

7.q: Which of the following statements best describes the function of an organisational breakdown structure (OBS)?
o: It sets out the required packages of work in a hierarchy
It assigns a specific cost to each member of the team
It shows the structure of roles and reporting within the project
It defines the sequence in which tasks are to be delivered
7.w: An OBS is a hierarchical view of how the project is organised, showing roles and who reports to whom.

7.q: Scope management is often said to have two core activities. Which pair best describes them?
o: Defining the required work, then controlling changes to it
Identifying the risks, then assigning owners to each
Scheduling the work, then levelling the resources across it
Estimating the budget, then reporting the actual spend
7.w: Scope management first defines the work required and then controls changes to it; the distractors describe scheduling, cost and risk activities.

7.q: What characteristic must an event have before it can be classed as a project risk?
o: It must be uncertain and capable of affecting the project's objectives
It must lie entirely outside the project team's ability to control
It must occur only during the execution phase of the project
It must be guaranteed to happen at some point during the project
7.w: A risk must be uncertain and able to affect objectives, whether positively or negatively.

7.q: How does a communication plan help a project manager direct communication effort where it is most needed?
o: By removing the need to report progress to the sponsor at all
By matching the type and frequency of information to each audience's needs
By fixing the project scope so that no updates are required
By requiring every stakeholder to receive identical daily updates
7.w: The plan matches information type and frequency to each audience, so the project manager focuses communication effort where it is most needed.

7.q: Which of the following statements best describes the overall function of project governance?
o: Creating the detailed work breakdown structure
Running the daily stand-ups and team meetings
Ensuring strategic direction, decision-making and control
Maintaining the project's daily risk log
7.w: Governance ensures the project stays aligned to strategy and follows agreed controls, decision-making and oversight.

7.q: A team lists its stakeholders then rates each on power and interest. What does this rating enable them to do?
o: Confirm the exact final cost of the project to the last item
Remove any stakeholder who might disagree with the project
Record only the contact details needed to send invitations
Plan an engagement approach proportionate to each stakeholder's position
7.w: Rating power and interest lets the team plan engagement that is proportionate to each stakeholder's position.

7.q: What is one benefit of applying a standard estimating funnel across an organisation's projects?
o: It replaces the need for bottom-up estimating
It fixes all estimates at the start of each project
It promotes consistent refinement of estimates across project phases
It removes the need for any contingency planning
7.w: A standard funnel provides a consistent approach to refining estimates as knowledge grows, aiding comparison across projects.

7.q: A sponsor wants independent confirmation, during delivery, that governance and processes are being followed. Which mechanism serves this best?
o: A project audit
A post-project review
A benefit review
A decision gate
7.w: A project audit gives independent assurance that governance and processes are being applied correctly.

7.q: A defect is found that stops key features working and will push delivery beyond the time tolerance agreed with the sponsor. How should the project manager treat it?
o: As a risk, because it might affect the project later
As a change request, because the scope has now altered
As an issue, as it has occurred and breaches tolerance
As a constraint, because it now limits the design
7.w: The defect has already happened and breaches the agreed time tolerance, so it is an issue to be logged, assessed and escalated to the sponsor.

n.0: A risk is uncertain and in the future, whereas this defect is already affecting delivery.
n.1: The scope has not been changed; a change request may follow from the agreed resolution, but the problem itself is an issue.
n.3: A constraint is a limit set on the project, not a problem that has arisen during it.

7.q: After a prototype is built it undergoes several tests to confirm it meets the client's requirements; which process is this part of?
o: Risk management activity
Quality assurance of processes
Quality control of outputs
Change management activity
7.w: Quality control includes testing outputs to confirm they meet the required standards and client expectations.

7.q: A project's main server crashes during a product launch. What should the project manager do first?
o: Replace the server without recording what happened
Log the issue and assess its impact on the project
Escalate the problem straight to the project sponsor
Cancel the launch until the server is restored
7.w: The first step is to formally log the issue and assess its impact so that an informed decision on the response can be made.

7.q: Understanding that a team is at Tuckman's storming stage, how should a project manager use this insight?
o: By helping resolve conflict and clarifying roles and goals
By disbanding the team and starting again
By assuming the team is fully mature and self-managing
By stepping back entirely and giving no direction
7.w: At the storming stage, conflict emerges, so the leader should facilitate resolution and clarify roles and objectives.

7.q: In the context of project management, how is a 'procurement strategy' best defined?
o: A matrix assigning internal team members to each work package
The overall approach to obtaining goods and services from suppliers
A record of the threats and opportunities affecting suppliers
A schedule showing when each supplier's work will take place
7.w: A procurement strategy sets out the overall approach a project will take to acquiring the goods and services it needs.

7.q: What is a key limitation of using email as a communication method?
o: It is the most suitable channel for urgent decision-making
It is not actually a written form of communication
It lacks tone and non-verbal cues, so it can be misread
It always ensures an immediate two-way exchange of views
7.w: Emails can be misinterpreted because they carry no tone of voice or body language.

7.q: A project audit examines whether the team followed agreed processes. What is the main purpose of carrying one out?
o: To assess adherence to agreed policies, procedures and governance
To assign blame to individuals for the project's problems
To plan the scope of work for the next project phase
To approve the final invoice submitted by the suppliers
7.w: A project audit checks whether project activities have complied with internal and external standards and governance requirements.

7.q: A cost breakdown structure (CBS) most directly supports which of the following financial activities on a project?
o: Setting out the responsibilities held by each stakeholder
Assigning individual tasks to named members of the team
Estimating, budgeting and monitoring the project's costs
Monitoring the project's risks and its open issues
7.w: A CBS provides a structured breakdown of cost that underpins estimating, budgeting and ongoing cost monitoring for control.

7.q: A project board rejects a change after assessment shows high cost for limited benefit. What does this demonstrate about change control?
o: It speeds up delivery through early implementation
It removes the need for any stakeholder input
It ensures that only beneficial changes are implemented
It supports uncontrolled changes to the project scope
7.w: Change control applies formal evaluation so the project is protected from changes that are unnecessary or harmful to its objectives.

7.q: When applying resource smoothing to a schedule, which constraint must always be respected?
o: The risk register must be cleared of all entries before smoothing starts
The available float must not be exceeded, so the completion date is protected
The project sponsor must approve each individual resource change first
The stakeholder analysis must be fully revised before smoothing begins
7.w: Resource smoothing works only within available float; the critical path and the project end date must remain unchanged.

7.q: You manage the day-to-day activities of a project, control its risks and ensure deliverables are completed on time. Which role are you performing?
o: Project team member
Project manager
Product owner
Project sponsor
7.w: The project manager runs the project day to day, managing time, cost, quality and coordination of the work.

7.q: What is a primary benefit of producing regular project progress reports for the sponsor?
o: They replace the project's risk register entirely
They remove the need to engage with project stakeholders
They finalise the agreed scope of the project
They inform sponsor decisions and enable timely intervention
7.w: Regular reports give the sponsor visibility of status, risks and deviations, supporting informed decisions and proactive corrective action.

7.q: Staff using a newly delivered finance system report confusion over some features and ask for more training. What is the most appropriate project response?
o: Log the feedback and assess the options for supporting the users
Disregard the request because the project has already closed
Escalate the concern straight to the governance board
Amend the business case to add the requested features
7.w: End user feedback should be acknowledged and addressed through support, training or further improvement to aid successful adoption.

7.q: Which of the following is NOT a standard step in the issue resolution process?
o: Analysis
Closure
Rescheduling
Identification
7.w: Rescheduling may be a consequence of resolving an issue but is not itself a formal step in the issue resolution process, which runs from identification to closure.

7.q: Several related projects are managed together to improve customer service and maximise value. What are they collectively part of?
o: A portfolio
A business case
A programme
A risk register
7.w: A programme is a group of related projects managed in a coordinated way to deliver benefits not available from managing them individually.

7.q: A project team includes members who only work part-time on the project. Which leadership challenge does this most likely create?
o: They will never need any direction from the project manager
Their limited availability may conflict with their other duties
They will always prioritise the project above all other work
They automatically remove all risk from the project
7.w: Part-time members split their time, so availability clashes with their other duties are a common challenge.

7.q: Which of the following correctly lists the main activities of a typical configuration management process?
o: Concept, definition, deployment, transition and benefits
Identification, analysis, response, review and closure
Planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit
Initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and closure
7.w: A typical configuration management process comprises planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit.

7.q: Infrastructure is delivered using a linear model while customer-facing features are developed and adjusted during delivery. What is this model called?
o: Extended
Agile
Hybrid
Waterfall
7.w: Mixing sequential and iterative components within one project is the defining characteristic of a hybrid life cycle.

7.q: Which outcome would a well-run quality management approach be expected to deliver?
o: A guarantee that no risks will ever materialise
A permanent freeze on the project's approved budget
Deliverables that reliably conform to their specifications
An automatic increase in the size of the project team
7.w: Effective quality management produces deliverables that reliably conform to their specifications.

7.q: An agile team forecasts remaining effort by extrapolating from its established average sprint velocity. Which estimating method does this represent?
o: Parametric estimating
Three-point estimating
Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
7.w: Applying a known unit rate, such as story points per sprint, to extrapolate a total is a form of parametric estimating.

7.q: A developer implements a requested change without anyone first analysing its effect on scope, time, cost, quality and risk. Which change control stage should have carried out that analysis?
o: Post-implementation review
Benefits review
Configuration audit
Detailed evaluation
7.w: Detailed evaluation assesses the impact of a proposed change on scope, time, cost, quality, risk and benefits so that a recommendation can be made.

n.0: A post-implementation review is not a stage of the change control process, and it would come too late.
n.1: A benefits review checks whether planned benefits are being realised, usually after the project.
n.2: A configuration audit checks items against their requirements and records; it does not assess proposed changes.

7.q: Without any schedule, a team is unsure which tasks to start and when. Which core purpose of scheduling is being demonstrated by its absence?
o: Recording configuration items under version control
Establishing the sequence and timing of activities
Defining the acceptance criteria for quality
Approving the project's overall business case
7.w: Scheduling establishes the order and timing of activities; without it, the team cannot know what to do when.

7.q: Midway through delivery, a steering group relies on progress reports to make decisions. Which benefit of reporting does this best illustrate?
o: It replaces the project's governance arrangements
It enables informed, timely decision-making
It guarantees the project finishes ahead of time
It removes all risk from the project entirely
7.w: Progress reporting gives stakeholders timely, accurate information, enabling informed decisions and effective control.

7.q: Which statement most accurately expresses the difference between a project and business-as-usual?
o: Business-as-usual has a defined end point, while projects continue indefinitely
Projects are delivered by a permanent team, while business-as-usual is not
Projects deliver defined change, while business-as-usual sustains current operations
Business-as-usual delivers unique outputs, while projects avoid any change
7.w: Projects create change and specific deliverables, whereas business-as-usual keeps existing services running.

7.q: An organisation with strong risk management is more likely to achieve its project objectives. Why is this the case?
o: Risk management removes the need for a project sponsor
Uncertainty is actively managed, improving the chance objectives are met
Risk management guarantees delivery below the approved budget
Risk management removes every possible threat before it can occur
7.w: Actively managing uncertainty improves the likelihood that the project's objectives are achieved.

7.q: How can a leader who communicates a clear and compelling vision of the goal influence team performance?
o: It removes the need to communicate progress to stakeholders
It reduces the clarity of individual responsibilities within the team
It can raise motivation and a sense of purpose, improving performance
It guarantees the project will finish ahead of its schedule
7.w: A clear, compelling vision gives the team purpose and motivation, which tends to improve its performance.

7.q: A project manager is drafting a communication plan. Which content should it include to ensure messages reach the right people?
o: The risk register, showing each risk owner and planned response
The work breakdown structure and the detailed activity schedule
Stakeholders, methods, frequency and communication responsibilities
The supplier evaluation criteria and the timetable for receiving tenders
7.w: A communication plan sets out who receives information, what and why, how and how often it is shared, and who is responsible for sharing it, so messages reach the right people.

n.0: Risk owners and responses are recorded in the risk register, not the communication plan.
n.1: The WBS and activity schedule plan the work itself; they do not set out how information reaches stakeholders.
n.3: Supplier evaluation criteria and tender timetables belong in the procurement strategy.

7.q: Which of the following statements best describes a milestone?
o: A scheduled event marking a key point, with zero duration
An activity with a defined duration and assigned resources
A period of contingency added to protect the end date
A document that lists every risk facing the project
7.w: A milestone is a significant point or event in the schedule and, unlike an activity, has no duration.

7.q: According to the APM, a project is best understood as a unique, transient endeavour undertaken primarily to achieve which of the following?
o: Coordinated benefits realised across several linked projects
Steady outputs delivered through repeatable routine tasks
Balanced returns from a managed collection of investments
Planned objectives that bring about beneficial change
7.w: A project is a unique, transient endeavour undertaken to achieve planned objectives, defined in terms of outputs, outcomes or benefits.

7.q: What key benefit does effective scheduling provide to a project manager?
o: Improved levels of motivation across the project team
Easier negotiation with influential project stakeholders
Reduced financial risk within the project business case
Clarity on task dependencies and the overall project duration
7.w: Scheduling makes dependencies visible and establishes how long the project will take, supporting sound planning and control.

7.q: A project manager creates an organisational breakdown structure (OBS). What is the main purpose of this tool?
o: To record the project's detailed work breakdown structure
To show the reporting relationships and lines of authority
To define the project's risks and their planned responses
To set out the methods used to communicate with stakeholders
7.w: An OBS sets out the project's organisational hierarchy, showing roles, reporting relationships and lines of authority.

7.q: Issue management differs from risk management chiefly because it deals with what?
o: The measurement of benefits after handover
The decomposition of deliverables into work packages
Problems that have already arisen and now need resolving
Uncertain events that have not yet happened
7.w: Issue management addresses problems that have already occurred, whereas risk management handles uncertain future events.

7.q: At handover a customer claims the product is unacceptable while the team believes it is complete. Which reference best resolves this dispute?
o: The procurement strategy
The communication plan
The risk register
The agreed success criteria
7.w: Pre-agreed success criteria give an objective standard against which acceptance at handover can be judged, resolving such disputes.

7.q: Members of a team with mixed experience are in conflict over task ownership. Which leadership challenge does this represent?
o: Slow approval cycles within governance
Inadequate quality assurance activity
Undefined roles and unclear expectations
Poor negotiation during procurement
7.w: Conflict over ownership usually signals unclear roles, and it is the leader's task to clarify expectations and responsibilities.

7.q: A sponsor wants the flexibility to refine requirements as user needs emerge. Which life cycle is better suited, and why?
o: Linear, because it freezes the scope right from the start
Iterative, because it removes the need for any planning
Iterative, because it supports evolving scope through continuous feedback
Linear, because it copes best with high levels of uncertainty
7.w: An iterative life cycle is designed to accommodate changing requirements, allowing scope to evolve through continuous feedback.

7.q: Why are success criteria considered at the start, during and at the handover of a project rather than only once?
o: To ensure they remain relevant and are used to steer and finally judge the project
To increase the number of governance gates the project must pass through
To transfer ownership of the criteria to a different stakeholder each time
To allow the project budget to be revised at each of the three points
7.w: Revisiting success criteria across the life cycle keeps them relevant and ensures they both guide delivery and provide the final measure of success.

7.q: During a project review, the sponsor asks for an overview of the project's current risks and how each is being managed. Which document should the project manager present?
o: The business case
The product breakdown structure
The project schedule
The risk register
7.w: The risk register is the central record of identified risks, their assessed severity, planned responses and current status, making it the correct document for reviewing how risks are being managed.

8.q: Which estimating method is most suitable for a project with high uncertainty in its early planning stage?
o: Analytical estimating
Parametric estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
8.w: Analogous estimating gives rough early estimates based on prior projects when detail is minimal and uncertainty is high.

8.q: Midway through planning, a team realises part of the scope is fixed and part is unclear. Why might a hybrid life cycle suit them?
o: It replaces the need for a project manager to coordinate the work
It combines predictable planning with adaptive delivery within one project
It lets them skip defining any requirements until the very end
It ensures no changes will ever be requested during delivery
8.w: A hybrid life cycle accommodates both fixed and evolving work by combining plan-driven and adaptive approaches in one project.

8.q: After stakeholder analysis, the project manager groups stakeholders for communication purposes. Why is this important?
o: It removes low-priority stakeholders from the project records
It establishes distinct categories of project risk
It creates a new reporting hierarchy within the project team
It tailors communication and engagement methods to each stakeholder type
8.w: Grouping stakeholders lets communication be made relevant, timely and appropriate to each group's level of involvement.

8.q: Against what standard should a project deliverable's quality ultimately be judged in practice?
o: The total budget that was spent on producing it
The requirements and needs it was created to satisfy
Its ranking against rival products in the marketplace
The number of premium features it happens to contain
8.w: Quality is judged against the requirements and needs the deliverable was created to satisfy, not cost or market position.

8.q: Which of the following is an example of the risk response known as avoidance?
o: Removing a high-risk feature from the project's scope entirely
Accepting the possibility of a small delay to final delivery
Buying insurance to cover possible damage to project equipment
Increasing the budget to cope with late supplier deliveries
8.w: Avoidance removes the threat completely, for example by taking the risky element out of scope.

8.q: How does understanding stakeholders' interests through analysis improve project communication?
o: It ensures only good news is ever shared with stakeholders
It enables messages to be shaped to each group's needs and concerns
It removes the need to consider how messages are received
It allows the same generic message to be issued to everyone
8.w: Knowing each group's interests allows communications to be shaped to their needs, supporting more effective engagement.

8.q: What does the estimating funnel primarily illustrate about project estimates over time?
o: The number of estimates required reduces to a single figure at the start
Costs always fall steadily throughout the life cycle
Accuracy improves and tolerance ranges narrow as more becomes known
Estimates become less reliable as the project progresses
8.w: The estimating funnel shows that estimate accuracy improves and tolerance ranges narrow as more detailed information becomes available.

8.q: In what way does unclear authority within a project team present a leadership challenge?
o: It can cause delays and disputes over who makes decisions
It increases the speed of every decision that is made
It removes the need for a project sponsor
It boosts accountability throughout the whole team
8.w: Unclear authority creates confusion and hesitation over decision-making, reducing efficiency and eroding trust.

8.q: Why does a risk require a different management response from an issue?
o: A risk is owned by suppliers and an issue by customers
A risk is recorded but an issue is deliberately ignored
A risk affects benefits while an issue never does
A risk needs planned responses in case it occurs; an issue needs action now
8.w: A risk is managed through planned responses ahead of time, whereas an issue has occurred and requires immediate resolution.

8.q: Which of the following statements best defines the term 'benefits management' in a project context?
o: The production and testing of the project's outputs before handover
The control of changes to the project's approved scope baseline
The scheduling of tasks so the project finishes by its agreed deadline
The identification, planning, tracking and realisation of a project's benefits
8.w: Benefits management is the identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of the benefits a project is intended to deliver.

8.q: Naming the person accountable for issuing each project report is which part of a communication plan?
o: The frequency of the communication
The responsibility, or sender, for the communication
The medium of the communication
The purpose of the communication
8.w: Identifying who issues each message defines the responsibility, or sender, attribute of the communication plan.

8.q: A project team uses the RACI model to assign responsibilities. Which type of tool are they using?
o: An organisational breakdown structure
A work breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A product breakdown structure
8.w: RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) is a common form of responsibility assignment matrix used to clarify roles.

8.q: At the start of a project a team decides the naming conventions, tools and responsibilities for managing controlled items. Which configuration management activity is this?
o: Verification audit
Identification
Status accounting
Configuration planning
8.w: Configuration planning establishes how items will be managed, including conventions, tools and responsibilities.

8.q: Which characteristic best distinguishes a hybrid life cycle from other project life cycles?
o: It follows one rigid sequence with no scope for iteration
It postpones all delivery until every requirement is agreed
It deliberately combines plan-driven and adaptive methods in one approach
It relies solely on adaptive methods with no fixed structure
8.w: The defining feature of a hybrid life cycle is its deliberate combination of plan-driven and adaptive methods within a single project.

8.q: A project manager uses a milestone to record the formal approval of the completed design phase. What does this milestone provide?
o: A checklist of quality requirements
An overview of team responsibilities
A schedule marker that shows progress
A register of the project stakeholders
8.w: A milestone marks a significant scheduled event, such as a phase completion or approval, providing a clear indicator of progress.

8.q: What is a common disadvantage of relying on face-to-face communication in a project?
o: It can incur higher costs through travel and scheduling
It is too formal to be used in iterative environments
It limits the opportunities for participants to give feedback
It reduces the level of trust between team members
8.w: Although effective for building trust, face-to-face communication can be costly and time-consuming to arrange.

8.q: Why is delivering far beyond the agreed requirements not necessarily a sign of quality?
o: Quality is unrelated to the requirements set for the deliverable
Quality always improves whenever more features are added
Quality is about meeting requirements, so over-delivery can waste resources
Quality is measured solely by how much is delivered
8.w: Since quality means conformance to requirements, delivering beyond them (gold plating) adds no quality and can waste resources.

8.q: What is a key difference between resource levelling and resource smoothing?
o: Levelling adjusts quality, whereas smoothing adjusts the cost
Levelling may extend the end date, whereas smoothing does not
Levelling applies only to agile, whereas smoothing is linear
Smoothing adds team members, whereas levelling removes them
8.w: Levelling resolves over-allocation by delaying activities and may extend the end date. Smoothing moves activities only within their float, so the end date does not change.

n.0: Neither technique adjusts quality or cost; both reschedule activities against resource availability.
n.2: Both techniques can be used in any type of life cycle.
n.3: Neither technique is about adding or removing people; both move activities in time.

8.q: Beyond audience, method and frequency, which further detail strengthens a communication plan?
o: The detailed cost breakdown for each work package
The named owner of each risk in the risk register
A means of gathering feedback from recipients
The supplier's internal reporting lines
8.w: Including a feedback mechanism makes communication two-way, confirming that messages have been received and understood as intended.

n.0: The cost breakdown belongs to budgeting and the CBS, not the communication plan.
n.1: Risk owners are recorded in the risk register, not the communication plan.
n.3: A supplier's internal reporting lines are its own affair; the plan covers the project's audiences and channels.

8.q: On a project, what distinguishes genuine communication from merely transmitting information to a group of recipients?
o: The volume of information contained in the message
The seniority of the person sending the message
The choice of digital rather than printed channels
The receiver's feedback confirming the message is understood
8.w: Feedback that confirms the message has been understood turns one-way transmission into genuine, effective communication.

8.q: A linear project fixes its deployment baseline once at the outset. How is the iterative equivalent best described by comparison?
o: Set only after the final product has been delivered
Re-baselined progressively as each iteration completes
Abandoned entirely because iterative work needs no baseline
Fixed once and never revisited after approval
8.w: In an iterative life cycle the deployment baseline evolves and is re-established as successive iterations refine the solution, unlike the single fixed baseline of a linear project.

8.q: An issue has occurred within a project. Which process is used to resolve it?
o: Configuration management
Change control
Issue management
Risk management
8.w: Issue management is the structured process for recording, assessing and resolving problems once they have occurred.

8.q: Why is the sponsor, rather than the project manager, held accountable for the business case throughout the project?
o: Because the sponsor produces the detailed cost estimates used in delivery
Because the sponsor owns the investment and is answerable for its benefits
Because the sponsor writes the technical specification of the product
Because the sponsor manages the project's day-to-day activities and tasks
8.w: The sponsor owns the investment and is accountable for realising its benefits, which is why the business case sits with them, not the project manager.

8.q: Which of the following best explains the distinction between change control and configuration management?
o: Change control evaluates proposed changes, and configuration management ensures approved changes are correctly implemented
Change control tracks scheduling milestones, and configuration management carries out product testing
Change control plans the use of resources, and configuration management defines the project team's roles
Change control manages procurement, and configuration management handles the project's budget reporting
8.w: Change control is the gatekeeper that assesses and approves changes; configuration management ensures approved changes are applied and maintained.

8.q: Which of the following statements best describes what is meant by a 'project'?
o: A temporary endeavour undertaken to deliver a defined and unique output
An ongoing operation undertaken to sustain routine business functions
A continuous process undertaken to provide day-to-day customer support
A permanent department established to deliver repeatable services
8.w: A project is a unique, transient endeavour with a defined beginning and end, undertaken to deliver specified objectives.

8.q: Why does describing a project as 'transient' matter when defining what a project actually is?
o: It guarantees the work produces identical repeated outputs
It shows the work will never involve any external suppliers
It signals the work has a defined start and finish
It confirms the work will always exceed its planned budget
8.w: Transience means a project has a defined beginning and end, unlike the continuous nature of operational business-as-usual work.

8.q: How does agreeing the success criteria at the outset help to secure early stakeholder buy-in to a project?
o: It lets each stakeholder pursue their own personal project goals
It removes the need to prepare a formal business case
It secures procurement discounts from the preferred suppliers
It aligns stakeholder expectations with the agreed project objectives
8.w: Involving stakeholders in setting success criteria aligns their expectations with the project's objectives from the start, encouraging commitment.

8.q: An agile team reviews scope at the start of each sprint and updates priorities from user feedback. How does this reflect iterative scope management?
o: The deliverables are set upfront and reviewed only monthly
The product evolves through ongoing review and stakeholder input
The team proceeds without defining any scope at all
The scope is fixed at the start and is never revisited
8.w: In iterative projects the scope evolves as work progresses, guided by continual review and stakeholder feedback.

8.q: As soon as a problem is confirmed to be affecting the project now, where is it first recorded in the resolution process?
o: In the business case during escalation
In the risk register during analysis
In the issue log at the identification stage
In the benefits plan at closure
8.w: A confirmed issue is first recorded in the issue log as part of the identification stage of the process.

8.q: A communication plan states that weekly status reports go to the steering group, issued by the project coordinator. Which attributes does this define?
o: The audience, method, frequency and responsibility for the information
The probability, impact and response owner for a risk
The severity, priority and closure date for an issue
The supplier, contract value and delivery date for procurement
8.w: It specifies what is communicated, to whom, how often and by whom, all of which are standard contents of a communication plan.

8.q: Which statement best describes the difference in timing between an issue and a risk?
o: An issue is a future possibility, whereas a risk is a current event
An issue is a current or past event, whereas a risk is a future possibility
Both an issue and a risk describe events that may occur in future
Both an issue and a risk describe events that have already occurred
8.w: An issue is a present or past event requiring resolution, while a risk is an uncertain event that has not yet occurred.

8.q: On an iterative software project, which stakeholder of the project management plan represents the users and owns and prioritises the requirements?
o: The project sponsor
The team leader
The governance board
The product owner
8.w: On iterative projects the product owner represents the business and users, owns and prioritises the backlog of requirements, and accepts or rejects completed work.

n.0: The sponsor owns the business case and approves the plan, but does not prioritise the detailed requirements.
n.1: A team leader organises the delivery work; they do not own the requirements on behalf of users.
n.2: The governance board gives direction and makes key decisions at gates, not day-to-day prioritisation.

8.q: Which of the following is a genuine benefit of regular progress reporting to the project manager?
o: It provides early warning of emerging variances
It removes the requirement to hold a baseline
It guarantees stakeholders will never raise issues
It eliminates the need to manage project risks
8.w: Regular reporting highlights variances early, allowing corrective action before problems escalate.

8.q: Warehouse staff who will operate a new inventory system daily are asked to test a prototype and give feedback. Which role are they performing?
o: Project manager
Project sponsor
Product owner
End users
8.w: End users are the people who will work with the project's deliverables day to day and can give practical feedback.

8.q: When should a project risk normally be formally closed?
o: At the very start of the project's initiation stage
When it is no longer relevant or has been fully addressed
Only after the post-project review has taken place
As soon as it has first been identified by the team
8.w: A risk is closed once it no longer poses a threat or opportunity, whether through response or expiry.

8.q: Which of the following would typically be discussed during a post-project review?
o: Lessons learned and performance against objectives
Plans for procuring brand new suppliers
Estimates for the costs of a new product
