Detailed technical rework of the product
8.w: Post-project reviews cover overall performance, stakeholder feedback and lessons learned to inform future projects.

8.q: What is the main output produced by the quality planning process on a project?
o: A project closure report
A project risk register
A change control log
A quality management plan
8.w: The quality management plan sets out how quality will be defined, managed and verified throughout the project.

8.q: Why might a project manager include milestones within a project schedule?
o: To remove the need for a formal project management plan
To guarantee that the project finishes ahead of schedule
To provide clear checkpoints for monitoring and reporting progress
To increase the total number of activities shown on the plan
8.w: Milestones give recognisable checkpoints against which progress can be monitored and reported to stakeholders.

8.q: A new data protection regulation takes effect during your design phase. Which analysis would help you understand its implications for the project?
o: A lessons-learned report
PESTLE analysis
A RAID log
Monte Carlo simulation
8.w: PESTLE assesses how external legal and political factors, such as new regulation, may affect the project.

8.q: What is meant by 'quality' in the context of a project?
o: Delivering outputs that meet the agreed requirements and are fit for purpose
Providing the most technically advanced solution available
Meeting customer expectations regardless of the agreed scope
Completing every task well ahead of its planned deadline
8.w: Quality is defined as meeting the specified requirements and ensuring the output is fit for its intended purpose.

8.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of quality assurance on a project?
o: Providing confidence that the processes can deliver the required quality
Inspecting and correcting individual defective deliverables
Giving objective, independent evidence about how the work is done
Checking that the agreed processes are being followed
8.w: Inspecting and correcting individual deliverables is quality control; assurance is process-focused and provides confidence.

8.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of a project milestone?
o: To track the unresolved risks within the project
To assign specific tasks to individual project team members
To measure product quality against the baseline specification
To mark a significant point or achievement within the schedule
8.w: Milestones are zero-duration events that flag key points such as phase completions or major approvals within the schedule.

8.q: A project manager wants to know whether current progress is ahead of or behind plan. Which tool most directly supports this?
o: The business case
The stakeholder matrix
The schedule
The risk register
8.w: The schedule provides the time baseline against which actual progress is measured, showing whether work is ahead of or behind plan.

8.q: How is the purpose of project management best distinguished from simply completing tasks?
o: It concentrates solely on cost, disregarding time and quality entirely
It assigns tasks randomly and reviews the results only at closure
It coordinates work purposefully to meet objectives within agreed limits
It focuses only on producing outputs, ignoring objectives and constraints
8.w: Project management purposefully coordinates work to meet objectives within agreed constraints, going beyond merely finishing individual tasks.

8.q: A project manager is developing a cost breakdown structure (CBS) for a project. What is the main purpose of this structure?
o: To record the issues and lessons learned during delivery
To break the deliverables down into manageable packages of work
To set out the reporting lines that exist between team members
To identify and track the costs of the project's individual components
8.w: A CBS breaks the project's costs down against its components, giving the project manager a structured basis for budgeting and cost control.

8.q: A PMO analyst finds that three portfolio projects are reporting schedule delays and inconsistent risk data. What is the most appropriate PMO action?
o: Replace the affected project managers without delay
Compile the performance data and escalate the trends to governance
Cancel the three projects that are reporting delays
Take over delivery responsibility for the projects
8.w: The PMO monitors and reports performance trends so that governance bodies can make informed decisions.

8.q: A configuration management plan is produced during initiation. What does this plan typically include?
o: A list of the approved external procurement providers
Roles, responsibilities, item tracking methods and audit schedules
The benefits realisation strategy for the whole project
A detailed cost breakdown of each individual task
8.w: The configuration plan defines the framework for managing items, including who is responsible, how items are tracked, and when audits occur.

8.q: Why are estimates at the top of the estimating funnel less accurate than those produced later?
o: Because the risk register has not yet been created
Because detailed scope and task data are not yet available
Because all projects rely on top-down budgeting at that point
Because agile approaches avoid planning at that stage
8.w: Early estimates rest on assumptions and high-level inputs because the detailed scope and work breakdown structure do not yet exist.

8.q: What is the result of a leader clearly aligning team tasks with the overall project objectives?
o: Increased scope creep across the project
Reduced accountability within the team
Less involvement from key stakeholders
Greater focus and improved team performance
8.w: When people understand the purpose of their work, motivation and focus increase, improving results.

8.q: During an induction session, how would you best explain to a trainee what the term 'project management' means?
o: The application of processes, methods, skills and knowledge to achieve specific project objectives
The ongoing balancing of an organisation's investments against its available resources
The grouping of related projects so that benefits are delivered beyond individual efforts
The continuous administration of repetitive tasks to sustain everyday business performance
8.w: Project management is defined as the application of processes, methods, skills, knowledge and experience to achieve the project's objectives; the other options describe operations, programme and portfolio management.

8.q: Which of the following activities would appear within an extended life cycle but not within a standard one?
o: Approving the deployment baseline before delivery begins
Reviewing whether forecast benefits have been realised in operational use
Defining the project's scope during the concept phase
Producing the detailed project management plan
8.w: Reviewing realised benefits after handover is characteristic of the extended life cycle, which continues beyond delivery of the outputs.

8.q: Which two elements together characterise a risk when it is first defined on a project?
o: Its uncertainty of occurring and its potential effect on objectives
Its exact cost and its confirmed completion date
Its assigned owner and its reporting frequency
Its approval status and its version number
8.w: A risk combines uncertainty of occurrence with a potential effect on objectives, unlike a certainty or fixed fact.

8.q: A project manager must define 'configuration management' for a new starter. Which description is correct?
o: The formal process for requesting and approving changes to scope
The technical and administrative control of a project's deliverables and their versions
The identification and engagement of the project's stakeholders
The evening out of resource demand across the schedule
8.w: Configuration management is the technical and administrative control of deliverables, their status and their versions.

8.q: Which sequence best represents the stages of a typical risk management process?
o: Logging, escalation, resolution and reporting
Identification, assessment, response and closure
Planning, execution, monitoring and closure
Concept, definition, delivery and handover
8.w: A typical risk management process runs from identification, through assessment (analysis) and response, to closure.

8.q: During delivery, which task most directly reflects what a project team member is responsible for?
o: Championing the project at senior board level
Approving the project's business case before work starts
Completing assigned work packages to the required standard
Deciding whether the project should proceed past each gate
8.w: Project team members are responsible for carrying out the assigned work packages and producing outputs to the required standard.

8.q: A linear project fixes all deliverables before work starts, while an iterative project adapts them over time. What does this show about scope management?
o: Iterative projects carry out no planning before delivery
Linear projects are inherently less reliable than iterative ones
Iterative projects manage scope incrementally as understanding grows
Iterative projects fail to define their scope at all
8.w: Iterative projects manage scope in increments, refining it as understanding of the requirements improves.

8.q: How does a cost breakdown structure (CBS) help a project manager with tracking project costs?
o: By allocating a named team member to each individual task
By linking a cost to each element of the project's scope
By listing the decision gates set throughout the project
By recording the lessons learned from earlier projects
8.w: The CBS links costs to defined elements of scope, allowing the project manager to track actual spending against the budget.

8.q: Which aspect of a team does Belbin's model primarily help a project manager to understand?
o: The order in which risks should be addressed
The reporting lines shown in an organisational breakdown structure
The stages a team moves through as it matures
The balance of behavioural roles within the team
8.w: Belbin's model describes behavioural team roles, helping the manager build a balanced and effective team.

8.q: A newly formed team works entirely remotely and rarely meets in person. Which leadership challenge is most likely to arise?
o: Preventing the team from using any digital tools
Building rapport and trust without regular face-to-face contact
Ensuring members never communicate outside meetings
Guaranteeing that no member needs any direction
8.w: Remote working makes building rapport and trust harder without the regular face-to-face contact that fosters it.

8.q: A sponsor wants a quick, high-level estimate based on a similar project completed last year. Which method should be used?
o: Analytical estimating
Parametric estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
8.w: Analogous estimating uses data from a comparable past project to give a fast, high-level estimate.

9.q: One event may happen next quarter; another has already stopped work today. How should each be classified respectively?
o: Both as risks, since both affect the project
The first as a risk; the second as an issue
The first as an issue; the second as a risk
Both as issues, since both are recorded
9.w: A possible future event is a risk; one that has already occurred and stopped work is an issue.

9.q: In an iterative life cycle, what term is commonly used for the short, time-boxed development cycles the team works in?
o: Milestones
Gateways
Phases
Sprints
9.w: Sprints are the short, time-boxed iterations used to deliver increments of the product in iterative and agile approaches.

9.q: Which statement best captures what the process of communication actually involves during project delivery?
o: Issuing instructions that require no response
A two-way process of conveying and confirming meaning
Recording information for audit purposes only
Broadcasting updates to as many people as possible
9.w: Communication is a two-way process of conveying information and confirming that its meaning has been received and understood.

9.q: Which statement correctly describes a project issue?
o: It is a problem now exceeding tolerances and needing escalation
It is an uncertainty relating to the project business case
It is a scheduled event that is recorded in the risk register
It is a constraint that has been imposed by the project sponsor
9.w: An issue is a problem that is breaching, or about to breach, delegated tolerances, so it is escalated to the sponsor to agree a resolution.

n.1: An uncertainty is a risk; an issue is certain because it is already happening.
n.2: Issues are unplanned and recorded in the issue log, not scheduled events in the risk register.
n.3: A constraint is a limit placed on the project, not a problem that has arisen.

9.q: A benefit review finds that only part of the forecast savings were achieved; what should the organisation do?
o: Analyse why the benefits were not fully realised
Treat the whole project as a complete failure
Cancel all future benefit reviews entirely
Ignore the results because the project has closed
9.w: The gap between expected and actual benefits should be analysed and captured as lessons learned for future projects.

9.q: Why might a project manager create a product breakdown structure before a work breakdown structure?
o: To create a baseline budget for the project
To determine the cost of the individual tasks first
To assign team members to their roles early on
To establish a shared understanding of the product to be delivered
9.w: The PBS clarifies the deliverables required, giving a shared understanding of the product so that the WBS can be built around it.

9.q: Within a business case, the expected benefits are weighed against which two factors to justify proceeding with the investment?
o: The costs and the risks of the investment
The schedule bar chart and the communication plan
The test scripts and the recorded defect logs
The team structure and the individual reporting lines
9.w: A business case justifies the investment by weighing the expected benefits against its costs and risks; schedules, team structures and test records are not what the benefits are balanced against.

9.q: A colleague argues that assembling the same standard kitchen unit for the thousandth time is a project. Why is this description incorrect?
o: The task is too small to require any planning
The task is not managed by a project sponsor
The task is repetitive and lacks any uniqueness
The task carries no financial cost to complete
9.w: Repetitive, routine work lacks the uniqueness that characterises a project and is better classed as business as usual.

9.q: How does an organisational breakdown structure (OBS) contribute to the successful delivery of a project?
o: It sets out the risk responses required to address external threats
It clarifies reporting relationships and lines of management control within the project
It defines the sequence in which project activities will be performed
It assigns costs to each of the project’s deliverables and work packages
9.w: An OBS depicts the project’s reporting lines and accountabilities, supporting governance and management control of the work.

9.q: A project manager omits the senior user when producing the project management plan. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Delivery costs will automatically increase tenfold
The sponsor loses all accountability for benefits
The plan may not reflect genuine user requirements
The schedule will no longer require any milestones
9.w: The senior user represents those who will use the output; omitting them risks a plan that does not reflect real user needs.

9.q: A general election is called midway through a public infrastructure project. Why would a PESTLE analysis be helpful in this situation?
o: It defines the contractual process for resolving disputes
It helps assess how the political change may affect the project
It calculates the project's critical path far more precisely
It improves the breakdown of the technical design work packages
9.w: PESTLE helps the project manager identify and assess external factors, here political change, that may affect the project, feeding risk identification and planning.

n.0: Dispute resolution is set out in the contract, not in a PESTLE analysis.
n.2: Critical path analysis comes from the schedule network, not from PESTLE.
n.3: Breaking down design work is done through the WBS, not PESTLE.

9.q: What is the primary purpose of a milestone in a project schedule?
o: To mark the completion of a significant stage or deliverable
To calculate the total float available on the critical path
To allocate the project budget across its work packages
To record the daily effort logged by each team member
9.w: A milestone is a key point in the schedule, usually marking the completion of a significant deliverable or stage; it has zero duration.

9.q: A possible delay to delivery is identified because a supplier may be overloaded with work. How should this be classified?
o: As a milestone, because it marks a delivery point
As a risk, because it has not yet happened
As a change request, because the plan must alter
As an issue, because it is affecting the project now
9.w: The delay is only a possibility that has not yet occurred, so it is an uncertain future event and is therefore a risk.

9.q: A team leader gives regular, specific and constructive feedback to team members. What effect is this most likely to have?
o: It reduces the leader's own accountability for the outcome
It fixes the project's deployment baseline permanently
It helps members improve and sustains strong performance
It removes the need for any recognition or reward
9.w: Regular constructive feedback helps team members learn and adjust, sustaining and improving their performance.

9.q: Why might a project manager use models such as Belbin and Tuckman when developing a team?
o: To understand team roles and development stages and adapt their approach
To calculate the project's overall budget
To replace the need for a project schedule
To decide the project's procurement strategy
9.w: Such models help the manager understand behavioural roles and development stages, so leadership can be adapted to support the team.

9.q: Which of the following is a core responsibility of the project manager?
o: Chairing the project steering group
Owning the business case and justifying the benefits
Authorising the release of project funding
Managing delivery against time, cost and quality
9.w: The project manager is responsible for delivering the project within the agreed constraints of time, cost and quality.

9.q: Stakeholder analysis identifies a group as both highly influential and highly resistant. What should the engagement strategy prioritise?
o: Reassigning them to a different project
Proactively engaging them to understand concerns and seek alignment
Sending them brief updates by email only
Ignoring them unless they choose to escalate
9.w: Highly influential yet resistant stakeholders must be actively engaged to reduce opposition and secure buy-in.

9.q: Which of the following is a key responsibility of the project sponsor?
o: Writing the detailed work breakdown structure
Maintaining the day-to-day project issue log
Producing the project communication plan
Approving key decisions and owning the business case
9.w: The sponsor provides direction, owns the business case and approves the major decisions and investment for the project.

9.q: In project scheduling terms, what does the technique of time boxing primarily help a project team to control?
o: The elapsed time devoted to a piece of work
The quality standards applied to the outputs
The reporting format used for progress updates
The number of stakeholders that are consulted
9.w: Time boxing controls the elapsed time given to a piece of work by fixing the period and flexing scope within it.

9.q: Which outcome would a project manager most reasonably expect from completing a PESTLE analysis?
o: A finalised critical path for the project schedule
A complete list of the project's internal stakeholders
A clearer view of the external context influencing the project
A signed-off configuration baseline for all deliverables
9.w: PESTLE produces an understanding of the external context; the other outputs come from scheduling, configuration and stakeholder work.

9.q: A trade union group with a history of resisting change is assessed as high influence and high interest. What is the most suitable engagement strategy?
o: Delay engagement until executive approval is granted
Withhold project documents from them
Assign a junior team member to manage the relationship
Engage them early and involve them in planning to address concerns
9.w: High-influence, high-interest stakeholders should be engaged closely and early to reduce resistance and gain their input.

9.q: A colleague expects the communication plan to contain the project's full risk scores. Why is this misplaced?
o: Risk scores are never recorded anywhere on a project
Risk scores must replace the audience details in the plan
Risk scores are the sole content of a communication plan
Risk scores belong in the risk register, not the communication plan
9.w: Risk scores belong in the risk register; a communication plan records audience, method, frequency and responsibility.

9.q: Which sequence best represents how work flows through a typical iterative project life cycle?
o: Delivery carried out entirely before any planning takes place
Concept, definition, delivery and handover performed once only
A one-off design followed immediately by closure
Repeated cycles of build and review until the product is complete
9.w: Iterative work progresses through repeated build-and-review cycles until the solution is complete.

9.q: A sponsor is frustrated that the concept-stage estimate later changed. How does the estimating funnel explain this?
o: Estimates are fixed once given and any change indicates poor planning
The original estimate should never have been shared with the sponsor
Early estimates are broad and refine as project detail increases
Later estimates are always less reliable than earlier ones
9.w: The funnel shows that early estimates are indicative and legitimately refine as more detail emerges through the life cycle.

9.q: What is the key difference between parametric estimating and analogous estimating when producing a project estimate?
o: Parametric uses historical per-unit data, while analogous compares whole completed projects
Parametric suits iterative projects only, while analogous suits linear projects only
Parametric is used only at handover, while analogous is used only at initiation
Parametric relies on expert opinion, while analogous applies statistical formulae
9.w: Parametric estimating scales historical cost or duration per unit, whereas analogous estimating draws on the overall data from a similar completed project.

9.q: A change initiative coordinates a new system, revised processes and staff training so that together they transform customer service. What is this?
o: Project management
Programme management
Portfolio management
Benefits realisation management
9.w: Coordinating related projects so that combined they deliver a shared transformation is programme management.

9.q: What takes place during the closure stage of the issue management process?
o: Assignment of ownership to a responsible person
Formal verification and sign-off that the issue is resolved
Implementation of the corrective action needed
Initial logging of the issue when it is first identified
9.w: Closure confirms and records that the issue has been resolved, with the necessary verification and sign-off completed.

9.q: Which of the following best describes the role of a change control board on a project?
o: A group authorised to review and approve or reject scope changes
An external panel appointed to audit the project's accounts
A board that owns the business case and secures project funding
A team that implements approved changes and updates configuration items
9.w: A change control board is the body with the authority to evaluate change requests and decide whether they are approved, rejected or deferred.

n.1: Auditing the accounts is an independent assurance activity, not the evaluation of change requests.
n.2: Owning the business case and securing funding is the sponsor's role, not the change control board's.
n.3: Implementing changes and updating configuration records is done by the project team after a decision; the board makes the decision.

9.q: What is the main benefit of extending a project life cycle to include a benefits realisation phase?
o: It allows the requirements to be changed freely throughout the delivery phase
It reduces the number of governance decision gates the project must pass through
It confirms that the intended benefits are actually achieved once the outputs are in use
It fixes the delivery budget more tightly before any work is allowed to begin
9.w: Adding a benefits realisation phase lets the organisation confirm the forecast benefits are delivered in operational use.

9.q: An iterative project has a loosely defined baseline at the outset. How is performance typically monitored?
o: By means of a post-project audit only
Through frequent comparison against the evolving baseline
Against a fixed plan set at project initiation
Against the supplier contract terms only
9.w: In iterative life cycles performance is monitored against a baseline that is reviewed and updated regularly.

9.q: Quality control is often described as a 'detective' activity. What does carrying it out actually involve?
o: Inspecting and testing outputs to find any that do not meet requirements
Auditing whether the correct processes are being followed consistently
Setting the quality standards and tolerances before the work begins
Planning how quality will be managed across the whole project
9.w: Quality control is detective: it inspects and tests outputs to find non-conformances, unlike planning or assurance which are preventive.

9.q: When a project team lists what is 'in scope' and 'out of scope', which discipline are they applying?
o: Procurement management
Risk management
Quality management
Scope management
9.w: Defining what is in and out of scope sets the boundaries of the project's work, which is a core part of scope management.

9.q: Which activities make up the benefits management process?
o: Updating the work breakdown structure
Identifying, quantifying, tracking and reviewing value
Planning the project's procurement routes
Monitoring individual team member performance
9.w: Benefits management systematically identifies, quantifies, tracks and reviews value to ensure it is realised.

9.q: A project manager reviews a checklist of common threats to spot what could affect the project. Which stage of risk management is this?
o: Risk response
Risk analysis
Risk identification
Risk closure
9.w: Using prompt lists or checklists to find potential threats is part of the risk identification stage.

9.q: A manager arranges a peer review of the team's process to confirm agreed procedures are being followed; what is this an example of?
o: Quality assurance of processes
Scope verification activity
Change control process
Quality control of outputs
9.w: Quality assurance confirms that project processes are being followed correctly so that quality outputs are produced.

9.q: What is a benefit of using instant-messaging platforms within a project team?
o: They support fast, informal exchanges that aid quick decisions
They remove the need for the team to hold any meetings
They create a formal, legally binding record of decisions
They eliminate the difficulties caused by differing time zones
9.w: Instant messaging enables rapid, informal collaboration, which is useful for fast-moving issues.

9.q: What is regarded as the primary objective of communication within a project?
o: To remove the need for formal project documentation
To ensure that all identified project risks are mitigated
To support shared understanding among the project's stakeholders
To reduce the total number of meetings that are held
9.w: The purpose of communication is to ensure that everyone involved understands the relevant information and expectations.

9.q: Which statement correctly matches a breakdown tool to its use?
o: The CBS structures project costs, while the OBS structures the teams
The CBS assigns responsibilities for each project work package
The RAM aggregates all project costs into reportable categories
The OBS lists the risks that could affect project delivery
9.w: The CBS organises costs and the OBS organises the people resources, each serving a distinct planning purpose.

9.q: A lead engineer resigns unexpectedly, work on their deliverables stops, and the delay now exceeds the schedule tolerance agreed with the sponsor. How is this best classified?
o: An assumption
A dependency
An issue
A risk
9.w: The event has happened and breaches the agreed tolerance, so it is an issue that must be escalated to the sponsor for a resolution.

n.0: An assumption is something taken to be true for planning purposes, not a problem that has occurred.
n.1: A dependency is a link between activities or deliverables, not an event that has happened.
n.3: A risk is uncertain and in the future; the resignation and delay have already happened.

9.q: What is the primary purpose of quality control within a project?
o: To document the interests of the stakeholders
To confirm outputs conform to specifications through inspection
To produce a detailed and costed business case
To manage the contracts held with suppliers
9.w: Quality control verifies outputs through inspection, measurement and testing to confirm they meet requirements.

9.q: A review finds a project failed to deliver key elements because scope was poorly controlled. Which process should have prevented this?
o: Scope management
Resource scheduling
Communication planning
Risk analysis
9.w: Scope management ensures that all required deliverables are identified, defined and controlled throughout the project.

9.q: A manager selects and prioritises all of an organisation's projects to align with strategy and balance resources. What are they managing?
o: A single workstream
A portfolio
A programme
A delivery team
9.w: Portfolio management selects and prioritises projects and programmes across the organisation to meet its strategic objectives.

9.q: Which of the following is true of a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM)?
o: It defines the physical components of the final product
It determines the order of the project's activities
It links organisational roles to the project's tasks
It sets the level of influence held by each stakeholder
9.w: A RAM matches roles from the OBS to the tasks in the WBS, ensuring each activity has clearly assigned responsibility.

9.q: How does an issue differ from a risk?
o: An issue is uncertain; a risk is certain to occur
An issue affects only cost; a risk affects only time
An issue is always positive; a risk is always negative
An issue has already happened; a risk may happen in future
9.w: By definition an issue has already occurred, whereas a risk is an uncertain future event.

9.q: Early feedback on a new IT system shows that users are confused by the interface wording. Which action best supports successful adoption?
o: Reassign the technical work to the users themselves
Transfer the concern to the sponsor as a risk
Arrange further end user engagement and training
Update the project governance plan
9.w: Engaging and training end users after handover helps embed the solution and maximise the benefits realised.

9.q: How can frequently changing project priorities pose a leadership challenge when managing a team?
o: They automatically improve the team's confidence
They simplify communication with stakeholders
They can cause confusion and resistance if not communicated clearly
They remove the need for any scope reviews
9.w: Shifting priorities can disrupt momentum and buy-in, so strong leadership and clear communication are needed to realign the team.

9.q: Which statement best defines quality control in a project setting?
o: Training the team members in various quality methods
Planning how the required quality will be assured
Monitoring results to check they comply with standards
Identifying lessons learned from earlier quality issues
9.w: Quality control monitors and inspects project outputs to confirm they meet the specified requirements.

9.q: The team agrees and carries out corrective actions to remove the effect of a logged issue. Which stage of issue resolution does this describe?
o: Logging
Escalation
Resolution
Identification
9.w: Agreeing and carrying out the corrective actions to deal with the issue is the resolution stage.

9.q: When resource smoothing is applied and the project end date must not change, what typically happens to the schedule?
o: Non-critical tasks are rescheduled within their float to even out resource demand
All tasks are moved onto the critical path so delivery is faster
The scope of several tasks is reduced to lower overall resource demand
Additional staff are recruited so that the work can be shortened
9.w: Smoothing keeps the end date fixed by rescheduling non-critical activities within their available float to level resource demand.

9.q: Which of the following statements most accurately captures the central focus of the quality planning process?
o: Escalating issues that exceed the manager's authority
Reviewing whether agreed procedures are being applied
Measuring completed products against their specification
Identifying the quality criteria and the means to satisfy them
9.w: Quality planning focuses on defining the quality criteria to be met and the methods and resources used to satisfy them.

9.q: Which of the following is most likely to make it harder for a project manager to develop team cohesion?
o: Frequent changes in team membership
Consistent leadership behaviour over time
Early engagement in team development
Shared values and common goals
9.w: Frequent membership changes disrupt trust and progress through the team's development stages, making cohesion harder to build.

9.q: What is the main purpose of a deployment baseline once a project moves into delivery?
o: To record the names and contact details of all project stakeholders
To provide a fixed reference against which progress and variance are measured
To capture the lessons learned for use on future similar projects
To list the recognised standards that the deliverables must comply with
9.w: The deployment baseline serves as the benchmark for monitoring performance and identifying variances during delivery.

9.q: Which of the following would not normally form part of a deployment baseline?
o: The planned resource requirements
The agreed delivery schedule
The defined scope of work
Benefits realisation tracking
9.w: Benefits realisation occurs after delivery within the extended life cycle and is not part of the deployment baseline.

9.q: Which of the following statements best describes the main outcome of carrying out critical path analysis on a project?
o: It documents the change requests raised during delivery
It assigns responsibilities using a RACI matrix
It calculates the financial return forecast for the project
It identifies which activities directly control the project duration
9.w: Critical path analysis identifies the activities that control the overall duration, distinguishing them from those with float.

9.q: The design specification is uniquely labelled and changes to it are authorised, but nobody has kept a record of its current version or change history. Which configuration management activity has failed?
o: Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
9.w: Status accounting records and reports the current status, version and change history of each configuration item. Without it, nobody can tell which version is current.

n.1: A verification audit checks that items match their requirements and records; it does not keep the records itself.
n.2: Identification uniquely labels the items, and the stem says the specification is already labelled.
n.3: Planning decides how items will be identified, controlled, recorded and audited; the failure here is in the recording itself.

9.q: A dispersed team relies on email for a complex negotiation, which drags on for days. Which disadvantage of email does this illustrate?
o: It provides an instant, written audit trail
It automatically records the sender and time
It handles nuanced, back-and-forth discussion poorly
It reaches large numbers of recipients at once
9.w: Email is asynchronous and text-based, making it poorly suited to nuanced, real-time negotiation that benefits from immediate two-way dialogue.

9.q: Why do estimates near the bottom of the estimating funnel carry tighter tolerances than earlier ones?
o: The sponsor insists later estimates match the first figure given
Fewer stakeholders remain involved to challenge them
Contingency has been deliberately stripped out of them
More detailed scope and information are available by that stage
9.w: As the project progresses, greater scope definition and information reduce uncertainty, allowing tighter estimate tolerances.

9.q: A team implemented a change straight after it was requested. Which stage should have evaluated its full effect on cost, time and quality?
o: Logging the initial change request
Closing the completed project
Implementing the approved change
Detailed evaluation of the change
9.w: Detailed evaluation assesses the impact of the change on cost, time, quality, scope, risk and benefits, so the appropriate authority can make an informed decision.

n.0: Logging captures the request; it does not evaluate its effects.
n.1: Closure is not a stage of change control and comes far too late to evaluate a change.
n.2: Implementation is what the team did too early; it does not evaluate the change.

9.q: A schedule shows that two activities must finish before testing can begin. What does this illustrate?
o: A task dependency
A work breakdown structure
A project benefits map
A scope verification check
9.w: A dependency exists where one activity cannot start until another is complete; scheduling identifies these relationships.

9.q: A team defines the improvements expected, then tracks whether they materialise after go-live. Which discipline are they applying?
o: Critical path analysis
Benefits management
Quality control
Configuration management
9.w: Defining expected improvements and tracking their realisation is the essence of benefits management.

10.q: Which review focuses mainly on capturing lessons learned to improve future projects?
o: A benefit review
A post-project review
A decision gate
A configuration audit
10.w: A post-project review captures lessons learned so future projects can benefit from them.

10.q: During which stage of the risk management process are risks assessed for probability and impact so that they can be prioritised?
o: Identification
Analysis
Response
Closure
10.w: Risk analysis assesses probability and impact, enabling risks to be prioritised for attention.

10.q: A communication plan records why each message is sent, such as 'to maintain sponsor confidence'. Which attribute is this?
o: The purpose of the communication
The frequency of the communication
The recipient of the communication
The medium of the communication
10.w: Recording the reason a message is sent defines its purpose within the communication plan.

10.q: A product owner postpones a planned feature so that a newly requested customer feature can be developed first. What does this decision demonstrate?
o: Formal change control escalation
Project risk avoidance
Backlog prioritisation and refinement
Project closure planning
10.w: Reordering the backlog in response to customer value is a core product owner responsibility.

10.q: What is a downside of relying too heavily on informal verbal communication?
o: It guarantees that information is always communicated accurately
Agreements may go undocumented and be misunderstood later
It removes the need for any defined escalation routes
It substantially increases the volume of project documentation
10.w: Informal verbal communication relies on memory, so agreements can be forgotten or misunderstood unless confirmed in writing.

10.q: Which of the following would you typically expect to find within a procurement strategy?
o: Preferred contract types and the criteria for evaluating suppliers
The models used to support development of the project team
The amount of float available on each of the project's tasks
The categories used to prioritise the identified project risks
10.w: A procurement strategy defines how suppliers will be chosen, including preferred contract types and evaluation criteria.

10.q: At what point in the estimating funnel is a detailed bottom-up estimate typically produced?
o: Immediately after the contract is signed
When the full scope and work breakdown structure are available
After the post-project review is complete
At the initial project concept stage
10.w: Bottom-up estimating requires a detailed scope and work breakdown structure, which are available mid-to-late in the funnel.

10.q: What is a benefit of using email for communication on a project?
o: It is always a fully secure and completely private channel
It provides a written trail that can be referred to later
It functions without any need for an internet connection
It removes the need to hold project meetings altogether
10.w: Email creates an auditable written record that is easy to store and refer back to throughout the project.

10.q: Which process ensures that changes to scope are formally approved so they do not adversely affect quality or budget?
o: Risk escalation
Resource allocation
Team briefing
Change control
10.w: Change control assesses, authorises and integrates proposed changes so the impact on quality, cost and time is controlled.

10.q: A product fails final testing because of a missed requirement, so the project manager formally records and recognises it. Which stage of issue resolution is this?
o: Closure
Analysis
Identification
Resolution
10.w: Formally recording and recognising the issue is the identification stage, which begins the resolution process.

10.q: Which of the following is a common tool used to carry out quality assurance?
o: Product inspections of the deliverables
Change request logs for the project
Issue registers maintained by the team
Peer reviews of the processes used
10.w: Peer reviews of processes support quality assurance by verifying that agreed procedures are being applied.

10.q: What is the role of configuration management once a scope change has been formally approved?
o: To carry out the approval of the original change request
To redefine the project's chosen life cycle for delivery
To ensure the approved change is applied and documented correctly
To communicate the approved change out to the stakeholders
10.w: After change control approves a change, configuration management ensures it is implemented, recorded and reflected in the controlled products.

10.q: A project is defined as being undertaken to achieve planned objectives. In what terms are these objectives usually expressed?
o: Outputs, outcomes or benefits
Departments, functions or teams
Profits, dividends or returns
Routine, repeated daily tasks
10.w: Planned objectives on a project are defined in terms of outputs, outcomes or benefits, distinguishing a project from operations, programmes and portfolios.

10.q: Which of the following would you typically expect to find within a well-structured business case?
o: The project closure checklist and lessons learned
Options analysis, investment appraisal and success criteria
A record of every risk the project has identified
A detailed daily stand-up schedule for the team
10.w: A business case typically sets out the options considered, the investment appraisal and the success criteria that justify proceeding.

10.q: A customer is uncertain whether the final deliverable meets their original needs. Which early activity would most likely have prevented this?
o: Holding more frequent team retrospective meetings
Assigning additional members to the project team
Producing a more detailed schedule as a Gantt chart
Defining the success criteria collaboratively with the customer
10.w: Agreeing success criteria with the customer early ensures a shared, documented understanding of the intended outcome.

10.q: Which of the following would typically fall outside the responsibilities of the project manager?
o: Tracking and reporting project progress
Managing the day-to-day project risks
Approving strategic funding and benefits realisation
Leading the creation of the project schedule
10.w: Approving funding and owning benefits realisation are sponsor responsibilities, not those of the project manager.

10.q: Who should ideally take part in a post-project review to make it effective?
o: The finance department only, reviewing the project’s final costs
Key stakeholders, project team members and project leadership together
The project manager alone, without input from any other party
External consultants only, engaged specifically for the review
10.w: A broad group of those involved in the project should contribute so that the review provides a balanced and comprehensive evaluation.

10.q: A chart divides a project into 'design', 'build' and 'test', each split into smaller work packages. Which structure is this?
o: Product breakdown structure
Work breakdown structure
Cost breakdown structure
Responsibility assignment matrix
10.w: A work breakdown structure decomposes the total work of a project into progressively smaller, manageable work packages.

10.q: On a supplier contract with staged deliverables, milestones are frequently used to trigger which of the following events?
o: Staged payments once agreed points are reached
The identification of new project-level risks
Automatic changes to the project's agreed scope
The levelling of over-allocated project resources
10.w: Milestones mark agreed points of achievement and are often used contractually to trigger staged payments on their completion.

10.q: How does the risk analysis stage differ from the risk identification stage?
o: Identification assesses probability and impact, whereas analysis simply lists the risks
Both stages only find risks, but identification also selects the responses
Both stages only assess impact, but analysis is done after closure
Identification finds the risks, whereas analysis assesses their probability and impact
10.w: Identification discovers and records the risks; analysis then evaluates each one's probability and impact so they can be prioritised.

10.q: Why is a cost breakdown structure (CBS) usually derived from the work breakdown structure (WBS) on a project?
o: Because the WBS identifies the work that then needs to be costed
Because the CBS defines the thresholds for approving scope change
Because the WBS controls how stakeholders are communicated with
Because the CBS sets the reporting line for each work package
10.w: The WBS defines the work to be done, and the CBS attributes cost estimates to those components, so the two structures align.

10.q: Why should the project sponsor be actively involved as a stakeholder in agreeing the project management plan?
o: Because the sponsor performs the day-to-day delivery tasks
Because the sponsor tests each deliverable for quality
Because the sponsor owns the business case and provides direction
Because the sponsor writes each work package personally
10.w: The sponsor owns the business case and provides strategic direction, so their agreement ensures the plan aligns with the organisation's aims.

10.q: How does a hybrid life cycle mainly differ from a purely iterative life cycle?
o: A hybrid is always shorter and cheaper than an iterative approach
A hybrid keeps predefined linear phases for part of the work, unlike a fully iterative approach
A hybrid abandons all upfront planning in favour of continuous change
A hybrid never gathers stakeholder feedback during delivery
10.w: Unlike a purely iterative life cycle, a hybrid retains fixed linear phases for the parts of the work that are stable.

10.q: A project manager regularly shares the vision, encourages initiative and supports team learning. Which leadership quality is being demonstrated?
o: Inspirational leadership that aligns the team
Purely reactive decision-making
Detailed cost and budget management
A command-and-control leadership style
10.w: Inspirational leaders energise and align their teams around a shared sense of purpose.

10.q: In Belbin's model, which team role is most focused on turning ideas and plans into practical, workable actions?
o: Implementer
Resource Investigator
Plant
Monitor Evaluator
10.w: The Implementer is disciplined and reliable, converting concepts and plans into organised, practical action.

10.q: An estimate is produced by applying a known average cost per feature module across the number of modules required. Which method is being used?
o: Parametric estimating
Three-point estimating
Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
10.w: Parametric estimating scales a known cost-per-unit value by the quantity of units to reach a total estimate.

10.q: What is an advantage of using physical, paper-based communication in certain project environments?
o: It prevents any form of miscommunication from occurring
It gives a tangible, lasting record that does not depend on technology
It is always the quickest way to distribute project information
It guarantees that recipients will actually read the information
10.w: Physical communication provides a reliable, permanent record in environments where technology access is limited.

10.q: Which of the following activities most accurately represents what project management involves when delivering a project's objectives?
o: Selecting which proposed initiatives should receive investment in each financial year
Planning, monitoring and controlling all aspects of a project to meet its objectives
Directing a coordinated set of projects to realise combined organisational benefits
Delivering identical outputs repeatedly to satisfy steady and predictable customer demand
10.w: Project management plans, monitors and controls all aspects of a project to achieve its objectives; the others describe business as usual, programme and portfolio management.

10.q: Which of the following outputs would typically result from the quality planning process?
o: A register of risks and their owners
A quality plan defining standards and responsibilities
A signed contract with a chosen supplier
A completed post-project review report
10.w: Quality planning produces a quality plan setting out the standards, methods and responsibilities for achieving quality.

10.q: A risk recorded earlier in the project has now actually happened. In project terminology, what has it become?
o: A milestone
A constraint
An issue
An assumption
10.w: When a risk materialises it becomes an issue: a problem that has occurred and now requires management action.

10.q: On a software project the team decides all deliverables must comply with a recognised standard; which aspect of quality planning is this?
o: Creating the change control procedures
Selecting the relevant quality standards
Defining the overall budget baseline
Documenting the lessons learned so far
10.w: Quality planning includes selecting the standards that will guide development and testing of deliverables.

10.q: How does an extended project life cycle differ from a hybrid life cycle?
o: Extended blends linear and iterative delivery, whereas hybrid adds operational phases
Extended adds phases after handover, whereas hybrid blends linear and iterative approaches
Both fix scope at the outset, but hybrid allows benefits to be reviewed later
Both remove the closure phase, but extended repeats delivery in short sprints
10.w: An extended life cycle lengthens the timeline to cover benefits and disposal, while a hybrid life cycle combines linear and iterative delivery approaches.

10.q: A cost estimate is produced by applying a standard cost per metre of road drawn from industry data. Which estimating method is this?
o: Parametric estimating
Expert judgement
Analogous estimating
Analytical estimating
10.w: Parametric estimating applies a known unit rate to a measured quantity, using historical or industry data.

10.q: A manager claims that project management is simply 'getting the work done'. Which correction is the most accurate?
o: It is the day-to-day running of a settled service once it has been established
It is the informal delegation of tasks to whoever happens to have spare capacity
It is the planned application of processes and skills to achieve defined objectives
It is the ongoing ranking of investments to match the organisation's overall strategy
10.w: Project management is a planned, structured application of processes and skills to defined objectives, not informal task allocation, operations or portfolio prioritisation.

10.q: A milestone marks the completion of system testing. What is its main purpose in the schedule?
o: To trigger a brand new stakeholder engagement plan
To give a checkpoint for monitoring and reporting progress
To move the project automatically into the final closure phase
To allow the risk register to be permanently archived
10.w: A milestone is a significant zero-duration event that acts as a checkpoint for monitoring and reporting progress and communicating key dates.

n.0: Reaching a milestone does not require a new stakeholder engagement plan.
n.2: Moving between phases is decided at a decision gate, not triggered automatically by a milestone.
n.3: The risk register is a living document kept up to date until the project closes.

10.q: Midway through delivery a project manager faces a trade-off between two options. How can the agreed success criteria help?
o: They remove the need to consult the project sponsor about the choice
They replace the change control process for that particular decision
They automatically approve whichever option costs the least money
They provide a reference to guide the decision towards the intended outcome
10.w: During delivery, success criteria act as a reference point that keeps decisions aligned with the project's intended outcomes.

10.q: Which group of stakeholders should contribute to a project management plan to ensure the delivered output can be operated after handover?
o: End users and operational staff
Competitors within the same market sector
Regulatory auditors external to the organisation
Members of an unrelated project's team
10.w: End users and operational staff must contribute so the plan reflects requirements needed for successful operation and handover.

10.q: Beyond simply naming suppliers, what does a well-considered procurement strategy aim to achieve for a project?
o: The detailed daily task schedule for the internal project team
Value for money and a sound, consistent approach to sourcing external work
A guarantee that no external suppliers will be needed at all
The elimination of every risk associated with using suppliers
10.w: A procurement strategy aims to secure value for money through a sound, consistent approach to sourcing external work.

10.q: How does the deployment baseline typically differ between a linear and an iterative life cycle?
o: Linear fixes time and cost; iterative fixes scope and quality
Linear has no baseline at all; iterative baselines the whole project
Both fix scope at definition and control it with change control
Linear fixes scope for the whole project; iterative lets it flex
10.w: In a linear life cycle the baseline is set for the whole project at the end of definition, with scope fixed and changes formally controlled. In an iterative life cycle time and cost are fixed and scope flexes, with detailed baselines set time box by time box.

n.0: This reverses the iterative approach, where time and cost are fixed and scope flexes.
n.1: Linear projects set a full deployment baseline at the end of definition.
n.2: Only the linear life cycle fixes scope at definition; iterative scope is refined and re-prioritised.

10.q: If change control operated without any configuration management, what problem would most likely arise?
o: No change could ever be authorised because there would be no approval route
The project would be unable to identify any of its stakeholders
Approved changes might be made without the resulting versions being recorded or traceable
The business case could not be written before delivery began
10.w: Without configuration management, authorised changes would not be recorded, so version control and traceability of items would be lost.

10.q: Which statement best defines project management as understood within the APM Body of Knowledge?
o: The application of processes, methods and knowledge to achieve defined project objectives
The routine monitoring of daily operational activities within a permanent department
The forecasting of resource requirements across the whole organisation each year
The assignment of repetitive tasks to staff within ongoing business functions
10.w: Project management is the application of processes, methods, knowledge, skills and experience to achieve the project objectives within agreed constraints.

10.q: A learner is confused between a programme and a portfolio. Which statement correctly distinguishes one from the other?
o: A portfolio always contains related projects, whereas a programme contains only unrelated ones
A portfolio delivers a single output, whereas a programme balances strategic investment
A portfolio's projects need not be related, whereas a programme's projects share a common objective
A portfolio is temporary, whereas a programme continues indefinitely as business as usual
10.w: A programme's projects share a common objective, while a portfolio groups projects and programmes that need not be related, selected to meet strategic goals.

10.q: Which of the following best describes the escalation step in the issue resolution process?
o: Recording the lessons learned after the issue is resolved
Logging the issue formally when it is first identified
Raising the issue beyond project authority for a decision
Assigning the issue to a stakeholder for resolution
10.w: Escalation is used when an issue exceeds the project manager's authority and requires a decision from a higher level of governance.

10.q: Before delivery, a sponsor and team use a product breakdown structure to agree exactly what will be produced. What does this most help avoid?
o: Misunderstandings about which deliverables are in scope
The need to schedule any of the work
The requirement to assign any responsibilities
The production of a project management plan
10.w: Agreeing the deliverables via a PBS creates a shared understanding of scope, reducing later disputes about what is in or out.

10.q: A project manager reviews risks at every team meeting rather than only at the outset. What benefit does this ongoing review bring?
o: It guarantees that no risks will materialise during delivery
It removes the need to maintain a risk register
It transfers all accountability for risks to the sponsor
It provides early warning of new and changing risks so responses stay current
10.w: Reviewing risks regularly gives early warning of new and changing risks, keeping planned responses current throughout delivery.

10.q: What is the primary responsibility of the product owner in an agile environment?
o: Producing the detailed technical documentation
Monitoring the delivery team's performance metrics
Prioritising the product backlog according to business value
Negotiating and managing the supplier contracts
10.w: The product owner ensures the most valuable features are delivered by managing and prioritising the backlog.

10.q: In an iterative life cycle, how is the deployment baseline usually treated for each time box?
o: Scope and quality are fixed, while time and cost flex
Time and cost are fixed, while the scope flexes
Scope and cost are fixed, while the time flexes
Time and scope are fixed, while the cost flexes
10.w: In an iterative life cycle time and cost are fixed for each time box and scope flexes, with lower-priority requirements deferred. Quality standards are protected, not traded away.

n.0: This reverses the iterative approach: scope is what flexes, and time and cost are fixed.
n.2: Time is fixed in a time box; the end date does not move.
n.3: Scope is not fixed in an iterative life cycle, and cost is fixed rather than flexing.

10.q: A project manager introduces an issue log and escalation route. What purpose does this primarily serve?
o: It records the estimated cost of each work package
It sets the acceptance criteria for the final product
It ensures current problems are captured and dealt with promptly
It forecasts uncertain events that may occur later
10.w: An issue log and escalation route ensure current problems are captured and resolved promptly, the aim of issue management.

10.q: A supplier requests a change to a component because of a manufacturing constraint, so the project manager raises a change request. Which process decides whether the change is accepted?
o: Change control
Scheduling optimisation
Risk escalation
Scope definition
10.w: Change control is the formal process used to evaluate a change request and decide whether the change to scope should be accepted.

10.q: A project's main server crashes, halting all progress. How should this event most accurately be classified?
o: As a risk, because it may affect the schedule
As a constraint, because it limits progress
As a milestone, because it marks an event
As an issue, because it has already occurred
10.w: The crash has already happened and is affecting delivery, so it is an issue to be managed and resolved rather than an uncertain future risk.

10.q: By the end of the concept phase in a linear life cycle, what is normally produced?
o: A signed acceptance certificate confirming benefits realised
An outline business case recommending whether to proceed
The fully tested product ready for operational handover
A detailed configuration management status report
10.w: The concept phase concludes with an outline business case that supports the decision on whether to continue into definition.

10.q: What must happen before a change can be applied to a project's baseline?
o: Declaration of a change freeze across the project
Renegotiation of the relevant supplier contract
Deletion of the affected configuration item
Formal approval through the change control process
10.w: No change should be applied to a baseline until it has been formally assessed and approved through change control.

10.q: Midway through delivery a client requests several enhancements to the agreed product. What should the project manager do first?
o: Submit a formal change request so the impact can be assessed and reviewed
Add the changes into the next stage of work in order to save time
Amend the configuration records directly to reflect the new requirements
Update the work breakdown structure and begin the changes straight away
10.w: Under change control, a formal change request must be raised and its impact assessed and approved before any change is implemented.

10.q: A project manager wants confidence that both the process and the product will meet requirements. Which discipline provides this?
o: Quality management
Risk management
Configuration management
Benefits management
10.w: Quality management addresses both process and product, giving confidence that requirements will be met.

10.q: During a gate review of the business case, what is the project manager's main role?
o: To determine the project's strategic alignment
To provide updates on justification and delivery feasibility
To chair the project governance board
To formally approve continued investment in the project
10.w: The project manager supplies delivery information that helps the sponsor present the case for continuation; approval rests with governance.

10.q: How do milestones assist a project manager specifically when reporting the status of a project to its stakeholders?
o: They set out the communication methods to be used for each group
They record the full technical specification of each project deliverable
They list the individual costs of every one of the project's activities
They provide clear reference points showing whether delivery is on track
10.w: Milestones give clear, recognisable reference points against which achievement can be reported, showing stakeholders whether delivery is on track.

10.q: How can a leader who addresses conflict within the team promptly and fairly influence performance?
o: It restores focus and cooperation, protecting performance
It transfers responsibility for morale to the sponsor
It removes the need to hold any team meetings
It guarantees that the project will meet its budget
10.w: Handling conflict promptly and fairly restores cooperation and focus, protecting the team's performance.

10.q: Partway through a project the team resolves its own disagreements and no longer needs frequent check-ins. Which Tuckman stage is this?
o: Performing
Norming
Forming
Storming
10.w: A performing team is mature and self-regulating, working effectively with minimal supervision from the leader.

10.q: In terms of stakeholder support, what benefit does a well-maintained communication plan bring to the project manager?
o: Well-informed stakeholders are more likely to remain engaged and supportive
Stakeholders no longer need to be consulted on any decisions
The project becomes exempt from its scheduled governance reviews
The project's approved budget is automatically increased in size
10.w: Timely, relevant communication keeps stakeholders informed and engaged, which helps sustain their support for the project.

10.q: A deliverable is completed on time and within budget, yet the customer is dissatisfied. Which success criteria were most likely overlooked?
o: Measures reflecting the schedule's baseline dates
Measures reflecting the supplier payment terms
Measures reflecting the project's risk tolerance
Measures reflecting user acceptance and satisfaction
10.w: Success criteria should capture user acceptance and satisfaction, not only time and cost, so that the outcome genuinely meets the customer's needs.

11.q: Why does having an agreed communication plan actually save the project manager effort during the delivery of a project?
o: It removes the need to maintain a detailed underlying schedule
It automatically resolves all of the disagreements between stakeholders
Communication decisions are agreed once rather than repeated each time
It eliminates every one of the project's risks well in advance
11.w: With communications agreed in advance, the project manager avoids reconsidering who, what, when and how for each message, saving effort.

11.q: On a new IT project you estimate the effort for your work packages, build the agreed components and report progress to the project manager. Which role are you performing?
o: Project sponsor
Product owner
End user
Team member
11.w: Project team members carry out the work and deliver work packages, provide specialist input and estimates, and report progress to the project manager.

n.0: The sponsor owns the business case and governs the project; they do not build components.
n.1: The product owner prioritises requirements and accepts work; they do not build the components.
n.2: End users provide requirements, help test and adopt the outputs; they do not build them.

11.q: How does a 'risk' differ from a 'certainty' in project management terms?
o: A risk lies outside the manager's control, whereas a certainty does not
A risk concerns team behaviour, whereas a certainty concerns the sponsor
A risk involves uncertainty, whereas a certainty does not
A risk always leads to failure, whereas a certainty leads to success
11.w: The defining feature of a risk is uncertainty: it may or may not occur, unlike a certainty.

11.q: Which stakeholder is primarily responsible for ensuring that the project management plan aligns with the organisation's strategic objectives?
o: A project team member
A supplier
The project sponsor
The product owner
11.w: The sponsor owns the business case and ensures the project remains aligned with the organisation's strategic goals.

11.q: What is the primary purpose of critical path analysis in project scheduling?
o: To identify the sequence of tasks that determines the project's duration
To define the overall scope of work for the project
To establish the stakeholder communication methods
To allocate team roles and responsibilities to members
11.w: Critical path analysis identifies the longest chain of dependent tasks with zero float, which sets the minimum project duration.

11.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between progress reporting and stakeholder confidence?
o: Frequent reports remove the need for stakeholder input
Clear, honest reports build trust and transparency
Reports should be withheld to avoid raising concerns
Reporting is the main cause of project scope creep
11.w: Transparent and honest reporting keeps stakeholders informed and engaged, which builds trust and confidence in the project.

11.q: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates work that would be classified as a project?
o: Answering routine user queries on a support helpdesk each day
Processing the organisation's payroll at the end of every month
Maintaining a client's existing software system throughout the year
Implementing a new customer relationship management system over six months
11.w: A time-bounded initiative delivering a unique output, such as a new CRM system, is a project; the others are ongoing, repeatable business-as-usual tasks.

11.q: Halfway through a critical online review, the connection repeatedly drops out. Which disadvantage of virtual communication does this show?
o: It can never involve more than two participants
It always takes far longer than a face-to-face meeting
It leaves no possibility of recording the session
It depends on reliable technology and stable connectivity
11.w: Virtual communication depends on reliable technology and connectivity; technical failures can disrupt or degrade the exchange.

11.q: A project manager maintains a risk register and reviews it each week. How does this best support project success?
o: It removes all remaining assumptions from the project management plan
It allows risks to be monitored continuously and responses to be actioned
It ensures the lessons learned are all documented before work begins
It prevents any further change requests from being raised during delivery
11.w: Regular review of the risk register lets the team act on emerging threats and opportunities before they escalate.

11.q: Before delivery begins, a project manager defines the standards the outputs must meet and how conformance will be checked. Which process is this?
o: Quality assurance
Quality planning
Configuration management
Quality control
11.w: Setting the required standards and how conformance will be checked, ahead of delivery, is quality planning.

11.q: A key risk recorded in the project's risk register has now materialised. What should happen next?
o: It should be ignored because it has already been analysed
It should be closed and recorded as a completed milestone
It should be deleted from the risk register without further action
It should be reclassified as an issue and managed accordingly
11.w: Once a risk actually occurs it becomes a current problem, so it is reclassified as an issue and handled through the issue management process.

11.q: What does version control help to ensure within the configuration management process?
o: That outdated documents are clearly identified and replaced
That the project's tasks are placed in the correct sequence
That the project's procurement rules are properly followed
That the entries in the risk register are correctly prioritised
11.w: Version control ensures that only the latest approved versions of documents and products are in use, and older versions are withdrawn.

11.q: A stakeholder submits a formal request to alter a key deliverable. What is the first step in the change control process?
o: Escalate the matter straight to the project board
Implement the requested change to the deliverable immediately
Log the change request and assess its likely impact
Update the configuration baseline before any review
11.w: The first stage of change control is to log the request and assess its impact on time, cost, quality and risk before any decision.

11.q: Why are milestones useful when monitoring the ongoing performance and progress of a project?
o: They provide the deadlines by which supplier contracts must be signed
They reveal slippage by comparing planned and actual achievement dates
They remove the need for any formal progress reporting on the project
They allocate individual tasks to named members of the project team
11.w: Milestones mark key events, so comparing planned and actual dates highlights schedule slippage and emerging risk to delivery.

11.q: In a delivery approach that uses time boxing, which element is deliberately held fixed throughout the work?
o: The duration of the period allotted to the work
The full set of features that are to be delivered
The total budget that is available to the project
The size of the team that is assigned to the work
11.w: In time boxing the time period is fixed; scope is the variable that flexes so the deadline is always met.

11.q: In an extended project life cycle, at what point does the life cycle normally come to an end?
o: When the outputs are handed over to the users
When the business case is first approved
When the planned benefits have been realised
When deployment has produced all the outputs
11.w: An extended life cycle continues through adoption and benefits realisation until the benefits promised in the business case have been realised.

n.0: Handover ends transition, which is where a standard linear life cycle stops, not an extended one.
n.1: Approval of the business case happens early, at the start of the life cycle.
n.3: Producing the outputs ends deployment; transition, adoption and benefits realisation still follow.

11.q: Which statement best reflects a purpose of risk management that goes beyond simply avoiding threats?
o: It removes all uncertainty from the project
It also identifies and helps exploit potential opportunities
It guarantees the project will finish under budget
It transfers accountability for outcomes to suppliers
11.w: Risk management addresses uncertainty in both directions, seeking to exploit opportunities as well as reduce threats.

11.q: A project is undertaken to deliver an output. How is that output most accurately described?
o: A permanent departmental responsibility
A sustained operational service function
A defined product, service or result
An adaptable ongoing support mechanism
11.w: APM describes a project's output as a defined product, service or result achieved within agreed constraints.

11.q: A total cost is built up from detailed specifications and individual work package estimates. Which estimating method does this describe?
o: Analytical (bottom-up) estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
11.w: Analytical, or bottom-up, estimating aggregates detailed estimates from individual work packages to produce the overall figure.

11.q: A supplier has failed to deliver a critical component, halting project work. How should this be classified?
o: An issue, because the problem has already occurred
A milestone, because it marks a point in the schedule
An assumption, because it was expected during planning
A risk, because it might affect the project later
11.w: A problem that has already happened and is affecting the project is an issue, not a risk.

11.q: An office build is estimated by applying a known cost per square metre to the floor area. Which estimating method is being used?
o: Expert judgement
Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Parametric estimating
11.w: Parametric estimating applies a known cost per unit to a measured quantity to derive the total estimate.

11.q: A project manager decides to buy in specialist development work from an outside supplier. Which document guides this approach?
o: The change request log
The risk register
The work breakdown structure
The procurement strategy
11.w: The procurement strategy defines whether work is delivered internally or bought externally, and the criteria for doing so.

11.q: An executive secured the funding and holds overall accountability for delivering the project's benefits. Which role is being described?
o: End user
Project manager
Project sponsor
Product owner
11.w: The project sponsor owns the business case, secures funding and is accountable for the realisation of the benefits.

11.q: In a project management plan, which role is chiefly concerned with confirming that the delivered outputs are usable and meet the needs of the business?
o: The project governance board
The product owner
The delivery team members
The end users
11.w: End users use the outputs in operation, so they are best placed to confirm the deliverables are fit for purpose and meet business needs.

11.q: How does the term 'quality' differ from the term 'grade' in a project context?
o: Quality always requires the most expensive materials available
Quality is meeting requirements; grade is a category of features
Grade measures conformance, while quality ranks features by luxury
Quality means a higher grade; the two terms are identical
11.w: Quality is conformance to requirements, while grade categorises features or characteristics; a low grade can still be high quality.

11.q: Which of the following activities best reflects the sponsor's particular role in relation to the project's business case?
o: Maintaining the project's day-to-day risk and issue registers
Championing and defending the investment at senior decision-making levels
Producing the detailed schedule and resource plan for the delivery work
Testing the completed deliverables against their acceptance criteria
11.w: The sponsor champions and defends the business case at senior level; scheduling, testing and register maintenance are project manager or team responsibilities.

11.q: Why is it important to establish project success criteria during the initiation phase?
o: To remove the need to prepare a business case
To allow the project to be closed sooner
To allocate individual tasks to team members
To define clear performance expectations that guide later decisions
11.w: Defining success criteria early gives a basis for measuring progress, guiding decisions and managing stakeholder expectations.

11.q: Why is risk management considered a proactive discipline throughout the delivery of a project?
o: It anticipates and addresses uncertainty before it affects objectives
It records lessons learned solely at project closure
It focuses purely on logging issues after they occur
It only reacts once problems have already materialised
11.w: Risk management is proactive because it identifies and responds to uncertainty before it can affect project objectives.

11.q: What challenge might a project manager face when trying to build motivation in a high-pressure delivery environment?
o: The team being consistently underloaded with work
Stress and burnout reducing morale and engagement
Receiving too much interest from stakeholders
Spending excessive time on detailed planning
