11.w: Sustained pressure can lead to burnout, which the project manager must manage to keep the team effective and motivated.

11.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of scope management in a linear project?
o: Frequent reprioritisation of user stories each cycle
Continuous negotiation of scope with the stakeholders
Formal control of changes once the initial scope is defined
Dynamic delivery of requirements as they evolve
11.w: Linear projects define scope early and rely on formal change control to evaluate and manage any changes thereafter.

11.q: What is the benefit to the project manager of defining a communication frequency within the plan?
o: It ensures updates are delivered regularly and predictably
It guarantees that suppliers will meet their commitments
It allows decisions to be taken without any discussion
It removes the need to keep any project documentation
11.w: Scheduled updates create consistency and reduce ambiguity, helping to build stakeholder trust.

11.q: In quantitative risk analysis, which technique might a team use to simulate many possible risk outcomes?
o: The Delphi technique
MoSCoW prioritisation
An Ishikawa diagram
Monte Carlo simulation
11.w: Monte Carlo simulation is a quantitative technique that models many scenarios to estimate the range of likely outcomes.

11.q: What is a key difference in how deployment baselines are managed in linear versus iterative life cycles?
o: Linear projects avoid the use of baselines completely
Linear projects rely on a fixed baseline, while iterative projects expect it to evolve
Iterative life cycles set one baseline and never change it
Both approaches exclude stakeholders from creating the baseline
11.w: Linear life cycles seek stability through a fixed baseline, whereas iterative life cycles embrace an evolving one.

11.q: A construction firm pours foundations in a fixed sequence but develops the building's smart controls in short cycles. Which life cycle is this?
o: Iterative life cycle
Extended life cycle
Linear life cycle
Hybrid life cycle
11.w: Combining a linear sequence for fixed work with iterative cycles for evolving elements within one project is a hybrid life cycle.

11.q: A previously settled team is joined by several new members who are unsure of their roles and look to the project manager for direction. To which Tuckman stage has the team most likely returned?
o: Adjourning
Forming
Norming
Storming
11.w: In forming, members are polite, unsure of their roles and dependent on the leader, who should give clear direction. A big change in membership often takes a team back to this stage.

n.0: Adjourning happens when the task is complete and the team disbands.
n.2: Norming is when ways of working are agreed and the team is cohesive, which is not the case here.
n.3: Storming involves open conflict and challenge to roles; here members are uncertain and looking for direction.

11.q: A work breakdown structure is being developed for a software deployment project. What level of detail should it provide?
o: A breakdown of all the work packages needed to complete the deliverables
The roles and responsibilities of each team member
Only the financial costs linked to each task
Only the task names together with their durations
11.w: The WBS should decompose the total scope into smaller, manageable work packages that capture all the work required.

11.q: Why is effective communication considered critical to success within a project environment?
o: It allows the project manager to avoid engaging with stakeholders
It removes the need for any project documentation to be produced
It ensures all decisions are made solely by the project sponsor
It enables collaboration and alignment between the project’s stakeholders
11.w: Effective communication keeps stakeholders informed and aligned, enabling collaboration and supporting project success.

11.q: A project manager applies Tuckman and Belbin, but a colleague expects them to remove all team problems. What is the correct view?
o: The models guide team development but do not guarantee a problem-free team
The models make leadership of the team unnecessary
The models ensure the team never reaches the storming stage
The models fix the project's budget and schedule automatically
11.w: The models guide team development and role balance but do not guarantee a problem-free team; leadership is still required.

11.q: Which of the following is most likely to be a portfolio management responsibility?
o: Selecting the right mix of projects to align with strategy
Ensuring two related projects are delivered in sync
Monitoring an individual project's risk register
Defining the detailed scope for a single project
11.w: Portfolio management ensures the right projects and programmes are chosen and prioritised to meet strategic goals.

11.q: Which of the following is not normally a responsibility of an end user during a project?
o: Controlling the project budget and schedule
Taking part in user acceptance testing
Providing feedback on usability and functionality
Adopting the new system or process after handover
11.w: Controlling budget and schedule is a project management responsibility and falls outside the end user's role.

11.q: A project fails to meet its key success criteria at a gate review; what is the likely outcome?
o: New scope is added without any assessment
The project may be paused or stopped
The project budget is increased without review
The team proceeds automatically to the next stage
11.w: Decision gates allow the organisation to pause, redirect or stop a project based on its current performance and alignment.

11.q: Beyond simply sending information, what must effective project communication achieve between the parties involved?
o: A shared understanding confirmed through feedback between sender and receiver
The largest possible volume of messages distributed to everyone
A permanent written record stored for audit purposes only
A one-way flow of instructions requiring no response
11.w: Effective communication achieves shared understanding, confirmed through feedback between sender and receiver, not merely the sending of information.

11.q: The agreed, integrated plan of scope, schedule, cost, resources and quality, approved by the sponsor, against which deployment progress is measured is known as what?
o: The benefits profile
The change log
The work breakdown structure
The deployment baseline
11.w: The deployment baseline is the approved, integrated plan against which deployment progress is measured and controlled. Once approved, changes to it go through change control.

n.0: A benefits profile shows when and how benefits are expected to be realised, not the plan for delivery.
n.1: The change log records change requests and decisions; it is not the plan itself.
n.2: The WBS breaks down the work to be done, but it is only one input to the baseline.

11.q: Why does benefits management typically continue after a project has been formally closed?
o: Because outstanding project risks can only be reviewed after closure
Because many benefits are realised during operational use rather than during delivery
Because the project baseline must be recalculated once delivery ends
Because the next phase of delivery must be planned after handover
11.w: Benefits such as cost savings or improved service are usually realised once outputs are in operational use, so benefits management extends beyond project closure.

11.q: One project is linear with a fixed baseline and another is iterative with rolling planning. What difference should you expect in how change is handled?
o: The iterative project avoids making any changes
Neither project requires change control at all
Only the linear project makes use of baselines
The linear project resists change, while the iterative one embraces it
11.w: Linear life cycles rely on stability, whereas iterative life cycles accommodate change more readily through adaptive planning.

11.q: Beyond simply issuing orders, effective project leadership is best characterised by which behaviour?
o: Avoiding contact with the team to remain impartial
Issuing detailed instructions and requiring strict compliance
Focusing solely on the project's budget and schedule
Enabling and empowering people to contribute their best towards the goal
11.w: Leadership enables and empowers people to contribute their best, going beyond merely issuing orders.

11.q: A project team is discussing whether their final product meets the definition of 'quality'. Which statement best defines quality?
o: Every project risk was successfully avoided during delivery
The final cost of the product came in below the initial budget
The deliverable includes as many additional features as possible
The output meets the defined requirements and serves its intended purpose
11.w: Quality means the deliverable satisfies its agreed specifications and is suitable for its intended use.

11.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between project, programme and portfolio management?
o: Programme management replaces portfolio management in smaller organisations
Projects are managed independently of any portfolio or programme structure
Portfolio management provides strategic alignment, while programmes coordinate related change
There is no meaningful overlap between the three disciplines
11.w: Portfolio management aligns all projects and programmes to strategy, while programmes coordinate related change and projects deliver defined outputs.

11.q: At its lowest level, what does a work breakdown structure typically break the work down into?
o: Work packages that can be assigned, estimated and controlled
Individual products and their raw materials
High-level phases only, without further detail
Departments responsible for the project
11.w: A WBS decomposes work to the level of manageable work packages that can be assigned, estimated, scheduled and controlled.

11.q: In a RACI responsibility assignment matrix, what does designating a person as 'accountable' for a task signify?
o: They are ultimately answerable for the task's completion, though others may do the work
They are merely kept informed once the task has been completed
They physically carry out every element of the task themselves
They are consulted for an opinion but hold no further involvement
11.w: In RACI, the accountable person is ultimately answerable for the task, even though responsible parties may perform the work.

11.q: A finance team updates spreadsheets and processes invoices every day. How should this work most appropriately be classified?
o: Business-as-usual, because it involves regular, repeatable tasks
Business-as-usual, because it has a sponsor and a budget
A project, because it is constrained by time and cost
A project, because it is carried out by a skilled team
11.w: Regular, repeatable work that maintains an ongoing service is business-as-usual, not a project.

11.q: In configuration management, what does the term 'configuration item' typically refer to?
o: A stakeholder's preferred method of receiving communication
A deliverable or document that is placed under version control
A resource that has been assigned across several tasks
A task that lies on the project's overall critical path
11.w: A configuration item is any product, deliverable or document that is identified and controlled through the configuration management process.

11.q: A developer flags a design flaw that could delay testing if it is not addressed. How should this be managed?
o: Record it in the risk register, as it is a possible future event
Add it to the work breakdown structure as a new task
Escalate it immediately to the project sponsor for a decision
Record it in the issue register, as it has already occurred
11.w: Because the delay has not yet happened and would only occur if the flaw is not addressed, it is an uncertain future event and belongs in the risk register.

11.q: Which configuration management activity maintains records of each item's current state and its history of changes?
o: Verification audit
Identification
Configuration planning
Status accounting
11.w: Status accounting keeps the records showing the current status and change history of each configuration item.

11.q: During delivery, a team finds that the original success criteria are no longer relevant. What is the best course of action?
o: Abandon the criteria and rely on team discretion
Continue using the original criteria regardless
Replace the criteria without consulting stakeholders
Revise and formally agree the updated criteria with key stakeholders
11.w: Success criteria must stay relevant and should be updated through agreed change control involving key stakeholders.

11.q: What does passing through successive decision gates help to confirm about a project during its life?
o: That its scope can never again be altered
That it remains viable and justified before further resources are committed
That the delivery team has followed every process correctly
That all of its benefits have already been realised
11.w: Decision gates repeatedly confirm the project remains viable and justified before more resources are committed.

11.q: A quality assurance review shows that a key process is not being applied consistently; what should happen next?
o: The findings should be ignored by the team
The project should be closed down immediately
Corrective actions should be identified and implemented
The product should be delivered without change
11.w: Quality assurance identifies process shortfalls so that corrective actions can realign work with quality standards.

11.q: A diagram breaks a new aircraft into fuselage, wings and avionics, then into their sub-parts. Which structure is this?
o: Product breakdown structure
Cost breakdown structure
Work breakdown structure
Organisational breakdown structure
11.w: A product breakdown structure decomposes the final output into its major products and their component parts.

11.q: Resource smoothing evens out resource peaks by rescheduling activities within which scheduling allowance?
o: The critical path duration
The project's cost baseline
Their mandatory dependencies
Their available float
11.w: Resource smoothing reschedules activities within their available float, evening out demand without moving the end date.

11.q: A team is building a new mobile app through short development cycles with regular end-user feedback. Which life cycle is most likely being used?
o: Extended
Hybrid
Iterative
Linear
11.w: An iterative life cycle delivers in small increments and refines the product through repeated cycles of stakeholder feedback.

12.q: A project manager keeps a single document listing each risk, its owner and its planned response. What is this document?
o: The communication plan
The risk register
The quality plan
The business case
12.w: A risk register is the central record of identified risks, their assessment, owners and planned responses, supporting ongoing risk management.

12.q: Which of the following is a common responsibility of a project management office (PMO)?
o: Providing assurance and support across multiple projects
Owning and controlling the project budget
Managing the scope and deliverables of each project
Acting as the primary user of the deliverables
12.w: A PMO offers governance, assurance, reporting and consistent support across projects or programmes.

12.q: A sponsor asks why the range on the cost estimate is much narrower at the end of definition than it was at concept. What best explains this?
o: More detail became known, moving the estimate down the funnel
An arithmetic error in the original estimate was corrected
A different comparison project was used for the revised estimate
An approved change request reduced the overall project cost
12.w: The estimating funnel shows that estimates become more accurate, and their ranges narrower, as more is known about the project through the life cycle.

n.1: Correcting an error might change the figure, but it does not explain the normal narrowing of the range.
n.2: Switching comparison projects changes the basis of an analogous estimate, not its accuracy range.
n.3: A change request alters scope and cost; it does not by itself narrow the estimating range.

12.q: How can appropriately delegating authority and trusting team members influence a project team's performance?
o: It always slows delivery because decisions take longer
It removes the leader's responsibility for the results
It can increase ownership and motivation, improving output
It prevents team members from developing new skills
12.w: Appropriate delegation builds ownership and motivation, which tends to improve the team's output.

12.q: Deciding whether to use a single supplier or several competing suppliers is a decision captured within which document?
o: The communication plan
The risk register
The quality plan
The procurement strategy
12.w: Supplier relationship decisions, including single versus multiple sourcing, form part of the procurement strategy.

12.q: Stakeholder analysis shows a group of community residents to have low influence but high interest. What is the recommended approach?
o: Avoid all engagement until after delivery
Monitor them only if they raise a concern
Manage them closely and involve them in every decision
Keep them informed through regular updates and consultation
12.w: Low-influence, high-interest stakeholders should be kept informed to maintain support and prevent misinformation.

12.q: Which three methods are recognised as typical estimating approaches within project planning?
o: Levelling, smoothing and crashing estimating
Predictive, iterative and hybrid estimating
Analytical, analogous and parametric estimating
Qualitative, quantitative and residual estimating
12.w: Analytical, analogous and parametric are the standard estimating methods identified in the APM Body of Knowledge.

12.q: Head office insists on face-to-face reviews, but the project team works across four countries. Which drawback does this most clearly expose?
o: It removes all ability to read tone and body language
It leaves no record whatsoever of any decisions taken
It can only ever reach a single person at a time
It is costly and impractical to gather everyone in one place
12.w: Face-to-face meetings require people to be co-located, which is costly and impractical for a geographically dispersed team.

12.q: Which statement best describes analytical, or bottom-up, estimating as used to produce a project estimate?
o: Building a total estimate by summing the estimated costs of individual tasks
Producing a top-down figure based on the overall size of the project
Reaching a figure through repeated rounds of anonymous expert consensus
Comparing the project with a previous initiative of broadly similar scope
12.w: Analytical, or bottom-up, estimating totals the estimates for individual tasks or work packages to produce an overall project estimate.

12.q: Which description best reflects the level and focus of a project's procurement strategy?
o: A high-level plan for how a project will source what it needs externally
A list of the internal skills the project team already possesses
A log of goods received and inspected against their specifications
A detailed cost estimate for every item the project will purchase
12.w: A procurement strategy is the high-level approach to sourcing externally, not a detailed estimate, receipt log or skills list.

12.q: A sponsor asks what project management is fundamentally there to accomplish on their initiative. What is the best reply?
o: To keep the initiative running indefinitely as a routine service
To guarantee the initiative faces no risks or changes whatsoever
To deliver the initiative's objectives successfully within the agreed constraints
To maximise the number of tasks the team completes each week
12.w: The key purpose of project management is the successful delivery of the initiative's objectives within its agreed constraints.

12.q: A project manager uses a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM). What is the key benefit of using this tool?
o: It tracks the financial cost incurred against each project phase
It allocates the packages of work to their related deliverables
It shows who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed
It breaks the project schedule down into its individual tasks
12.w: A RAM, often using RACI, maps who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each task, giving clear role accountability.

12.q: Once a work breakdown structure is complete, which subsequent planning activity does it most directly enable?
o: Approving the project's business case
Estimating and scheduling the identified work packages
Selecting the project's governance board
Realising the project's long-term benefits
12.w: The WBS defines manageable work packages that can then be estimated, scheduled and assigned for control.

12.q: What is the main purpose of a decision gate within project governance?
o: To approve the contracts held with suppliers
To assess whether the project should continue
To carry out the lessons learned sessions
To delegate new work packages to the team
12.w: Decision gates provide control points where continuation of the project is reviewed against performance and objectives.

12.q: At which stage of the change control process is a change formally approved, rejected or deferred?
o: Before the change request is logged
Only once the change has been implemented
At recommendation, after the evaluation
During the transition phase exclusively
12.w: At the recommendation stage, once the change has been evaluated, the sponsor or appropriate authority decides to approve, reject or defer it.

n.0: Nothing can be decided before the request exists and has been logged.
n.1: The decision must come before implementation; otherwise the change is uncontrolled.
n.3: Change requests can arise and be decided at any point once the baseline is set, not only at transition.

12.q: According to APM terminology, a risk may have what kind of effect on project objectives?
o: Only a negative effect, never a positive one
No effect on objectives whatsoever
A guaranteed effect that is always realised
Either a positive or a negative effect
12.w: APM defines risk as covering both threats and opportunities, so its effect may be negative or positive.

12.q: A team uses a product breakdown structure (PBS) to represent the end product. What is its primary purpose in scope management?
o: To allocate costs to individual project activities
To estimate the overall schedule for the project
To define the deliverables that make up the final product
To assign team members to each project task
12.w: A PBS breaks the end product down hierarchically to define the deliverables that make up the final product.

12.q: Which of the following best defines leadership in a project context?
o: Recording risks and issues in the relevant registers
Enforcing compliance with procurement procedures
Monitoring the budget and updating the schedule
Providing vision, motivation and direction to the team
12.w: Leadership is about inspiring and guiding people towards achieving the project's objectives, rather than administering controls.

12.q: Why is risk analysis carried out before deciding on responses in the risk management process?
o: So that the project budget can be finalised and fixed
So that the responses can be chosen at random for fairness
So that every identified risk can be immediately closed
So effort can be focused on the most significant risks first
12.w: Analysis prioritises risks by probability and impact so that responses target the most significant threats.

12.q: Which situation is the strongest reason for a project to adopt a hybrid life cycle?
o: Some parts are predictable while others need flexibility
All requirements are fixed and fully understood
The product is simple, small and repetitive
The customer has minimal involvement in delivery
12.w: Hybrid life cycles are chosen when some components need firm, predictive control while others benefit from adaptive delivery.

12.q: Which of the following statements best describes what a schedule provides to those delivering a project?
o: A time-based plan of activities, dependencies and resources
A record of quality standards the outputs must meet
A list of stakeholders and their communication needs
A justification of why the project should be funded
12.w: A schedule is a time-based plan showing activities, their dependencies, durations and required resources.

12.q: Before delivering a major milestone presentation, why would a project manager consult the communication plan?
o: To review the supplier's procurement performance
To approve an outstanding change request to scope
To confirm the audience, delivery method and timing of the update
To reassess the risk thresholds and escalation triggers
12.w: The communication plan defines the who, what, how and when of key information sharing, so it confirms how the milestone update should be delivered.

12.q: Which of the following best illustrates a risk on a project?
o: The project sponsor has already resigned from their post
A key supplier has already defaulted on an agreed delivery
The team has already exceeded the budget agreed for the phase
Adverse weather could delay the construction work later in the year
12.w: Adverse weather is an uncertain future event that may delay delivery, so it is a risk; the others have already happened and are issues.

12.q: A PMO introduces a lessons learned process across all completed projects. What is the primary benefit of doing this?
o: It identifies who to blame for previous project failures
It speeds up future procurement decisions
It supports continuous improvement across the project portfolio
It justifies staff changes within the delivery teams
12.w: Capturing lessons learned helps future projects avoid repeat mistakes and adopt proven good practice.

12.q: A project manager describes a deliverable as being of 'high quality'. What does 'quality' mean in the context of a project?
o: That it meets the agreed requirements and is fit for purpose
That it was completed ahead of its planned schedule
That it includes more features than were originally specified
That it exceeds recognised industry standards for the sector
12.w: In APM terms, quality means the deliverable conforms to its agreed requirements and is fit for its intended purpose.

12.q: A sponsor asks how the team ensures their processes consistently produce quality outputs; which process is most relevant?
o: Quality assurance of processes
Procurement planning work
Quality control of outputs
Stakeholder analysis activity
12.w: Quality assurance focuses on the processes used to ensure that quality outputs are consistently produced.

12.q: Which single feature is most fundamental to something being classed as a project rather than another type of organised work?
o: It continues indefinitely without a planned end point
It is managed by a permanently established department
It generates a recurring, predictable stream of income
It is unique, producing outputs not delivered before
12.w: Uniqueness is a defining characteristic of a project; each project delivers something not produced in exactly that way before.

12.q: Why does an approach based on time boxing depend heavily on clear prioritisation of the work to be done?
o: Because prioritisation removes the need to set any deadline at all
Because the period is simply extended to accommodate all of the work
Because the scope is fixed and therefore cannot ever be reduced
Because only the highest-priority items can be guaranteed within the fixed period
12.w: With time fixed, prioritisation ensures the most valuable items are completed first, as not all scope can be guaranteed in the period.

12.q: A product meets every technical specification, yet customer feedback is negative. What most likely went wrong?
o: The deployment baseline was disregarded
The success criteria did not include user satisfaction
Too much emphasis was placed on iterative delivery
Stakeholders were engaged too frequently
12.w: Success criteria focused only on technical outputs can omit qualitative measures such as user satisfaction.

12.q: In which situation is analytical (bottom-up) estimating least appropriate?
o: When little or no detailed data is available
When a detailed work breakdown structure exists
When resource-level planning is required
When the design has been fully specified
12.w: Analytical estimating relies on detailed data, so it is least reliable when little or no such information is available.

12.q: Your sponsor asks for the business case to be updated to reflect recent inflation. Which section should you review first?
o: The investment appraisal
The record of team roles
The success criteria
The scope statement
12.w: Inflation affects forecast costs, so the investment appraisal is the section that must be revisited.

12.q: A council forms a temporary team to build a new leisure centre, disbanding it once the centre opens. Which characteristic marks this as a project?
o: The team and funding are permanent and ongoing
The output is identical to previous deliverables
The work repeats on a fixed monthly cycle
The endeavour is transient with a defined end point
12.w: A project is transient, having a defined beginning and end, after which the temporary organisation is disbanded.

12.q: The sponsor has requested a progress report on the project. What should the project manager most appropriately include?
o: Updates on schedule, budget, risks and key deliverables
Strategic alignment assessments and funding approvals
Benefit realisation figures and post-project audit results
Detailed staffing contracts and future hiring plans
12.w: Progress reporting communicates performance against schedule, budget, risks and deliverables so decisions can be made.

12.q: In a linear project life cycle, in which phase are the detailed schedule, budget and project management plan normally finalised?
o: Definition
Concept
Deployment
Transition
12.w: Definition is where requirements and detailed plans are developed, the project management plan is produced and the deployment baseline is set before the work begins.

n.1: Concept develops the idea and outline business case; detailed plans come later.
n.2: Deployment carries out the work against plans that were finalised in definition.
n.3: Transition hands over the outputs and closes the project.

12.q: What is the main purpose of a procurement strategy in project management?
o: To schedule the internal resources needed to complete project tasks
To identify and document the risks that face the project
To define how goods and services will be acquired from external suppliers
To assign roles and responsibilities to project team members
12.w: A procurement strategy sets out how external products, services and resources will be obtained to support delivery.

12.q: Which estimate would you most expect to find towards the narrow end of the estimating funnel?
o: A comparative estimate made at concept from a past project
A rough order estimate given before the need is understood
A wide range estimate used early to test the outline business case
A detailed estimate built from the WBS later in the life cycle
12.w: The funnel narrows as more is known. A detailed, bottom-up estimate built from the WBS later in the life cycle has the narrowest range.

n.0: Comparative (analogous) estimates are quick and used early, so they sit at the wide end.
n.1: An estimate made before the need is understood is at the widest point of the funnel.
n.2: Estimates used to test an outline business case are early, wide-range estimates.

12.q: Which of the following best defines 'quality planning' in the context of a project?
o: Controlling any slippage against the schedule
Determining how quality requirements will be defined and met
Documenting the risk responses that were chosen
Inspecting the finished deliverables to find defects
12.w: Quality planning determines the quality standards required and how they will be achieved across the project.

12.q: Which of the following would NOT be classed as a project risk?
o: Potential cost savings from adopting a new item of technology
Confirmed damage that has already occurred to a delivery vehicle
Expected delays caused by forthcoming changes in legislation
Possible supplier delays arising from future industrial action
12.w: A confirmed event that has already happened is a current issue, not an uncertain future event, so it is not a risk.

12.q: A configuration audit finds that several different versions of the same document are in active use. Which activity has failed?
o: Configuration identification
Configuration control
Verification audit
Configuration planning
12.w: Configuration control should prevent unauthorised or duplicate versions from being released and used across the project.

12.q: A team agrees its delivery scope, timeline and budget, and this is recorded and approved before work begins. What has been established?
o: A procurement strategy
A risk threshold
A communication plan
A deployment baseline
12.w: An agreed and approved reference for scope, time and cost before execution describes the deployment baseline.

12.q: Which of the following is typically recorded during the closure stage of issue resolution?
o: The stakeholder responsibility matrix for the project
The proposed escalation route for the issue
The date the issue was resolved and the actions taken
The estimated likelihood of the issue recurring later
12.w: At closure the resolution date and a summary of the actions taken are recorded to confirm the issue is complete.

12.q: A project manager reviews economic, legal and environmental trends affecting a new facility. What is the purpose of examining these together?
o: To build a rounded picture of external influences on the project
To confirm the internal budget allocation for the facility
To measure the quality of the facility's finished components
To assign responsibilities to the facility's construction team
12.w: Considering these factors collectively, as in PESTLE, gives a rounded view of the external environment shaping the project.

12.q: Which of the following is a common challenge when building a project team?
o: Ensuring that every member has an identical working style
Relying on communication being clear from the first day
Balancing team members' roles, personalities and availability
Removing every difference in members' skills and experience
12.w: Forming a cohesive team requires balancing individuals' roles, personalities, skills and availability.

12.q: A business case usually evaluates alternative ways of meeting the identified need. What is this particular section commonly called?
o: The options appraisal
The risk register
The responsibility matrix
The configuration log
12.w: Comparing alternative approaches, such as 'do nothing', 'do minimum' and 'do something', forms the options appraisal within the business case.

12.q: Why can face-to-face communication be less effective in certain project delivery environments?
o: It provides too much written documentation for the team
It can be impractical for dispersed teams or tight schedules
It excludes body language from the exchange of information
It removes the need to consider cultural sensitivities
12.w: For geographically dispersed or fast-moving projects, arranging in-person meetings can be costly and time-consuming.

12.q: Which statement best characterises how estimate tolerance behaves as a project moves through the estimating funnel?
o: Tolerance stays constant from concept through to delivery
Tolerance widens steadily as the project progresses
Tolerance narrows progressively as knowledge and detail increase
Tolerance is only ever expressed as a single fixed value
12.w: Estimate tolerance narrows progressively through the funnel as increasing knowledge and detail reduce uncertainty.

12.q: Which document does the sponsor use to demonstrate the strategic value of a proposed project to the organisation?
o: The quality register
The risk register
The business case
The work breakdown structure
12.w: The business case sets out the value proposition and links the project to the organisation's strategic goals.

12.q: Why is a communication plan especially valuable when stakeholders change during a project?
o: It removes the need for any formal handover activity
It shows who needs what information, when and how
It allows new stakeholders to ignore past agreements
It prevents any future misunderstanding from occurring
12.w: The plan sets out who needs what information, when and how, so new stakeholders can quickly be brought into the right communication routine.

n.0: A communication plan supports handover; it does not replace it.
n.2: New stakeholders are still bound by agreed decisions; the plan does not change that.
n.3: A plan reduces misunderstanding but cannot prevent it completely.

12.q: An audit is carried out to assess whether the project's quality procedures are being applied correctly; which process is this?
o: Project scheduling activity
Quality assurance of processes
Requirements gathering work
Risk assessment activity
12.w: Audits are a form of quality assurance used to confirm that established quality procedures are being followed.

12.q: What is a key benefit of summarising a verbal discussion in a follow-up email?
o: It guarantees the eventual success of the whole project
It removes the need for the original discussion to take place
It removes every possibility of the message being misread
It provides a record of what was agreed and the next steps
12.w: A written summary creates a record and reinforces shared understanding of what was agreed verbally.

12.q: Which of the following best defines configuration management in the context of a project?
o: Measuring the project's performance against its agreed baselines
Planning the allocation of resources across the packages of work
Estimating the level of budget reserve the project should hold
Identifying, controlling and tracking the project's products and their changes
12.w: Configuration management is the technical and administrative activity of identifying, controlling, accounting for and verifying a project's products throughout their life.

12.q: What is the main difference between a product breakdown structure and a work breakdown structure?
o: The PBS shows the deliverables and the WBS shows the work to create them
The PBS sets the deadlines and the WBS sets the budgets
The PBS shows the work and the WBS shows the associated costs
The PBS supports communication and the WBS supports risk management
12.w: The PBS defines what the project must produce, while the WBS defines the work needed to produce those deliverables.

12.q: A supplier-capacity risk has been successfully dealt with through earlier delivery. What should the project manager do next?
o: Close the risk and record its outcome in the register
Leave the risk open in case the problem returns later
Remove the supplier from the project altogether
Escalate the risk to the project sponsor for a decision
12.w: Once a risk has been resolved it should be closed and its outcome documented to keep the register accurate.

12.q: A quality control check finds that several components fail to meet the specification; what should happen next?
o: Ignore the failures because most components passed
Adjust the original scope to match the output
Change the requirements to suit the output
Report the failure and decide on corrective action
12.w: Non-conformance found in quality control should be reported so that corrective action can be taken to meet the standard.

12.q: A senior stakeholder wants to understand how reporting will work across the project's several teams. Which structure should the project manager refer them to?
o: The product breakdown structure (PBS)
The organisational breakdown structure (OBS)
The work breakdown structure (WBS)
The cost breakdown structure (CBS)
12.w: The OBS shows reporting lines and how roles fit within the project's organisation, which is exactly what the stakeholder is asking about.

12.q: A new starter asks what separates an issue from an assumption in project terms. Which explanation is correct?
o: An issue is a problem that has occurred; an assumption is something taken to be true for planning
An issue and an assumption mean effectively the same thing
An issue is a future possibility; an assumption is a current problem
An issue is a benefit; an assumption is a cost to be recovered
12.w: An issue is a problem that has already occurred, whereas an assumption is something accepted as true for planning purposes; they are different concepts.

12.q: A project manager is preparing to advise the board whether to launch a new venture. Why include a PESTLE analysis?
o: To show the external factors that could shape or threaten the venture's success
To record the detailed costs of each deliverable in the budget
To confirm the internal reporting lines within the project's governance
To allocate individual work packages to named members of the team
12.w: PESTLE reveals the external factors that could shape or threaten success, informing the launch decision.

12.q: In a project, leadership is most closely concerned with which of the following?
o: Establishing direction and motivating people to achieve shared goals
Inspecting deliverables to confirm they meet their requirements
Aggregating the project's costs into reporting categories
Recording and controlling changes to the scope baseline
12.w: Leadership is chiefly about establishing direction and motivating people towards shared goals, unlike technical control activities.

12.q: A work breakdown structure contains items such as 'code user interface' and 'test module'. What does this structure help to define?
o: The procurement process for the external suppliers
The financial framework underpinning the project
The structure of the client's own organisation
The work required to produce each project deliverable
12.w: The WBS breaks the scope into the work required to complete each deliverable, expressed as manageable work packages.

12.q: During a typical iterative life cycle, when is stakeholder feedback most commonly gathered?
o: Never, because the scope is fixed at the outset
Only once, at the very end of the project
At the close of each iteration to shape later cycles
Only before the first iteration begins
12.w: Iterative delivery seeks feedback at the end of each cycle so subsequent iterations can respond to it.
